You will not find it cheap.

Will my hon. friend dare
assert that Hon. John Oliver, Hon. Mr. King and Hon. Mr. Farris, who represented the province of British Columbia at the Liberal convention, did not reflect Liberal

opinion in their province? But let me come down to the Maritime Provinces.
Do not skip Quebec and Ontario.

My hon. friend says, "Do not skip Ontario." My hon. friend will be busy enough in Ontario at the next general election. He will he lucky if the party of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) does not carry away so many Tory seats from my hon. friend's party in Ontario that neither he nor any of his associates will again be returned to this House.
But let me go down to the Maritime Provinces. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) took great comfort in saying that the Maritime Provinces had only eleven members here to support the Opposition. Let me say to my hon. friend that from the province of Nova Scotia alone we have to-day four representatives on this side of the House, and if it had not been for the manipulations under the Military Voters' Act we would have nine members from that province. Let me say further in regard to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island: Look well to yourselves and never mind the Liberal party. If my hon. friends will only give the people an opportunity of expressing their views they will very soon see where the representation will come from. They will see that the Maritime Provinces, the great West, and the provinces of Quebec and Ontario will vote want of confidence in this Government with such an overwhelming majority as has never yet been recorded in the history of the Dominion. That is what will happen.
In conclusion, let me say to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia, that when he speaks of the "remnants" of the Liberal party, those "remnants," as soon as an appeal is made to the country-and the sooner the better-will be back here doing business at the stand now occupied by himself and his friends.

Mr. Speaker, since the legions on the other side seem to have faded away, I will gladly resume the debate. May I at the outset extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address on the very excellent way in which they acquitted themselves of that duty? May I also extend my hearty congratulations to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) on the position which he has attained, although in his case there is a
certain feeling of sympathy mingled with my congratulations? Amidst some outstanding imperfections my right hon. friend possesses many good qualities, and he certainly displayed wonderful courage when he consented to be the sacrificial lamb after the right hon. gentleman (Sir Thomas White) who was elected in Leeds in 1917 refused to play the leading part in what has become a funeral procession.
Sir, we have met this session under very special circumstances-circumstances upon which I wish to briefly dwell, and which have compelled my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to move the amendment which we are now discussing. That amendment is a direct demand on this Parliament to uphold honour in public life. It is an assertion of the will of the people of Canada never to abdicate the position of master to take up the duty of servant. As that great exponent of British Liberalism, Mr. Asquith, said on a memorable occasion: "Democracy implies that the will of the people must prevail." The House of Commons must reflect the opinion of the country and the national will. Parliament and the people must be of one mind, and when they cease to agree power should revert to the force that dispensed it. We have to-day in this country a Government that pretends to govern, and a Parliament that pretends to legislate, for unmistakable signs and innumerable evidences have shown very clearly that public confidence, the mainspring, the life breath, of Government and legislation, has withdrawn equally from the one and from the other. The present Government is at this moment in the most humiliating and disgraceful position which any government has held in this country since the days of what has become known as the "nest of traitors," and when they resort to quibbling and contrivances [DOT] of procedure for the purpose of clinging to office until 1922; when they resort to subterfuges, even dignified under the name of party strategy; and when they do that under the pretence that there is unrest in this country, they are delivering against themselves a judgment which the country needs only to register when the proper time comes. This government measures up to the well-known definition of Toryism: "Distrust of the people qualified by fear." The statement that it will not yield to public opinion but will go to the full limit of its time is a challenge that will be taken up.

The amendment of my hon. leader and the denial of the right of the present Parliament to legislate are justified on three main grounds. First, the election of 1917 was held and a majority obtained under the special conditions of the war, by means of a franchise which was specially framed for what was described as the only purpose Of the election, and was for the duration of the war. Second, since this election a new reign has been inaugurated; a new Administration has been formed; a new Prime Minister has been appointed; a new party has been created, and new questions have arisen which were not only submitted to the electorate, but were specifically excluded fiom their consideration and from their verdict. Third, this Government and Parliament do not possess the confidence of the people of this country; and cogent evidence has been shown not only of the swinging of the pendulum, but of a deeply rooted national distrust in the ministerial leaders. The speakers who have preceded me have related extensively the conditions under which the last election was held. I shall not go over the ground again; I shall not quote the written and spoken pledges of the members of the Government, from the right hon. Prime Minister down to the last member of the Administration. An Election Act was passed picking the electors who were to select the Administration. The Prime Minister of that time asked the people of Canada to suspend for the time being all their political views and the consideration of all questions which were controversial between the parties, and a Union Government was formed with the distinct understanding that it was only to last for the duration of the war. Thousands of Liberals voted for the hon gentlemen opposite, believing in the sincerity of those pledges. Those who voted against the .Government were branded as disloyal, as being allies of the Kaiser, as not being good Canadians- because it was pointed out that the only issue was the carrying on of the war; that all the other issues had been temporarily suspended. It was stated that no loyal Canadian, Mr. Speaker, could vote otherwise than for the Union Government, however strong, however divergent, may have been their views on ordinary political questions. My hon. friends opposite cannot deny that; there is not one of them that did not say so. The electors of Canada know that, and the continuance in 
office of the present Government under the circumstances, constitutes a gross and palpable injustice to Canadian democracy. That is the very reason why so many men in this country who would be inclined otherwise to support my right hon. friend are opposed to his continuance in office, because as between him and public morality and national honour, they choose the latter. Take the case of. the soldiers- it is the most glaring one. Thousands of young Canadians voted for this Government because circulars were freely sent to all the military camps in France, Britain and Canada, even in the United States, and to the troops in the trenches, telling those young men that this was a war election; that the only issue was selective conscription; that the only question was the carrying on of the war; that the mandate they were called upon to give was a mandate for that purpose and no other, and that there would be another election when the war was over. In many cases the soldiers did not know who were the candidate^ to whom they were giving their suffrage. Indeed, in the Yukon Territory the votes of the soldiers were registered before there was any candidate in the field. Fourteen members of this House, Mr. Speaker, who had been defeated in Canada sit in this Parliament to-day by virtue of the soldiers' vote. I do not protest against the soldiers having exercised their right to vote. When I used the same argument in the city of Peterborough, I was taken to task by some newspapers, and the Montreal Gazette said that I had protested against the votes given to the soldiers, though paying me the compliment that I was generally more careful in my words. Sir, I do not and did not complain about the votes of the soldiers. The war is over; those issues are past; the only ones who want to keep them alive are the members of the present Government, who refuse to elect a peace Parliament, and who remain in office by virtue of a mandate given to a war Parliament. What I said in Peterborough and what I say in this House is that, to the soldiers of Canada who gave a vote under such unprecedented and special circumstances, on their being told that they were giving that vote for a special time and a special purpose, it is very unfair to use and abuse that mandate for the settlement of other questions, especially when those young men from one end of the country to the other are asking

the Government to give them an opportunity and the right to vote on the domestic questions of Canada. I do not wish to be understood as stating that the Government has no right to legislate on anything that, at the time of the election, it did not explicitly declare that it would deal with. The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) put up a man of straw to knock him down when he referred to that matter, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), in labouring extensively on that topic and quoting Sir Wilfrid Laurier and other constitutional authorities to that effect, was losing his time, as nobody will deny what he attempted to prove. But when a government specifically state that they will not deal with particular matters or things which are in controversy between the parties, when upon that assumption thousands of Liberals vote for that government, and when now, in spite of that pledge and declaration, they proceed to deal with and legislate upon matters which they themselves specifically excluded from the verdict they asked for from the electorate, I cannot comprehend the ethics or sense of honour of men who would do that in the face of such declarations. The question is not so much one of power or legal right, it is one of public morality, of common honesty. The action of the Government in this regard is a gross breach of faith, as gross a breach of faith as ever disgraced the political history of this country, and made all the more gross by the fact that the men who are guilty of it claim the law and the Constitution as their defence. It is a well known fact that the cleverest deceivers usually manage to keep within the four corners of the law. It is to be regretted that Canadian public men put themselves in the position of a man who will lure on a friend to make a bet and then refuse to pay, because the debt is not recoverable at law.
The second point of my argument is that we have confronting us to-day a new Administration, a new party, a new Prime Minister, and a new ministry, none of which has ever received the endorsation of the Canadian people. Immediately after the close of last session, there was announced to the Canadian public the setting of a star and the rising of a new one. It was at the same time announced to the world that the Canadian Unionist party had passed out of existence and that a new party had taken its place. The other day the Prime Minister claimed that this new party is the legitimate descendant of the former party. I quite admit that it is the descendant of
the other, but I have my doubts as to its legitimacy. Legitimate children, as a rule, are proud to bear the name of their father. The new party was shy, if not ashamed, to go throughout the world retaining the name of its generator, and the hyphenated appellation of "National Liberal and Conservative," which means everything on earth and, for that reason, nothing at all, was used.
I admit that there was not avery discernible solution of continuity between the Unionist party and this one. The new party, however, was cut out, drafted, painted red, white and blue, and varnished with the blessings and good wishes of the special interests which always controlled its predecessor. The former member for Peterborough West, to whom I give credit for being one man who kept his pledge to his electors, asserted that the National Liberal and Conservative party, like Topsy in Uncle Tom's Cabin, was not born, it "growed." Lord Hugh Cecil, speaking a few days ago to his constituents, intimating that he would sit on the Opposition side of the House with his distinguished brother, used these words:
Parties, like poets, are born, not made. They arise out of circumstances, spontaneously, not out of plans and plots.
If the British statesman is right and a party cannot arise out of plans and plots, I wonder what is the real character of the aggregation that controls the Government to-day. The Government and the ministerial press proclaimed to the world that a new party had been formed. When the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie), quoted as an excuse to refuse an election, the precedent of Sir John Macdonald being replaced by Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, and Sir Charles Tupper; that of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), being replaced by Mr. Murray; that of Mr. Walter Scott being replaced by Mr. William Martin; that of Sir Lomer Gouin being replaced by Mr. Taschereau, without a general election being held; they forgot to mention, or rather took good care not to mention, that in each one of those cases there was only a change in' leadership, and in no case was there a new party or a new programme.
Moreover, the ministry which is on the treasury benches is far from being the ministry to which a mandate was given in 1917. The men who were in the ministry of 1917 formed a fairly able combination. Indeed, we were told at the time that it was a combination of the best brains

of the country. But surely not even the most sanguine supporter of the present ministry would make such a claim in favour of this Administration. Most of the ministers who gave prestige to the Unionist Administration have withdrawn, and their places have been taken by gentlemen whose main qualifications for office were that they occupied seats where there was less danger of losing an election than in others. The present Cabinet is notable more by the men who are not now of it than by those who are in it. It is a Cabinet of shreds and patches, and if the few additions which are mentioned in the papers as likely to be made in the near future are made, they will serve only t^ magnify the oddness of the complexion and the preposterous appearance of the crazy-work. The most ingenious patching will not suffice to make the old Tory-Unionist Government garment cover our large national limbs. Patching serves only to display more conspicuously the imperfections of its cut and texture.
The right hon. Prime Minister claimed the other day that this Administration is young, having been returned to office in 1917. I will point out the numerous changes that have been made in the Cabinet since that day; I will point out the striking difference between what it is to-day and what it was two years ago, and perhaps my right hon. friend will permit me to apply to his ministry these words of the great satirist Juvenal: Facies tua computat annos

"Your very face betrays your age." Before leaving this subject I have a word or two to address to the very, very few gentlemen who still describe themselves as Liberals and form an appendage to this reactionary Administration. One of these gentlemen proclaimed yesterday his articles of faith. Now-I am going to speak my mind very frankly-as between an insincere Liberal and a candid Tory, give me the Tory every time. It does not cheapen the political currency. It does not degrade the morality of our public life. Sir, Liberalism is not, and cannot be, represented in this Cabinet or elsewhere by men who in recent years have been on every sicle of every public question, and never loyal to any. Monsieur Foucher, a Prime Minister under Napoleon, was said to have taken at various times seven different and contradictory oaths of allegiance. I think some Canadian public men could quite easily rival that record without seriously hurting their convictions. In this connection I

desire to quote the words of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) at Saskatoon. I shall quote from what hon. gentlemen opposite will regard as a very authoritative newspaper the Ottawa Journal, of November 13, 1920:
Mr. Calder said that three years ago he did not understand the tariff question as well as he did at the present time, for the reason that he had never had occasion to study it. "I was," he said, "more or less of a parrot, just as other people are parrots. I got up in our Legislature and advocated free fertilizers when I did not know the first thing about it, and forty other members knew no more."
My hon. friend said he was a parrot, and did not know anything about the tariff.
I ask you, Sir, in what light the hon. gentleman appears when his leader, the right hon. Prime Minister, said in his speech the other day that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization is and always has been consistent. The only mean- [DOT] ing could be that he was still consistently -a parrot; he still repeats and registers his master's voice-only the master has changed. In Moosejaw, my hon. friend said that he was a Liberal, but not a Mackenzie King Liberal. Sir, Liberalism is a creed, it is a doctrine, it is a set of principles, but if my hon. friend wishes to refer to the Liberals in this House or in this country as King Liberals, and at the same time claims that he is still a Liberal, the only inference is that he is a Meighen Liberal, which is a species unknown both to zoology and common sense. Why, when my hon. friend was in the West singing a love duet with the right hon. the Prime Minister-I admit this is not in the newspapers, but it was repeated to me by many Liberals in Regina and other western cities-sitting around the dinner table he told the people there: "The Liberals in the House of Commons are not serious about an election. They do not want an election.
"There are members in the House who told me last year that if the Government was in danger of being defeated they would absent themselves when the division came." Sir, on behalf of the members of this side of the House, I ask my hon. friend as a gentleman to substantiate that slanderous statement. Let my hon. friend or any other gentleman give the name of any member who said that. Even now press correspondents are saying that we are not serious about asking for an election; yet in the very next column they stultify themselves by asserting that we on this side

of the House are refusing pairs, are most unfair, and are willing to take any sort of advantage to defeat the Government. Could two statements he more contradictory? The one statement answers the other. The people of Canada will be able to judge of the sincerity of those who say these things.
The third reason in favour of the amendment is that this Government is no longer in harmony with public opinion and has utterly lost the confidence of the country. Indeed, it has not only lost the country's confidence; it has earned its contempt. No government has the moral right to pass legislation under such circumstances. The result of the by-elections cannot be misread; they are bold, definite and unequivocal. The Canadian people have made it clear that they want a new government. They will not let the country pass through two more years of dishonourable history in order to allow a group of political gentlemen to show their consistency in their vices as well as in their virtues, and to gratify the human disinclination of my hon. friend, the Minister of Militia (Hon. Mr. Guthrie), to become once more a private man. As my hon. friend the member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), pointed out in the course of his admirable speech, out of fifteen elections held since 1917 the Government lost ten and won only five, but in each of these five in glorious victories they had themselves selected the constituencies; and, in four of the five, Cabinet ministers were candidates. Every time an election was forced upon this Government by the natural course of events they have been overwhelmingly defeated. Yet, Heaven nows the expedients to which they resorted in order to check the threatening adverse march of events. My right hon. friend the new Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), has always been noted for the cleverness of his electoral devices and he has worked out a new scheme. He is running his elections on the instalment plan. Last year seven elections were held on the same day. In two of the constituencies members of the Government were candidates, and the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Tolmie), were elected. But on the same day there was an election in Glengarry, there was one in Assiniboia, there was one in Victoria and Carleton, and there was one in the good constituency known as Quebec East; and in every one of these the Government was snowed under by overwhelming majorities. In the County of Prince, Prince Edward Island, my hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), was elected by acclamation. In the county of North Ontario the election was postponed owing to the death of one of the candidates, but the Government was defeated when the election was held. This year, under the new business methods of the new Prime Minister, instead of having the by-elections on the same date, as has always been the custom, and as is only proper, we are having them in slices; as I say, it is the instalment plan, and it is being operated in a very irregular manner; the debt that is overdue is not given preference over the new one. The county of East Elgin became vacant by the death of the sitting member on February 14, 1920; the election was held on November 22, 1920, nine months afterwards. Yet the county of St. James Montreal had become vacant at about the same time, and the election was held immediately. The county of Peterborough became vacant by Mr. Burnham's resignation on July 15, 1920, and the election was held on February 7, 1921. Yet at the same time, in the middle of July, 1920, the county of Yale became vacant by Mr. Burrell's appointment to public office and the election was held on November 22, 1920. The two counties of St. John and Colchester became vacant on the 16th and 13th July, 1920, respectively, and the elections in these constituencies were held November 22, 1920. Why this difference in the treatment accorded East Elgin and Peterborough as compared with others. And we are now told-at least I have read in the Montreal Gazette-that an election may be held pretty soon in the county of York-Sunbury which is actually vacant; but as regards the county of Ya-maska, it is said that the province of Quebec is so largely represented in Parliament that there is no need of an election in that constituency. When an election is over in one constituency the electoral machine of the Government is transferred to another place. East Elgin and Peterborough have witnessed and have withstood the tremendous and costly experiment of the new organization which my right hon. friend referred to in his speech, so much so that the honest people in these two important ridings were asking themselves with amazement the question: "Where does the money come from?" But the Government's machinery was of no avail, and public opinion asserted itself in a ringing man-

ner against this discredited Administration. Hon. gentlemen opposite are now trying to minimize the importance of these elections. Indeed, my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), stated, amidst the cheers of his followers on the other side, that the election in Peterborough constituted a mandate to the Government to carry on, to use the stereotyped words of the former member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White). I shall not discuss this further than to express the hope that my right hon. friend was more logical and displayed more common sense when he represented our country at the League of Nations recently. The Prime Minister, the ministerial candidate in Peterborough, and all the ministerial forces, claimed that the issue of the election was the tariff policy. Am I right in stating that? We stated that the issue was the usurpation by this Government of administrative power, and that this Parliament had outlived its existence and its mandate. On this issue the member from West Peterborough, (Mr. Gordon), fought and won. Now the Prime Minister states, with great satisfaction, that the verdict was not against the tariff. The Minister of Justice follows and declares that the verdict was not against the right of the Government to continue in office. These were the two issues according to them. Who is right, the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice? Was the verdict against the tariff policy of the Government or, to use their own words, against its right to carry on. Hon. gentlemen opposite are entitled to their choice but they must, at least, reconcile their views in the matter. The only alternative would be that the verdict is against^ the new Prime Minister personally, and is simply a notification that the electors do not want him. Sir, the Prime Minister went to Peterborough and said that the election was most important, that the return of the Government candidate was imperative, that all eyes in Canada were cast on Peterborough. He said the same thing in East Elgin. Why should he now try to take all those Canadian eyes off Peterborough and East Elgin? The result doubtless does not substantiate the statement which my right hon. friend made in my own province in the city of Sherbrooke, that the Liberal party outside of the province of Quebec was extinct. He has to modify his tune in that respect. Still even the Minister of Militia had the 
temerity to make this wicked assertion. There is one party in this country to-day which is extinct. It has practically disappeared from the Provincial Administration of all the provinces of Canada, and in this Federal arena it has taken concealment under a new equivocal name. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) also went to Peterborough, and again the eyes of all Canadians were described as being cast in the direction of that now famous constituency. The right hon. gentleman even said-I read it in the press; the defeat of the Government candidate would be the first drop of poison. I gave credit to my right hon. friend that he was sincere, and he obviously showed the effect of that drop of poison on his political constitution when, instead of defending the Government in this very dangerous period, that great parliamentary fighter of so many battles used his time to advocate the League of Nations before a House which is unanimously in favour of that great organization. The electors of those various constituencies have clearly expressed the determination of the people of Canada to restore true responsible Governmment and to be ruled by men who are elected by the people in a normal and constitutional way. Yet the Prime Minister states that he will not yield to this public intimation. The Salvation Army says of all mankind that a man may be down, he is never out. But my right hon. friend is wrong when he thinks this is also true of the Government. When a Government is down it has to go out. It is important that it should be so. When it is obvious that a Government does not command the support of the majority of the people, its decisions carry no influence, it has no more authority. Individual members cannot speak here with authority when everybody knows that they no longer speak the voice of their constituents, that their tenure in this Parliament is precarious. Such a thing does not make for the dignity of parliamentary institutions. It reduces the House of Commons to the level of a mock parliament, and patriotic statesmen have no right to inflict that on a great country. It does not make either for independence or freedom of action. The member who knows that he cannot secure the renewal of his constituents' mandate is tempted to support the existing Government in everything through thick and thin, because he knows that when they cease to swim he will have to sink. Rather

than swimming in a hazy obscurity he is tempted to avoid anything that may bring down the Government however divergent from theirs may be his views on the particular subject under discussion. The worse the prospects for the Government afforded by an election the surer is the pressure exercised on individual weakness. I do not hesitate to say that the votes cast by many hon. gentleman when a division comes will not mean confidence in the Government so much as confidence in themselves to retain a little longer seats which are already moving away from under them. I am sure the Minister of Militia appreciates that feeling. The Prime Minister said that his Government has the confidence of a majority in this House and that so long as he retains that majority he has a constitutional right to carry on. I shall endeavour to show that that position is unsound, and that the Government must also command the support of the majority of the people.
But, Sir, can my right hon. friend say that he has still a majority in this House which allows him to rule with honour and dignity. The majority of seventy in 1917 has dwindled to twenty, probably to fifteen to-day. And yet the hon. the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) has the gall-I do not know whether that is a good English word-to refer to us as a "remnant." Remnant! Remnant! What is the hon. gentleman himself? What is the Government that faces us in this House? Remnant! The only "remnant" that I see is this Government, which had a majority of seventy, three years ago and which is now struggling to keep a bare majority, and being unable to do it by the ordinary way of electoral victories, is adopting the rather humiliating process of trying to get recruits from the ranks of its opponents by methods which I do not care to describe, in order to postpone the shameful defeat that awaits it at the polls. I hurl back in the Minister of Militia's face this mean appellation that he applied to the Opposition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is exceeding the proprieties of debate when he accuses another hon. member of applying a "mean appellation." I think that upon reflection he will realize the impropriety of the expression and will withdraw it.

I will with pleasure withdraw the remark, Mr. Speaker. Your Honour knows that I am not an adept in
the use of the English language. As I said, the majority of seventy of three years ago has dwindled to about twenty to-day. Cabinet reorganization cannot be undertaken, the best men in the party cannot be called to the Council table lest the dangerous adventure of by-elections conduces to a still greater reduction of that majority. Yet reorganization is badly needed. Friends and panegyrists of the Prime Minister in the press state that he is practically alone in the Cabinet. I would not like to say that, and I hope I have not hurt the feelings of any of the members of the Cabinet in repeating the statement. It is the ministerial press that says that my right hon. friend is the one man in this Administration, and that he is surrounded by gentlemen of whom we might say, after the manner of a former British Prime Minister, that they are all ciphers, he being the unit that gives value to them. I do not agree with that statement, far from it, and I am free to confess that if I had been given a vote-and I hope my right hon. friend will permit me to say so-when the selection of a new Prime Minister was made, there is one gentleman in the Cabinet whom I would have voted for rather than for my right hon. friend. I will not name him,-so every other minister may think that he is the man. I would make only one exception

I beseech my hon. friend the Minister of Militia not to think so. I have quoted the statement which is made by newspapers friendly to the Government. Is it in the interests of the good administration of this country that a Government should be so weak and impotent? After having stated for the last two years that we had in Ottawa a Government without a leader-that is what the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal Star used to say very frequently-shall we have the misfortune now to have a leader without a Government?
Other expedients are used to preserve that vanishing majority. The other day, during the speech of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) your honour ruled that he was bound to describe the right hon. gentleman who was elected in Leeds in 1917 as "the member for Leeds." Still I do not hesitate to say that this right hon. gentleman under the law has forfeited his right to his seat. What is the law on this matter? Section 15, chapter 10, of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, reads, in part, as follows:
If any member of the House of Commons accepts any office or commission, or performs any service for the Government of Canada, or

for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is paid or to be paid .... the seat of such member shall thereby be vacated and his election shall thenceforth be null and void.
The preamble of the schedule to the Act which was passed last year concerning the acquisition of 'he Grand Trunk railway provides that one of the parties to the agreement is called the Government; and clause 6 of this schedule, which forms part of the Act provides:
That the value of the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be determined by a Board of three arbitrators, one to be appointed by the Government.
And the first sentence of clause 21 of the schedule reads as follows:
Each of the parties to this agreement shall pay its own costs of and in connection with the arbitration subsequent to the date of this agreement, including the remuneration of the arbitrator appointed by it.
The amount of the remuneration is not fixed in the law, but it is specifically stated that the arbitrator who shall act in the matter shall be remunerated by the Government. I say, Sir, that under the circumstances there should have been an election in Leeds and that there should be a member from that constituency voting on the amendment to the Address.
There is another matter to which I wish to direct your attention, Mr. Speaker. On July 21, 1920, the hon. member for Ste. Antoine, Montreal (Sir Herbert Ames), delivered a very eloquent address before the Empire Parliamentary Association in London on "The Dominions and the League of Nations." This address was printed, and I have a copy of it in my hand. With your permission, I will read the following words from page 5:
Now, X have just returned from a hurried visit to Canada. Mr. Balfour has alluded to the double capacity which I occupied at that time, and for the moment still occupy. For sixteen years I have been the representative of Western Montreal in the Canadian House of Commons. My resignation is in the hands of the Speaker because I have found that my new work is quite enough to occupy all the time and attention that I am capable of giving to it.
This was on July 21, 1920. Why should the electors of St. Antoine, Montreal, be disfranchised? Why has the resignation of Sir Herbert Ames been kept secret and withheld? I am sure that it must have been intercepted on its way to Your Honour, because you could not have it in your hands without acting upon it-but that is always the humiliating method of avoiding IMr. E. Lapointe.]
an election and evading a defeat. Shall this be permitted to continue? Will the Canadian people stand for that much longer? Sir, the Government does not own the people of Canada, body and soul, by feudal right.
My right hon. friend, in his characteristic way, discarded as ridiculous and unworthy of attention the argument that the Government must not only have the support of a majority in the House, hut must also have the confidence of the people, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) followed in the same vein. I take issue with my right hon. friend and these hon. gentlemen. It is in direct violation of the spirit and traditions of the British constitution that a Parliament should continue its existence when it is clear that it no longer represents, carries the support, or enjoys the confidence of the people. Against the opinion of the Canadian Prime Minister, who struggles frantically to remain in office against the will of the country-and the Minister of Militia issued yesterday a challenge that I shall now take up-I shall oppose the opinion of a great British Prime Minister, who, placed in similar though less unfavourable circumstances, deemed it his duty to let the people rule and select a government which had their confidence. To the Meighenian-if my hon. friend will permit me to use the expression-views of the duty of a constitutional Prime Minister, I shall oppose the Gladstoijian standard. Mr. Gladstone had been returned to office at the election of 1868, and in 1873, two years before the expiration of the mandate of that parliament, seeing that the by-elections were going against the government, and that he did not carry any longer the support of the majority of the people of Britain, he dissolved Parliament and Mr. Disraeli was returned by a large majority. Mr. Gladstone took his seat in the British House of Commons as the leader of the Opposition, and you will permit me to read a few words which he uttered in his speech on the Address in the next session following the election. You will find those words at page 80 of the Debates of the British Parliament of March, 1874, volume 218:
My hon. friend seems to think that there is but one important element In the position of a government, and that is the numerical amount of its majority. Now, upon that point I join issue with my hon. friend. I think he fundamentally misunderstands the constitution of this country if he supposes that the actual majority that a government may posses!! in an existirg House of Commons is sufficient to

give it more moral and political strength for the discharge of its arduous duties, after it has become apparent or when it is becoming clear that the possession of that majority is not agreeable to the sense and the convictions of the country. Now, Sir, there is the whole difference between my hon. friend and myself.
Further, on page 81, he says:
Because in this country we watch the signs and currents of public opinion. We recognize the general title of the country to be governed in conformity with its wishes and its intelligence ; and the mere possession of a parliamentary majority, satisfactory as it is when it is a true indication of the actual current of feeling and opinion of the country, is no adequate support and no adequate warrant for the continuance of a government in office if it has become clear, or when there is reasonable ground for supposing that the desires of the country are in an opposite direction.
On page 84 here is what he says:
Yet, as an Englishman, as one attached to the institutions of the country, and as one who held an office which bound him to regard the principles of the constitution, I cannot regret a dissolution which has given to the people of this country an opportunity of pronouncing their opinion upon the conduct of affairs, though I think the judgment which has been passed is an erroneous one.
Gladstone spoke as an Englishman and I commend his words to both the Prime tvlinister and the Minister of Militia and Defence. They are repeated by one who is not an Englishman, who has not one drop of Anglo-Saxon blood in his veins, but who is a true lover and admirer of British principles and who wants to uphold them in this country.
Later on in that session, Mr. Gladstone was still being attacked in the British House of Commons for having so dissolved Parliament two years before the expiration of his Parliamentary term and so brought on an election in which he was defeated. I wish to quote only a very few words *which the House will find on page 1126 of the same volume of the British Hansard. Mr. Gladstone said:
Therefore, my regret is, not that the dissolution took place when it did, but that it did not take place before, for I am not willing to hold office under any circumstances, with a minority either in this House or the country. It is repugnant to my feelings, and not compatible with the best interests of the country that a Government should continue to govern, even with a numerical majority, when its strength is falling away, and when there are daily increasing evidences that it no longer represents the will and opinions of the constituencies. That is the regret of which I have to make a frank expression. Had I known as well as I know now what was to take place, it would not have been upon the 24th of January or the 24th of December, nor upon any day in January or December, but at a much earlier period, that my colleagues and myself would have advised the Crown to dissolve.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) the other day, and the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) yesterday stated that the opinions which we have quoted in this debate were the opinions of men who were out and wanted to go in, in which, they said, they were like members on this side. The words of Mr. Gladstone were uttered after the election, not for the purpose of getting in, as those hon. gentlemen said, but to explain why he had advised the Crown to dissolve, namely, because it was made clear to him that the majority of the people of the country were opposed to his continuing in office. This is the first precedent.
The Minister of Militia and Defence quoted as a precedent the Government of 1892 to 1895 when Mr. Gladstone had withdrawn and had been replaced by Lord Rosebery. It is true Mr. John Redmond presented to the British House of Commons a motion asking for dissolution of Parliament in 1895, but at that time, what were the conditions? The British Parliament had three years of existence, and out of, I think, nine by-elections which had taken place, the Government had gained and had lost and the net gain to the Opposition was only three seats in the House of Commons. Is there any similarity to the position of a Government which had a majority of seventy in this House, which majority is reduced to twenty-three? Yet, this is what Mr. Balfour said in the British House of Commons on that occasion:
I have never observed in the history of this country that any party or any Government have gained credit for hanging on to office in the vulgar sense, without power, and with only the insignia of office-for hanging on to their places when they were deprived of all real influence over the course of events, and when the general trend of opinion was against them. Under such circumstances, a Government may possibly do good administrative work; it may possibly continue to hold its tenure of office for one month, two months, or even for a year or more, but you will never And, in the history of this country, that this had the result of increasing the credit of a Government with those in whose favour their fortunes must ultimately rest.
In 1895, Lord Salisbury was returned to power with a large majority, and in 1900, there was held that election which was referred to by the Minister of Militia and Defence as the "Khaki" election. This was during the latter part of the South African war. Two years afterwards, Lord Salisbury resigned and was replaced by Mr. Balfour, and then by-elections began to go against the Conservative or Unionist



administration of Britain. I will quote the words of two of the leading English statesmen of that time as I find their utterances recorded in volume 150 of the British Hansard. This is what Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman said, as reported at page 71:
It is common for us to say, and it is true constitutionally, that the Minister of the Crown in this country is selected and appointed because he is the man who commands a majority in the House of Commons. But what does that mean? It means that the command of the majority of the House represents the feeling of the country. The moment the House of Commons gets out of touch and harmony with the country, then that plea for retaining office dissolves; and the right hon. gentleman has no right to entrench himself behind the confidence and support of his friends here after it is known to all mankind and to himself. as well as to any of them, that he has lost the confidence of the country. When I say it is known to himself, it is obviously so, because, if he was not aware he had lost the confidence of the country, why should he show any reluctance to appeal to the country and immensely strengthen his position by securing a favourable verdict from it?
In the same debate, at page 117, Sir Edward Gray is reported as making this statement, speaking of the right hon. Mr. Balfour:
Does he expect to get any good result in Parliament from prolonging the life of the present Government? The last election took place upon the war, and it could not have counted as an ordinary election. To all Intents and purposes this House of Commons is ten years old. Does the Prime Minister suppose he can restore it to a vigorous and healthy condition now? He knows he cannot, and the House knows he cannot, because they know it is out of touch with the country as a whole. The longer the Government attempts to go on keeping the House of Commons working, the more they will damage the House of Commons as an institution, and the longer they go on, I sincerely hope and trust, the greater will be the resentment of the country when they have the courage to appeal to It.
My hon. friend the Minister of Militia slipped very quickly over this precendent, and he was in error in the last part of his statement with regard to it. These words were uttered in July 1905, and five months afterwards, on the 4th of December, 1905, two years before the expiration of the parliamentary term Mr. Balfour did not dissolve parliament but resigned his position as Prime Minister. Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman was called upon to form a ministry on the 5th of December, 1905. The elections were held in January, 1906, and the government of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman was returned by a large majority. There is one feature, however, of the precendents quoted by my hon. friend the Minister of Militia with refer-
IMr. E. Lapointe.!
ence to the government of Lord Rosebery in 1895, and the government of Mr. Balfour in 1905 which will be followed in this country, and it is this: Both these governments were defeated and swept out of office when the electors had a chance to pronounce their opinion. I have quoted the opinion of leaders in the public life of Great Britain, and I may say that on the principle there is no difference of opinion. They may have differed as to whether the circumstances at different periods justified the application of the principle, but on the principle itself they all agreed. I shall now quote the opinion of constitutional writers. I call your attention to what Sir William Anson says in his "Law and Custom of the Constitution'' at page 372:
We must not forget that the possible violation of the laws is not the only reason why a Ministry should retire when it is shown to have lost the confidence of the House or the country- Ministers are not only Ministers of the Queen, they represent the public opinion of the United Kingdom,; when they cease to impersonate public opinion they become a mere group of personages who must stand or fall by the prudence of their action. They may have to deal with disorders at home or hostile manifestations abroad ; they will have to meet these with the knowledge that they have not the confidence or support of the country; and their opponents at home and abroad would know this too.
Professor Dicey in his "Law of the Constitution" says:
The reason why the House can, in accordance with the constitution, be deprived of existence is that an occasion has arisen on which there is fair reason to suppose that the opinion of the House is not the opinion of the electors. A dissolution is allowable or necessary whenever the wishes of the Legislature are or may fairly be presumed to be different from the wishes of the nation .... The essential point to notice is the principle that the authority which ultimately determines the right of a Cabinet to retain office is the nation. The authority of the House of Commons is derived from its representing the will of the nation, and the chief object of a dissolution is to ascertain that the will of Parliament coincides with the will of the nation .... The precedents show that in modern times the rules as to the dissolution of Parliament are like other conventions of the Constitution, intended to secure the ultimate supremacy of the electorate as the true political authority of the State.
The constitutional historian, Mr. J. R. Green, writes as follows:
A minister availing himself of the temper of a parliament elected in some moment of popular panic, and refusing to appeal to the country would be, even if legal, a criminal.
I would advise my hon. friend the Minister of Militia, if he were here, to be

4G7
more careful in issuing challenges. Of course, I cannot quote an instance which is analogous to the present, of a government changing its membership, forming a new administration, selecting a new leader, forming a new party, formulating a new platform, as was done in July, 1920, and not going to the country. There is nothing similar in British history, because it never was done. My hon. friend, if I may be allowed to call him so, though he is no longer a member of this House, the late member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), said:
There is no precedent in history of a group of men holding up two parties and running away with the government.
Those words are not mine but they will serve to show that it is rather difficult to find a situation quite identical to the present one. I will quote another instance, a very recent one, which took place in one of the British dominions. Last year, I think it was in May or June, 1920, General Smuts, the prime minister of South Africa, was returned to office under peculiar circumstances at a general election. He was the leader of a party called the South African party.
That party elected 44 members to the House. There was the Nationalist party under General Hertzog, which also secured 44 seats in the House of Representatives. There was another party, the Unionist party, under Sir Thomas Smart, which elected 25 members. And finally there was the Labour party with a membership of 21. General Smuts had no majority over all the other parties combined, but he succeeded in enlisting the support of the Unionist party, and to a large extent of the Labour party, and managed to carry on the affairs of the Commonwealth without any great difficulty. Indeed, he had a good majority in the House. But after the session was over he considered that those conditions were rather precarious and he tried to form an alliance with the Nationalist party. A conference was held, but the extremists of the Nationalist party could not modify their views to a sufficient extent to allow General Smuts and themselves to co-operate. Then he made an appeal to Sir Thomas Smart of the Unionist party and succeeded in forming a new permanent party which has retained the name of the South African party but of which Sir Thomas Smart and his Unionist followers are members. General Smuts had a majority in the House of Representatives of South Africa. But what did
General Smuts do? He had no mandate from the people of South Africa to carry on the affairs of the country with a new party formed of a combination of the South African party and the Unionist party. General Smuts is a Liberal; General Smuts is a statesman; General Smuts is a great British constitutionalist; and he found that it was his duty to secure a mandate from the people of South Africa. Yet, from his point of view, it was a dangerous course to pursue; it was a very close fight. But it is always safer to trust the people, and General Smuts to-day is Premier of South Africa, and when he proceeds to the Imperial Conference in June he will go there speaking in no unmistakable way as the representative of the South African people.
This leads me to say a word or two with regard to the Imperial Conference. The conference has been heralded, promised, postponed, and finally called. It is to be a gathering of momentous importance. The destinies of Canada, the national status of Canada, and questions of most vital and sacred interest to this nation, are to be discussed. Problems of extreme gravity, the solution of which may involve tremendous responsibility on our part, will be brought before that conference. Just to show that I am not exaggerating, I shall read the very words that are used in the calling together of this conference. Here they are:
The Dominions are invited to attend the Imperial Conference in June on the lines of the Imperial War Cabinet Meetings which took place in 1917 and 1918, to deal with the many-urgent problems of common interest which call for the co-ordination of policy and action by the different governments of the Empire.
From the speech from the Throne delivered a few days ago in the British Parliament I extract the following words:
I hope the Prime Ministers of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland. as well as the representatives of India, will be able to visit London during the coming summer. I am confident that discussions that will take place during their visits will be of the utmost value in bringing about co-ordination, both in the external and internal policy of the Empire.

Mr. Lloyd George, the British Premier, speaking in the House of Commons, is reported in the Montreal Star, of February 16, 1921, as follows:
Mr. Lloyd George speaking in the House last evening declared that it was too much to ask of these small Islands that they undertake the whole burden of the defence of a gigantic Empire in every sea, and that at the forthcoming conference of Prime Ministers of the Dominions in London the whole problem of Imperial Defence must be considered. There must

be, the Prime Miister went on, co-ordination not only between the various services, but between the several parts of the Empire. Mr. Lloyd George stated that the Conference of Empire Premiers to be held in London in June will be the most momentous event in the history of the Empire.	.
Now, Sir, after having read that extract, standing here to-day in this Canadian Parliament, fully conscious of the responsibility that attaches to my words, I emphatically state that the gentlemen who pretend to govern Canada at the present time have no right to represent our country at that conference, because they do not enjoy its confidence and are not entitled to speak the national voice; and we will not consider ourselves bound, either legally or morally, by any decision or agreement which they may reach there. It may be said that any such decision will have to be ratified by the Parliament of Canada before it can become binding. But, Sir, the deliberations and discussions that precede the decision are important, and Canadians have the right to confer, deliberate, and discuss matters with the statesmen of the various sister nations of the British Commonwealth, through representatives who carry the support and enjoy the confidence of our people. It has been stated in the press, and indeed my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice clearly suggested it in this House last year, that representatives of the Opposition might be invited to attend the conference as associates of those representing the Government. Sir, I do not hesitate to say-and I know that in this statement I voice the views of my hon. leader in this respect-that no such proposal can be entertained. It would be a mere subterfuge for the purpose of giving to the Government a semblance of authority; it would be, on the part of the Opposition, the mere lending of itself to a violation of the rights of the people. The people of Canada have the right to be represented there by a Government which has its support and confidence. It has the right to be represented by men delegated by a Parliament which has a clear mandate, and has been elected in a regular and constitutional way. What authority and influence is attached to the representatives Who would propose to negotiate in the name of a country which loses no opportunity of repudiating them with all the power of which it is capable? You would not negotiate on a weak foundation, or rather on no foundation at all, and the other parties to the negotiations know the political conditions prevailing in this country. Will you [Mr. E. Eapointe.l
let me read what the Canadian correspondent of the London Times, a Tory if I am not mistaken, sent to that paper and which appeared in the Times edition of January 7th:
Empire Peace Cabinet-Strong Canadian Opinions.
(From our Canadian correspondent.)
The Prime Minister of the Dominion will not discuss the attitude of Canada toward proposals which may be submitted to the meeting of Empire Prime Ministers in June next. Mr. Meighen succeeded to office only a few months ago. Since then there has been a re-organization of the Cabinet, and another re-organization is imminent.
It follows from all this that there is nothing very constructive in proposals from Canada for the Empire Peace Cabinet. No doubt naval defence will be considered, but for the time Canada is reluctant to shoulder new or heavy obligations. The political outlook is uncertain, the government is troubled by the difficulty and complexity of domestic problems, and ministers have still to determine their own attitude towards many questions of national as well as of Imperial concern.
I say, Sir, that it is the clear duty of the Government to let the people elect a new Parliament, select a Government which possesses its confidence, before any gentlemen undertake to proceed to the Imperial Conference and speak on behalf of Canada. Let us set our own house in order before undertaking to rebuild the British Empire or attempting to modify the constitutional structure of other nations. Let us first purify our own political atmosphere and clear away this abnormal parliament which in no way reflects the safe, sane, sober and normal opinion of the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have already spoken much too long, although I would like to express now my views about some of the matters which are to come up at the Imperial Conference. I believe, however, that having by an amendment challenged the right of this Parliament to legislate under the circumstances, we must first take the sense of the House before discussing the problems of the day. I was surprised to hear some gentlemen in this House blame the leader of the Opposition for having acted as he did. I would simply advise them to consult Bourinot, page 97, and they will see that the course followed by the leader of the Opposition was the legal and constitutional course to adopt.
In bringing my remarks to a conclusion I appeal to hon. gentlemen-though I am not greatly confident that my appeal will be heeded by all-to yield to the clamour

of the people and restore to the Canadian democracy full control over its political institutions. Members of the Government, especially the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, have told us on previous occasions, have painted a very deplorable picture, of the arduous duties of Ministers of the Crown, of how much work they have to do and the sacrifices they have made. Sir, the people everywhere feel that the crown of martyrdom is too heavy for my right hon. friend and his associates. They all want to give them a rest. I invite the Prime Minister to recall those words of Lincoln which would certainly apply to our present political situation:
In this age and in this country public sentiment is everything. With it nothing- can fail, against it nothing can succeed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Two references in the speech of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) make it highly essential, I think, that the position of the Chair should be stated clearly and beyond all question. First with respect to the ruling given by the Chair when the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) was speaking. That ruling merely had reference to the well-known rule of the House that an hon. member alluding in debate to another hon. member should do so as the member for a certain constituency, and not refer to him by name. My ruling on that occasion had no reference whatever to the point as to whether the late Minister of Finance is or is not a member of this House. In any event the ruling of the Chair would have no bearing upon that question; but inasmuch as there is no official intimation before me that the seat in question has been vacated I felt that even although the subject might be open to question it was far better to refer to the late Minister of Finance as the member for Leeds.
The second reference to which I wish to allude has to do with the statement credited to the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) that his resignation was in the Speaker's hands. The House will at once realize that it would never do for the impression to go abroad that the Speaker was a party to withholding a document of that character.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I therefore deem it my duty to make it clear to the House that I have not in my possession the resignation of the member for St. Antoine nor have I
ever received a document which was, or which purported to be, the resignation of his seat in this House. I thought it undesirable to interrupt the hon. member for Quebec East while he was speaking, but I felt that at the earliest possible moment the House should be apprised of these facts.
Mr. Speaker, I desire to repeat what I said in the course of my speech that I knew that such resignation had not reached Your Honour's hands, and it must have been withheld on its way.

Mr. Speaker, the brilliant lawyer and parliamentarian who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lapointe) occupied many minutes of the time of the House in recalling the deeds of some of my ancestors many of whom have been dead for fifty years. It was intensely interesting to me to hear what these fine fellows did but I am more interested to-day in the question, "Where are we going from here, and what are we going to do?" than in what other men did fifty years ago. If there ever was a time when the people are asking "Where are we going from here, what is your platform?" it is to-day? They are asking these questions in a manner more intensely earnest than ever before.
Following the time honoured custom, Sir, permit me to offer my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. They did their work ably, conscientiously and effectively, I should like to say to my hon. friend the mover of the Address (Mr. Mclsaac) that from the first day he appeared in this House he always seemed to know his own mind, always knew the way he was going to vote, and loyally followed his leader. Perhaps being more of a pathfinder myself, I can appreciate what loyalty and service of this kind mean better than some others; therefore I congratulate the hon. gentleman and his constituents, and I hope that he will be long spared to represent them and to support his leader loyally in this House.
To my hon. friend the seconder of the Address (Mr. MacKelvie) I wish to convey my opinion that his speech was the most eloquent maiden effort that I have yet heard; and that I was not alone in thinking this is apparent from the words of the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) who twitted my hon. friend slightly on falling under the influence of the apple. It is well known,

[ think, to all hon. members who have long been in this House that the hon. member from Cape Breton has himself for many years been under the subtle influence of iron and steel in his own province, and apparently that was his Scotch way of complimenting the hon. member for Yale.
To my right hon. (friend the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) I would say that he has reached his high office through no assistance of mine-not wittingly at least. But, on the other hand, I am very glad to be able to congratulate him and Canada and myself on his becoming Prime Minister. If ever there was a time when the people were looking for clean-cut, open-hearted talking so that they can get at the facts, in my judgment, Sir, it is now. From the first day that my right hon. friend became leader of this Government there was no doubt in my mind where he stood on the tariff question, and I do not think there was any doubt in the minds of any other Canadians. I believe that his unequivocal stand has had a good effect all over the country, because the people are looking for the truth. And at least his definite announcement of where he stood on the tariff question cleared away any doubts in my own mind on the subject, and I stand before you to-day, Sir, transformed, so far as Canada is concerned, from the nebulous free trader of a year ago, into as clean-cut and as unequivocal a protectionist on principle as the right hon. the leader of the Government himself.
It might not be without interest to some hon. members to follow the steps by which I reached this conclusion. It was quite unexpected in my own mind. In fact, the statement of the right hon. the leader of the Government came to me as a direct challenge, which I accepted as such, and I started out to collect a bundle of facts with which to bombard the right hon. gentleman this session, but I had not got very far in my search before I discovered that I was collecting two sets of facts. I found, almost without exception, that it was hard to discover a first class political economist who did not, at least in theory, agree with the principles of free trade. On the other hand, I found, with one notable exception -my native land-that practically the whole civilized world was protectionist. That, to my mind, was just as much a fact as the other, and had to be dealt with as such. I started in to find the reasons for that condition of affairs, and for a

while I put it down to original sin and went on building up my platform. I got quite a bundle of facts bolstering up my free trade platform, but when I turned them over I found original sin there, and something told me that if I came to this House with such a theory I would get punctured. So I had to find some better reason, and the conclusion I came to was that men do not accept free trade principles for about the same reason that they do not practice religion. But it is the fact, that they are afraid to do so, and the reasons of their fear are so real and so apparent that to refuse to acknowledge them is to be irrational. People still lock their doors when they go away. There is a reason for it-there are thugs in the world. But it took me some time to reach that conclusion-and after the most eloquent speech of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) yesterday, I think hon. members will understand what I was up against, because free trade, whatever else it has been, whether it is right or whether it is wrong, has undoubtedly been a great success in England.
But I had to find out why all other countries had not adopted something which has been such a great success in England, and for a while I was stuck, but eventually I played that old children's game which my grandchildren are now starting to play -I pretended. I pretended first I was a Frenchman-I stepped across the Atlantic and I looked at the world from the other side; then I pretended I was a German; later on I pretended I was an American; later than that I pretended I was a Canadian; later even than that I pretended I was a Canadian farmer; later even than that I pretended I was a Canadian manufacturer; later even than that, Mr. Speaker, I imagined I was a Canadian statesman; and, last of all, I stepped out of those shoes and got into the shoes of a man of the world-I tried to look at the world from the shoes of a man of the world in a world of men, and the results were extraordinary.
The first great discovery I made was that for thirty long years I had been looking at the question of free trade, thinking the group thoughts of the men with whom I was raised in my early days, and whose interest, I can now clearly see, it was to be free traders. For thirty years I had been thinking on this subject as an Englishman rather than as a Canadian. And the next great discovery I

made was that while free trade was undoubtedly to the best interests of the British people themselves, it by no means followed that it was in the best interests of the people of other countries differently situated.
Another point of view was brought to my attention during my plan of campaign. It did not come in a day, it did not come in a week, it did not come in a month; it took time to reach my present conclusions. I wondered where we were going from here, because my constituents are going to ask that question. I will have to answer it, and every hon. gentleman in this House will have to answer it. I thought, now, looking back over the ages, what has been the progress of men as men. We are undoubtedly better off to-day than our cave-dwelling ancestors were; no sane men in this age would like to exchange places with them. It is a long step from Stonehenge to Westminster; it is a long step from the trade and commerce of Lower Canada, where rum was the chief article of barter, to this honourable House, with its stringent dry laws. We have passed over a very hard road, but we have made very real progress. I do not know whether I ever told you the story before, Mr. Speaker, but once on leave I was invited to Scotland. Almost the first thing, my host, being a Scotchman, pointed out to me, with some considerable detail-more than I thought was necessary at the time- was the battlefield of Bannockburn. He said: "This is where my ancestors whaled the stuffing out of yours." But I had just come from the other side, where Scotchmen and Englishmen and Canadians and Frenchmen and Australians and New Zealanders were standing shoulder to shoulder. The English and the Scotch had had their fight and had shaken hands, and now they were fighting in a common cause.
That, Mr. Speaker, has been the history of the progress of the world. What is the lesson of the war? It is absolutely this, that no country, no matter how big or how well organized, can to-day stand alone. Every soldier who left Canada knows deep down in his heart that Canada alone could not have won the war. Great Britain alone could not have won the war; every soldier who fought over there knows it, just as he knows that no country can to-day stand alone. We passed that stage years ago.
It is here, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to make a reference to a remark made by
the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), who, I regret to say, is not at the moment in his seat. The hon. gentleman says that Canada never will do this and never will do that, but the time has long since passed when he or any other member can say what Canada never will do or never shall do. The member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), who is not now in his seat, I regret to say, asked the right hon. leader of the Government the other day what certain words of Lloyd George meant. I say to him that the words of Lloyd George mean exactly what they say, and the sooner he or other hon. gentlemen who have aspirations to leadership in this country find that out, the better-it is their job. There is no excuse for ignorance in this matter; you can find it out for a five cent stamp, and they will be glad to tell you.
Now, with the permission of the House, I wish to read a short extract from an article which is entitled "The Yellow Peril." The writer says:
Let us take the broadest possible view of the racial map of the globe as it existed before the recent war. Out of a total number of human beings amounting to 1.700,000,000, 550,000,000 were white, 1,150,000,000 were coloured. Thus the coloured races out-numbered the whites more than two to one. The white world consists of Europe, North America, the southern part of South America, the Siberian portion of Asia, and Australasia. The coloured world consists of the bulk of Asia, virtually the whole of Africa, and most of Central and South America.
This is the point to which I wish to direct attention:
The great bulk of the white race is concentrated in the European continent, and in 1914, before the war, the population of Europe was approximately 450,000,000. Four-fifths of the entire white race lives on less than one-fifth of the white world's territorial area. The remaining one-fifth is scattered to the ends of the earth, doing their best to hold the tide of colour. A century ago the impulse of the white race rolled aggressively eastward; precisely the opposite condition now prevails. The white races are more or less in an attitude of defence against the tremendous wave that is beating on their shores, a wave that is likely to become more tremendous now that the yellow races have learned so much in the course of our lamentable war.
I leave to the imagination of hon. gentlemen what will happen to this continent of America if the powerful white races of Europe are permitted to disintegrate. Four hundred and fifty millions live there; one hundred millions, odd, live here. What will happen? Millions of these colored men to-day

are on the move. At least sixty millions of them are among the most efficient and modern fighters in the world. Mr. Speaker, I claim no great superiority for the white race. For the existence of every one of the great religions, including the Christian, under whose flag I have the honour to stand to-night, the white man is indebted to men of colour-and it owes them much besides. On the other hand, the white race can give much to the coloured races. I could not help thinking when my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) was speaking on the League of Nations, that if we could only have with us to-day that learned and distinguished Chinaman to whom he referred, he would agree that it would be far better if we could bring his people up to our standard rather than that they should bring ours down to theirs.
There is not the slightest doubt in my mind-and I believe there is not the slightest doubt in the mind of any thinking man -that one more war like the last, or one more fight between the white races, will settle this civilization and settle it for good. While I am quite sure that the interests of Canada, of the United States, of England, of Europe, are absolutely one, it does not matter what I believe or what I think; it is what the other fellow thinks and believes that counts. So far as we are concerned, Canada is to-day a nation. The time is coming, and it is not in the far distant future, when Canada will have to make up her mind whether she will take the white man's road, with or without the assistance of America, just as she did in the war.
This brings me to the question of the markets of the world, about which we have heard so much during this debate. My hon. friend from Marquette looks with longing eyes to the big market to the south of us. So do I, and God grant that he will be able to build up a good big trade down there; it is a thing we all want to do. He says they have 120,000,000 people down there and hope to have 200,000,000 in so many years. But let us have a look at Europe. There is a market there, too, for she has 400,000,000 people to-day

not to-morrow or at some distant time in the future-400,000,000 people who need everything that this country produces in order that they may be brought back to normal conditions. If we permit them to disintegrate, we are ruined; the white race is ruined. Is not that a market worth cultivating, too? Is not the

cultivation of that market a job worthy of any man or of any nation? I think so. Let me tell the House about that little island across the sea whose success was so ably presented yesterday by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark). That little island to-day produces for export practically nothing but coal; the reason why she can send her ships to all parts of the world and bring back produce is that she can load her ships both ways, and she is the only country on earth that can do that. That is what ruined Germany. Germany tried to grow wheat and to force her manufactured goods on other countries. She gave three years' credit to niggers because she could not afford to take their products back. What would become of our wheat if England were to produce wheat? As I have said, England produces for export practically nothing but coal; she sacrificed the development of her agricultural industry because she wanted to become a manufacturing nation with world-wide markets. It is or has been in her interest to have free trade. Let us take a look at this big market to the south of us. It is not a little island twenty-one miles away from a market of 400,000,000 white men, but it is a large continent producing almost everything that modern man requires, with the exception of tea and coffee. I can think of no other product that man wants that she does not produce in quantities. Which of these countries is likely, in the ordinary course of events, to be the best market for this country, and which country has been the best in the past? Without bothering the House with a lot of figures which I obtained from the statistical office and which, with the permission of the House, I will place on Hansard, I will briefly state that the exports in the last twenty years from Canada to Great Britain exceeded the exports from Canada to the United States by $1,807,604,367. That is the history of the past.
