There should he no difference of opinion as to which would be likely to become the best market-200,000,000 people against 400,000,000-and there would be no difference of opinion, except for two things. The first is the will of our people-we cannot do anything without their will-and the second is Canada's enthusiastic desire to remain a nation. I have endeavoured, as best I know how, to come to a sane conclusion, but I must at this point absolutely disagree with my hon. friends to my left. This pamphlet which I hold in
my hand is called the " New National Policy as adopted by the Organized Farmers of Canada in the Farmers' platform drafted and issued by the Canadian Council of Agriculture at Winnipeg on November 29, 1918," and in it, at page 13, I find the following:
By reducing the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual, uniform reductions be made in the remaining tariff on British imports that will ensure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada in flve years.
That is their platform, and while a year ago I would have jumped at it, today, I am not in favour of free trade in one year or five years with Great Britain or any other country on earth, without a quid pro quo. My reasons are briefly these. The whole foundation of our present society in Canada rests upon the tariff, and if we take away the tariff, the whole structure will fall down. I will support that contention by recounting one solitary statement of fact, given in sworn evidence before the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) this summer. If my memory serves me right, the subject under discussion was Yale locks, and the manager told the Minister of Finance that it cost him 40 per cent more to manufacture these locks in Canada than it did in the plant of the parent company in the United States. The Minister of Finance was apparently astonished and he asked:	" How do you
account for that?" Like a flash came the answer:	"We have in the parent company in the United States one machine that cost $60,000 and which performs one function. It will perform that function for all the keys in Canada in one week and it will stand idle here for fifty-one weeks in the year." In other words, while you can have a $100,000 machine in a country with a population of 100,000,000, you cannot have a $100,000 machine in a country with a population of 8,000,000.
It has been said that the tariff has been abused, but that is no argument against the principle of protection. Even if the tariff has been abused, I have just this to say on that subject:	We are still a
nation of men; we are not absolutely at the mercy of all the organizations that like to put up prices. Like myself all the other members of the House have thought this matter out and I will, therefore, not take up a minute of the time of the House in discussing it; but I have just this to say, that while protection may not always protect and while it may have sometimes

been abused, as I believe it has, we are still a democratic people; we are self-contained, and when we make up our minds to get after these people, such a movement cannot be withstood and these people will stand at the bar of outraged public opinion. If any man is taking advantage of my patriotism or the patriotism of other Canadian men who desire to be self-reliant, then some day he will answer for his action.
In conclusion, free trade as practised in England has proved to be no panacea for unrest, no panacea for profiteering, and no panacea for war. In fact, I believe the fierce competition for foreign markets, which was so ably described yesterday, had a great deal to do with bringing about the war. Until a few years ago, it was almost universally believed that to maintain peace you had to prepare for war and to have big armaments. Some people believe it to-day, but millions of people know that it is a lie. Millions of women know that it is a lie; millions of soldiers know that it is a lie. We have had the biggest preparation for peace in the shape of war material, the world has ever seen, yet we have had the bloodiest war, and in the knowledge that it is no guarantee of peace, no panacea, lies, to my mind, the hope of the world. If you once get enough people making up their minds that a certain thing is desirable, they are going to get it; they always have got it, and when there are two roads, one leading to destruction and absolute annihilation-that is war-and some other road, if you can get enough people looking for that other road they will find it. Here is a ray of hope. Already there has been published in the last year a book by a Major Douglas. I have not the time nor the ability to review his book, but I have read it, and can commend it to every hon. gentleman in this House, and to every banker and every labouring man in this country. It is not Bolshevism; it is not Socialism; it does not pull down, but it does show a way whereby we can build up and avoid war.
I think the members of our Government who attended the Peace Conference have caught the spirit of this new day too. I listened with great joy to the eloquent words of the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) when he told us that at this meeting of the League of Nations, Canada was there as a nation in reality and in truth, and that she was a stronger nation for her connection with the British Empire. I also listened to the words of the hon. member for Durham, the ex-

President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), who in no uncertain words said: "The world is on the march and Canada is in the van." Thank God for that. We are not hanging back and letting George do it.
This brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the amendment. I want to point out to hon. members that while we have hopes of a better day Douglas's plan is not yet in existence, and I am quite sure the millennium is not here; but we have got the amendment. That, I think, will bring almost any man out of the clouds. It did not take me very long to make up my mind what I was going to do with respect to it, but it did make me think a little bit just the same. I asked myself the questions: What are you here for? Who sent you? What is your job? And I came to the conclusion that I had been sent here under very definite instructions to carry out what was the real issue-the Conscription Act. I do not know what all my constituents thought on all the planks that have been carried out by the Government since, but on that one issue there is no doubt in the world where they stood, because it was the sole topic in my election. I came down here to help push that thing through with all my force, and I did it. I believed in it, and I have this to say about that Act. If we have another war, we will have conscription not only of the men from 18 to 25, but of every man in this country, and in saying that I have not the faintest doubt that I represent the overwhelming opinion among the men who fought in the war. This idea of letting a few men do it

"letting George do it"-is played out. The next thing that I came down to do, in my opinion, at least, was to see that the men who were crippled and the widows and orphans of the war got all this country could afford to pay them. I made up my mind to fight for them. The next thing- well, perhaps the less said about that the better.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that if ever there was a time when the people wanted to know what they were up against, it is now. The first requisite of an appeal to the country at the present time is a definite, clear-cut issue, and on the fiscal policy, if possible, so far as I am concerned. This the leader of the Opposition is apparently determined we shall not have. The next requisite to my mind, is a fair redistribution of seats. This the leader of the Opposition also firmly declines to have. If we do not have redistribution before the election w'e will have,

in effect, more people disfranchised five times over than were disfranchised in 1917. We should certainly have at least one or the other of these requisites, if not both, namely, a clear-cut issue and representation by population. I shall therefore vote against the amendment.
' Mr. WILLIAM ASBURY BUCHANAN (Lethbridge) : Mr. Speaker, I usually speak briefly, but I question very much whether I can conclude my remarks in the short space of time remaining before the House will adjourn for this sitting, but I do not object to making a start and then adjourning the debate. In the effort to condense my remarks I cannot avoid saying what has been said by other speakers in the debate, and that is a word of congratulation to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), I am going to say that I thought so highly of the Prime Minister at the time, not because I agreed with his policy or his past course, but of the man personally, that I sent him my congratulations while I was travelling west on the train. I want to say this of the Prime Minister, and it is something that has not been mentioned. He has demonstrated during the time I have been in parliament real industry, and in that respect he is an example especially to the younger men who come into this House, because if we do not display industry we will not get very far. The Prime Minister has been a remarkable example of tireless industry.
What I have arisen for is largely to explain my position. Still, I question very much whether there is any reason why I should explain it, because last year when sitting on the Government side of the House, I expressed my own views on public questions. In order to have more freedom, and especially since a new government, with a new leader, had been formed-I would not say a new policy had been announced-I felt I would be much freer in what has been termed No Man's Land. First of all, I want to say that from the beginning, and for months prior to the formation of the Union Government, I was an advocate of a Union Government, and when the Union Government was formed I supported it for the purposes for which it was formed, and that was for the conduct of the war. I agree entirely with the position that has been taken by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). I went back from this city in 1917 to my constituency, and my old party friends supported me because I told them I was supporting conscription, and supporting Union Government, to carry out that policy and all other necessary war measures, but that in every other respect I was adhering to the principles I had always advocated in this House.
That is my position to-day, and for that reason I am not prepared to support the Government that has been constituted since the last session of Parliament. The people returned to power in 1917 a Government headed by the late Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). The Prime Minister who led that Government has resigned, and a new Prime Minister with a new policy and a new name for his party has assumed office. Now, holding the views I do, I cannot accept the policy of that party, though I have the very highest admiration for its leader. My judgment is that the people in 1917, when they voted for the candidates in that election, voted with a war mind. The war was the foremost question in their minds, and consequently their decision was based upon their desire to win the war, and with no thought whatever about the domestic problems that might develop as a result of the war. That being the case, the people should have an opportunity of (expressing themselves on the policies that are uppermost at the present moment, the domestic questions that are engaging their attention just now. A Gov-vernment that satisfied the people on war issues may not satisfy them on peace issues; they may differ entirely in their views in these two respects. As I said, I did not abandon the views I held in peace times; I consider that we have again reached the peace stage and I therefore, stand by the principles which I advocated in the past.
Another thing that we should keep in mind is the fact that spart from the selection of a new leader, the constitution of a new party, and the outlining of what has been called a new platform, there are other reasons, why the people should have an opportunity to express their views at the present time. The official Opposition has a new leader, and there has come into existence an entirely new party with a platform. Why should not the people be given an opportunity to express their opinion on the merits of the respective parties that exist to-day? May I say, at this juncture, that we have not had an election in Canada on purely domestic problems since 1911? Ten years have elapsed since we have had an election in which the issues of ordinary times could be discussed

and decided. The only election we have had between 1911 and the present date was the election of 1917, which was fought out entirely on a war issue, and it is very important at the present time that an election should be held. My attitude last session, to which I still adhere, was that it was possible to have a census and redistribution, and to have an election in 1921. I maintained that it was possible to do so if an effort had been made to expedite the census. We could have had early returns of the population of this country and could have had redistribution and an election. My statement at that time was to this effect:
I believe it would be only necessary to have one session of Parliament following the present session before we could have redistribution and before an appeal could be made to the country on the basis of representation in accordance with the census of 1921.
I am going to be quite frank and say that if the Government give to me and to this House an assurance that they will carry out the purpose of the amendment to the amendment I shall be satisfied for the present. But I go further and say that no contentious questions should be brought up in this House until a redistribution bill has been drafted and we are ready to go to the country. I am put in this position: If I vote for the amendment to the amendment, I am practically saying, and I do say, that it is possible to have a redistribution this year, to have the census taken, and to have an election. But I know that the Government we have here at the present time must exist to formulate that redistribution, and they may come back and say: "We cannot guarantee that we can carry out what is asked for in the amendment to the amendment; it depends upon whether we have the support of the members."
Naturally, too, it depends upon whether they have my individual support; and I am not prepared to pledge my support to the Government or any party in this House on any question until I know what it is and exactly what is going to be discussed. The Budget debate will come up later if the Government decide to carry out their programme, and if they are going to carry out the policy they have outlined in the address, I am bound to differ from them and, therefore, to vote against them. But I know what will be said. It will be stated that if I want this redistribution before an election I must support the Government in order to get it. Now, I cannot go so

far. The Government should give us an assurance of a real desire on their part to provide redistribution this year, to expedite the census, to have an election immediately, and to avoid during this session the discussion of all controversial questions, or give me freedom to act as I think best in the interests of the country.
I believe that Western Canada is entitled to increased representation at this time; but if I must support the Government on other questions in order to keep it in existence so that that representation may be provided, I am placed in a position in which I do not wish to remain. I am not going to tie myself up to any party on any question in order to have something-done which I think is necessary at this particular time. I feel that the West would be deprived of its proper representation in this House for probably four or five shears if we had not a redistribution, but I do not want to be tongue-tied or to be held down by any promise to support the Government until it decides to have a redistribution and go to the country. If it accepts the proposal that it should go to the country this year under the terms of the amendment to the amendment and along the lines I have mentioned, I shall be satisfied. I am going to try to conclude before the House rises, although I had intended to speak at greater length. However, I can place my views on other matters briefly before the House'. I came into this House in 1911 and during all the time I have been a member, I have been an advocate of a clear-cut policy which is in entire contradiction to the views expressed in the address in regard to the tariff. Now, if I accepted the views put forward by the Government in the Address I should be contradicting the position I have taken in this House from 1911 up to the present time. It is not a question of consistency on the part of those who have advocated tariff reduction in the past. The question that concerns me, is: what attitude have I taken; have I been consistent; and do I intend to remain consistent? I am not looking forward to the future, but I intend to remain if I possibly can a consistent advocate of policies which I believe are in the best interests of the country. I know that the Prime Minister has attempted to put all those who believe in a low tariff, or people who believe in freedom of trade, into a certain category, the free trade class. I

refuse to be placed there. But I am an advocate of free trade wherever it is in the best interests of the majority of the people. I am in favour of low tariff where it is in the interests of the bulk of the people. I am not prepared to destroy industry and capital, and that is the bugaboo that has always been raised. But I am satisfied that in the budget that will be brought down by the Government the outstanding principles of the national policy will be maintained.
Because we find those men in the country who have long been advocates of high protection loyally supporting the Prime Minister. Well, I cannot join in the support of the Prime Minister along with individuals who agitate high protection; they would not be proper company for me with the views I hold.
Now, having promised the people who returned me in 1917 that I would not abandon the principles that I supported in the past, and having reached the stage where there is a definite declaration on the part of the Government that it is going to adhere entirely to the principle of protection as it has been in existence in this country for forty years, I have come to the parting of the ways. If it is impossible for the Government to concede the point that I have mentioned in connection with redistribution, I cannot possibly vote confidence in a government that expresses opinions of that sort, because I would be declaring confidence in a government in whose principles I did not believe. That would not be fair to the Government, it would not be fair to me, and it would not be fair to the people who have elected me in the past.
And so my position is this:	Now that
we have passed the war stage and are reaching what we hope are normal times I am still in the position that the Prime Minister was always in and adhering to the views that he advocated prior to the war. That is all. I am there and that is where I intend to remain until I am convinced that I am wrong. Up to the present I have not been so convinced. It was my intention to speak on other questions this afternoon but I shall have an opportunity of doing so later. I shall therefore close my remarks, feeling that I have placed before the House in condensed form my views on the amendments and on the main motion.

speechtext: Consideration of the motion of Mr. Janies Mclsaac for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King, and the proposed amendment to the amendment of Mr. Campbell, resumed from Wednesday, March 2.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall, if it will not be too much for the right hon. leader of the Government to bear, open remarks by offering him my sincere congratulations upon his attainment of the high position which he now occupies. He has brought dignity to the office; he fills it with dignity, and the worst wish that any hon. member on this side has for him is that he will not be permitted to bear that dignity too long.
It was of great interest to me to listen the other night to the speech delivered in this House by the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie). One reason why I listened to his speech with such interest is that we have sat in this House a long time together, and the other and principal reason if his absolutely chameleon-like change of policy. It appears to be customary that the moment a man, no matter what his former political views may have been, attains office, and perhaps, in order that he may retain office, the old faith and the old shibboleths go and he seems to cut his coat according to his cloth in the way of politics; a strange virus seems to get into his blood, something that was not there before, something that, I may say, does not seem to suit him very well.
My hon. friend launched into an argument on the tariff, and he stated that the Opposition had done everything in its power to avoid the issue. He said further: What we want to know is just where they stand. If I know anything of the members of the Opposition, they are not attempting to avoid any issue as regards the tariff. When the tariff is brought down and when the proper time comes to discuss the tariff, every hon. member on this side will be found amply prepared to state his position. There is before the people to-day only one issue and it is not the tariff. What my hon. friends opposite would like, and what
they are endeavouring to do on every available occasion, is to draw the tariff herring across the track so as to keep the people from thinking of the real issue, which is whether my hon. friends opposite should resign or not. It has been proved in the by-elections that that is the issue to-day, and on that issue I purpose speaking.
As I have already stated, a most chameleon-like change has come over the Minister of Militia and Defence in regard to his fiscal ideas. It is not so long ago that members on this side of the House introduced certain resolutions in regard to the tariff, the first one that I remember being in 1914, and another one in 1917. The first resolution was introduced in 1914 by Mr. Knowles of Moose Jaw, who was then a member of this House. This is Mr. Knowles' resolution:
That in the opinion of this House the time has arrived when, in the interest of the farmers, and consequently in the interest of the whole of Canada, the duties on agricultural implements should be forthwith removed.
The present Minister of Militia and Defence had some words to say upon that subject and they were no uncertain utterances; they were as clear-cut as they possibly could be. This is what he said, in speaking in this House on the 11th March, 1914, as reported at page 1566 of Hansard:
Mr. Hugh Guthrie (iSouth Wellington) : I desire, before the motion is put, to offer a few remarks upon what I consider to be one of the most important questions with which this House has had to deal during the present session. We on this side of the House, and, I fancy, some members on the other side of the House, are not quite satisfied with the wave of the hand by which the right hon. the Prime Minister sought to relegate this important matter to the ash heap, or, at all events, to some place outside the precincts of this Chamber. The question is too big and too far-reaching in its consequences to be dealt with by the Prime Minister in a ten-minute speech, and by the silence of the members of a party numbering 130 or 140 in this Chamber. I have no doubt that there are many hon. members, supporters of the Government, who are very keenly interested in this matter-many of them representing rural ridings; many of them representing, as I do, both rural and urban populations-and who desire to give free expression to their thought and opinion upon this grave question.
And so on. I read that simply as an introduction to the speech which he delivered. Later in his speech the hon. gentleman referred to the Prime Minister of that day ami said of that right hon. gentleman:
He had not heard the case very fully argued ; he said the Government would consider the question, but he stated, as deliberately as a

man could state it in the House, that on account of the trusts and combines of the United States it would not be possible to give free agricultural implements to the people of Canada. There is only one thing left for him to do, and that is to reduce the tariff on agricultural implements to a minimum. In my view, that will not be as satisfactory as the complete abolition of the duties upon agricultural implements.
Further on he said:
If these trusts cannot take possession of the British market, which is a free market, how could they take possession of the Canadian market if it were made a free market? To my mind, there is nothing in the argument of the Prime Minister. It was not a reason for refusing to abolish the duty; it was the merest kind of an excuse.
Then he went on:
I rose on this occasion chiefly because I think that some member from the province of Ontario should interject some remarks into this debate to show that the demand for agricultural implements is by no means limited to the western provinces of Canada. The riding which I have the honour to represent in this House is about equally made up of urban and of rural inhabitants. I am satisfied that, irrespective of party, the people engaged in agriculture in the county of Wellington, north or south, would hold up both hands for the boon of free agricultural implements.
Then he continued:
So I believe it is in the great province of Quebec and in the Maritime Provinces; certainly it is in the great western provinces of Canada. From the Atlantic to the Pacific, the demand is as broad as is the country. I then ask the Government: Why not accede to a demand of that kind when your revenue is going to suffer so little and when no Canadian industry is going to be injured?
He said further:
I desire in a few words to show that the removal, the entire abolition of the Canadian duties on agricultural implements, would not do an injustice to a single manufacturing establishment in Canada.
Therefore, in 1914, the present Minister of Militia and Defence was absolutely certain that free agricultural implements would be a great boon to the people of the Dominion; that it would help in cheapening food, and that it would not do one iota of injury to Canadian industries. Those are three very good reasons, and I submit that they still hold good to-day. Just one more quotation from my hon. friend's address:
I, for one, believe that of all the industries in Canada the agricultural implement industry is the one now best able to stand without the support of any customs tariff at all.
That was on the motion of Mr. Knowles. In 1917, this motion was moved by the Hon. Frank Oliver, then member for Edmonton:

That in the opinion of this House it would be in the public interset if the Customs Tariff Act were so amended as to provide:
1.	That wheat, wheat flour, and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list.
2.	That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery, and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
What did the Minister of Militia say at that time with respect to clause 2 of the resolution? He said this:
I therefore favour that portion of the amendment which provides that agricultural machinery shall be upon the free list. I favour the whole of the free list as set out in paragraph 2 of the amendment.
He further says:
And when I look at the trade returns and find that in item after item which it is now proposed to put upon the free list the revenue collected is so small as to be negligible, it seems to me clear that the time has come when the relief asked for in this clause of the amendment should be granted.
The Minister of Militia the other night directed his attention principally to the Farmers' party. He produced a catalogue and declaimed loudly against it. Well, that is quite within his privilege, so far as I am concerned, but I want to ask this:	If the
Farmers' party go on advocating, as they do advocate, and as we on this side of the House have advocated, that certain articles should be put upon the free list, does it lie in the mouth of any hon. member of this House, even the Minister of Militia himself, to find such fault with the Farmers' party that one would think they were doing some great national harm in expressing their views? Even if the farmers do not buy their agricultural machinery at home, but in the United States, there is this much to be said: the duty goes into the treasury of the people of Canada, and not to the manufacturers. Why, Sir, the Minister of Militia talked as if it was a matter of absolute disloyalty to buy anything outside of one's own country. Sir, until the millennium comes I think the people are going' to buy where they can buy cheapest. It struck me as I heard that portion of the Minister's remarks, that I could see the beginning of the old flag waving again. Disloyalty for the farmers to buy in the cheapest market? Who has the right to accuse of disloyalty any class that acted so well as the farmers have done during the past few years? I say that such language comes not well from the Minister, and that that sort of argument should not be made.

In passing, I noticed the other day the report of a speech hy an hon. member of the Senate, expressing the opinion that in view of the Fordney Bill which has just passed both houses in the United States there should be reprisals by the Dominion of Canada. Now I do not believe that that is a proper policy, or ever will be a proper policy, to pursue, either for the nation or for the individual. You will never get far down the road by adopting reprisals as a nation along these particular lines. The thing for the people of this country to do, so far as that question is concerned, is to keep their heads level and to attend to their own business along fiscal lines as it should he attended to, and let the other nations look out for themselves.
I desire now to take up what to my mind is the real issue before the people of this country. The Minister of Militia the other evening quoted many precedents to show that so far as the Government was concerned it was carrying out the will of the people in retaining office. Well, if precedents are to count, all I can say is this, that my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), in the excellent speech he made yesterday, with the precedents that he quoted absolutely swept the ground from under the feet of the Minister of Militia. I do not believe there is any judge who, hearing the matter argued legally, would not say that the precedents quoted hy the hon. member for Quebec East outweighed the precedents quoted by the Minister of Militia. But, Sir, I am not concerned with precedents in this case. They do not appeal to me here, and for this reason: precedents ought not to weigh in the case before us because there was an absolute promise by this Government that on the conclusion of the war they would go to the country. It was plainly and distinctly understood, if ever anything in this world was understood, that that Government was formed for war purposes, and war purposes only; that it would endure only during the life of the war; and that when the war was concluded the people would he consulted. Why should the Government not have consulted them before now? The people of Canada have realized in the last year more than they ever realized before-because up to last year they had not taken the matter into their serious consideration-that since 1911 they have not had one single iota of a chance to pass upon questions affecting the Dominion of Canada. There has been no discussion upon public platforms; there 31
has been no dissemination of opinion; there has been no attempt so far as our own political questions are concerned to educate the people. Therefore, I say that in view of that promise, which the people of Canada absolutely believed would be carried out, there is one thing, and one thing only for this Government to do, and that is to dissolve Parliament and appeal to the people.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have referred to the by-elections. Let us take the last five by-elections. The Government won three out of five. Now three of those elections were absolutely hand-picked, and in two of them ministers of the Crown were running. Can that he considered an expression of public opinion? Does anybody mean to say that because a few thousands of the millions of voters in Canada have expressed their opinion, that is a mandate for the Government to continue in office? I distinctly say it is not, and I believe the people of this country take the same view.
The Minister of Militia seemed to feel rather badly-perhaps his were only crocodile tears-about the "remnant" of Liberalism in Ontario. Let us admit for argument's sake that there are not many in this House, hut what they are makes up for any lack of numbers. I want to tell the Government this: There is the healthiest "remnant" of Liberalism in the province of Ontario that there has been for many years, and it just wants a chance to act. There is Liberalism in the province of Ontario, the same old Liberalism it has always been, standing for freedom of thought and freedom of speech, well-settled theories and policies; and the Liberals of Ontario are quite content that these theories and these policies and these doctrines shall be tested out at the earliest possible moment. If the minister is so confident that there is only a remnant of it left, and that that remnant cannot accomplish much, one would at least suppose that under such circumstances the Government would have sufficient courage to go to the country and stand by the result. But the great trouble is that they lack any courage. This Government is like the clinging vine; it shoots out its tendrils in the direction of little byelections which they calculate upon winning. Sometimes the tendrils do not find any purchase, they break, and down comes the vine; although occasionally the tendril succeeds in hanging on. But in each case in which it has hung on, the success has been



of no credit to the Government, because the constituency has been hand-picked. But while, in my opinion, at any rate, no Government knowing, as this Government knows, the attitude and the frame of mind of the people of Canada, should continue in office. Nevertheless this Administration persists in hanging on, it still clings tenaciously to its position. It will not be responsible to the people of Canada, whose opinions and desires it absolutely disregards. Why, under these circumstances, the Government continues to carry on, is a state of mentality on its part which I cannot grasp. I would at least say, in their position: Come on and we will have a fight; it will not be bloody; there will be a good deal of gas but that will not matter so long as we fight it out and see who is the winner: let us find out whom the people want as their servants, and when they have made their choice we are ready to obey their commands. Surely that is only logical and right, and I ask the Government to take this course. But, to my mind, the milk in the cocoanut was spilled by the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) before he sat down. It is quite evident why they do not want to go to the country. We got a little inkling of it from the hon. member for St. Hya-cinthe (Mr. Gauthier), but we got it all from the Minister of Militia; and that was that on the grounds of equality there would be many times greater representation in the cities than in the rural districts. The Government know that their policy appeals to the big interests, and the big interests live in the cities. So that with a redistribution such as they propose to give them, the cities shall send such representatives as will vote in their interests. The rural representation, they expect, will be cut down to as great a degree as possible, while the urban they will build up, and build up, as I have no doubt they will do if they last long-enough to make a redistribution-and make it in such a way that only their own supporters shall come from the cities. That is the reason there is no election and no appeal to the people; that is the reason why public opinion is being flouted day by day and the public are being told by this Government, wrho forget that they are the servants of the people: You attend to your own business and let us alone and we will attend to ours, and when we are ready we will ask for your advice. That is the whole kernel of that portion of their propaganda. The Minister of Militia the other night, by sort of process of elimination, finally figured out that although the Government did not

deserve the confidence of many portions of the Dominion of Canada, still they had the confidence of some, and then at length he got down to the supposed fact, which he stated with great vehemence:	"At least
we have the confidence of the House of Commons." Well, it would appear to me when I arrived here about two weeks ago that possibly they had and possibly they had not. But I thought that if there was one thing which they did not have it was the confidence of the Commons; and I have no doubt to-day that if hon. members sitting on the other side of the House voted as their hearts dictate and not as the glory of office impels, they would vote in such a way as to show quite plainly that this Government has not the confidence either of the people or of the House of Commons.
Sir, I say again that precedents matter not. There was a promise and that promise should be absolutely carried out. We have the strange spectacle of two ex-ministers of the Administration sitting on this side of the House, both having resigned for the same reason and both of them now antagonistic to the Government. Is not that palpably an evidence that the Government has not the confidence of the House and certainly not of the pepole? When any Government, as this has done, has seen its followers leave it day by day, month by month, and year by year, it surely can come to one conclusion only, and that is that it is not wanted and that another is wanted in its stead. The great bete noir to hon. gentlemen opposite is the Farmers' party. Well, I hold no brief for that party, but I do say, as a Liberal, that if the farmers want a party of their own and desire to express certain views, they should be at perfect liberty to carry out that idea. This is an absolutely free country. Why, therefore, should there be any bitter feelings against any section of the people who desire to give expression to their views? Surely it has not come to such a pass in Canada that none can get together and express views or advance theories. It it has, then it is a sorry plight for this Dominion. But I do not believe that such is the case.
Now, I have only this to ask the Government, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that they trust the people. The people are not often wrong. In this strong, virile young country the people know pretty well what they want, and if they do go wrong they will very quickly get right again. I say, therefore, that the Government ought to trust the people and give them an opportunity

to say what Government they want at the present time. In other words, I commend to the members of the Government, in all fairness to the people of Canada, this exhortation: "Play up, play up, and play the game!"

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I deal with
the subject matter of the Address, may I express regret that the right hon, gentleman (Sir Robert Borden), who led the Government previously to the present Prime Minister, is in such a state of health that he is unable now to take any large share in the affairs of the country. I should like also to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address and to express my appreciation of the manner in which they discharged their duties in this respect.
In 1908, when the present Prime Minister first sought election, I was a constituent in his riding and ineffectually did my best to keep him from coming here. I can now congratulate him on his brilliant and rapid rise to the position of Prime Minister. He is to my certain knowledge a true Conservative, tenacious of principles, and able in the advocacy of them, and the times are going to demand a man of such characteristics as their champion. These opinions are all going into the crucible, and they will have to undergo considerable refining and much change. While Union Government lasted, under the former Prime Minister, I endeavoured to give it my full support, and did so support it in all matters for which it was primarily formed. But it was inevitable that, in view of the procedure followed in the formation of this Government and the new issues, I must seek new alignments. Hence I find my. self in "No Man's Land."
There is no political terminology apt in description of Union Government: It was not one party, it was not a coalition, it was not a fusion. When we first met in joint caucus I was surprised. During the war I said nothing, but in the second session I advocated a change to a coalition basis. I discussed this with some of the ministers. In the third session there was a caucus of Liberal Unionists to consider the future course. The decision was, to go on for the present as we had been doing. With that decision began the disintegration of the Liberal Unionist group and the present difficulties of the Government.
Sli
Because of lack of clear political definitions no political action in the constituencies was possible. When the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Calder) recently told the West that the Government had been too busy for political activity he talked bunkum. If we had been a coalition each member could have organized; but as the case stood we could do nothing. For a Conservative Unionist to organize, looked like throwing the Liberal Unionists overboard; and for a Liberal Unionist to organize was to seek a separate career and throw the Conservative Unionists overboard. We could not appeal to both until the future course was in some measure determined. The consequence was that as time went on confusion grew in the ridings; and as elections must be faced the confusion must be ended. As no preparation had been made in the ridings it only remained for the Government party in the House to attempt a fusion. This fusion is no wider than the House. If the Peterborough election demonstrates anything it is that the fusion has not included the electorate. Many Conservatives deprecated but they will finally accept it. Many Liberal Unionists doubted it and will finally reject it.
There were two opportunities for a coalition-one when the Government was formed and one after the war. Both were lost. The result is that the Government finds itself to-day out of touch with the electorate and generally unprepared for an election; and it needs time, desperately needs time.
Though forseeing the present position for myself, I supported the Government last session because it proposed to balance its expenditure with taxation. As the whole is greater than any part, so it seemed to me that to get a balance of taxation over expenditure was more important than an exact justice in any of the items making up that taxation. I had differed with the Government in its 1919 Budget, and last year re-stated some of my objections to its tariff policy. The member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has said he was smoked out. He and some of his associates think I stayed until I bear on my garments the odor of the smoke that expelled him. I assure him that the fire never touched me.
In 1919, in association with a distinct group of Liberals in coalition, I could have continued in support of the Government, for issues had arisen which seemed to me important enough to justify such a course

could I have had assurance such as a coalition of that sort could give. Without such assurance, in complete surrender to the fiscal opinions held by four-fifths of the Government supporters, I found myself, on other issues, in fundamental disagreement, and so departed.
In the main I agree with the Progressive platform-at least as interpreted by the leaders of that party. The recall I would never accept, as' it is not consonant with our system of representative government and degrades a member no matter what may be his service. I agree also with the leaders of the party that it must extend its membership with all classes of the community and free itself of any class organization or control.
With regard to the Liberal party, the presence in their ranks of many strong protectionists hampered Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier throughout his career, and forced him to opportunism on this question. At this, stage in our affairs, despite the fact that this fiscal question is not of the essence of Liberalism, it is desirable that a government should come in unanimous as to protection or decided tariff reductions. The Liberal leader has not spoken with the same voice in the East as in the West; this opportunism is inopportune now. If he could tell the West his sympathy with its desires for reductions, he should be able to say to Montreal something thereon beyond this-that it is overshadowed by the larger question of restoring representative government. If the Liberal party had in 1911 to suffer the loss of its Toronto protectionists, 1921 may be the time to lose its Montreal protectionists; the omens forecast it.
The foregoing sufficiently discloses the attitude I shall take on the tariff. Let this be added. In examining the tariff it should be borne in mind that we have had practically the same policy for over forty years. No country will accept protection but on the principle that eventually competition among the encouraged industries will bring prices to the general world level. Canada before the war was one of the dearest countries of the world to live in. Have we got the competition expected? If not, why? Have combines defeated it? Has our tariff become an Old Age Pension instead of a Mother's Allowance?
This nation is now the upholder of Stat-ism in its operation of a combined system of transportation by railways and steamships. The freight rates decision and policy thereon of the Government, have

not been fully satisfactory to the country and I trust there may be laid before us some plan of getting better results. The operation of the railways calls for large improvement and possibly this will be effected when the Grand Trunk is finally taken over. If the Government woiild appoint a committee of the House to reporf thereon, I believe the country would approve.
In the past I have urged the attention of the House and the Government to consideration of a committee on Estimates as a great improvement in means of retrenchment. In other respects as well, this would have important results. The Minister of Finance led me to expect that a committee to consider and report thereon would be favoured by the Government and I take the earliest opportunity to refer to it. Discussion of it will be possible when a resolution now on the Order Paper is reached.
On the question of Imperial Relations, I have been pleased to see that the last two Prime Ministers of Canada have been in agreement in policy. This is a subject that should not come into party politics, and I regretted yesterday to hear the utterance of the member for East Quebec (Mr. Lapointe) thereon. Not a regard for the public interest, but party acrimony spoke them. I trust an opportunity to discuss on the floor of the House, the policy Canada shall pursue may be afforded.
The excess profits tax has long been marked for extinction as an unjust system in peace and directly making for inflation. As the British Government has announced that there it will be discontinued, it is to be hoped that it may be reformed out of existence here.
The natural resources are more strongly than ever being demanded by the Western Provinces. The position of those provinces as inferior members of Confederation must be reformed so that the same principles shall prevail in all, that no grievance as to status may mark our full stature of nationhood.
Finally, with regard to the sub-amendment which I have seconded, its first consideration is the country's interest, and not the tactics of party strife. The Government's supporters who demand redistribution, as I did last year, must recognize that without a miracle the Government must disappoint them. As it cannot recognize, and may very probably be defeated, any Budget adopted this year cannot settle business conditions. If the Government can carry its Budget, and as obviously it

seeks to make the tariff the next issue, it cannot let that issue stale by postponing its appeal to 1922. Add the three components -inability to organize until the eve of an election, unsettled business, and an issue shaped to its liking, and the result is undoubtedly an election this fall. If the interests of the country are consulted, a redistribution will be made before this session closes and a House properly representative will be returned to deal with all the many great and disputed questions.
Mr. JOHN A. MAHARG (Maple Creek) : Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I wish to associate myself with all that has been already said in a complimentary way of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and also of the mover and seconder of the Address. I particularly desire to associate myself with what was said by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid). I think in the few words he contributed he gave excellent advice to the Prime Minister.
Now, coming to the particular questions before the House, it is not my intention to devote very much time to the resolution, for I think the ground has been almost entirely covered; there may be one or two phases of it which I may touch upon if time will permit. In the meantime I wish particularly to direct my remarks to some of the matters discussed by the right hon. the Prime Minister during his tour of Canada shortly after his elevation to the chief citizenship of the Dominion. Some of those statements reflect specifically on the people whom he describes as being particularly represented by this group. In justice to myself, to our organization and to the people referred to, I deem it my duty to deal with some of those statements.
The Prime Minister directed his attention to the farmers first, I believe, during the by-election in Colchester, when he described them as being in alliance with, I think he termed them, seditionists, wreckers, Bolshevists and other people whose doctrines were preached only in one country in the world at the present time. To this statement, Sir, I take the strongest exception.
4 p.m. I do not think that a grosser misrepresentation was ever made of any class or group of people. I shall therefore give a few illustrations to show to hon. members and to the people just the position that the farmers assumed during the crucial period in the history of our country. It is not pleasant for me to have to deal with this matter, and up to the present time I have refrained from
referring to it in this House, but my duty now compels me to demonstrate the absolute baselessness of the statement of the Prime Minister. I will be as brief as I can and will commence at a point shortly after the wpr broke out.
In the month of February, 1915, we held a convention of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Association and a movement was started, known as the Patriotic Acre Movement. At that time a plan was undertaken whereby every member in our organization who possibly could would make a contribution towards a fund by donating a certain number of bushels of wheat produced on his land. The net result of that movement was that during the following summer an entire trainload of wheat, consisting of forty cars, was delivered at the port of Montreal free on board a transport to the order of the British Government. My hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) corrects me-it was a trainload of flour consisting of forty 80,000-pound cars. This meant quite a large contribution. But in addition to that trainload of flour an additional $20,000 remained in the fund, and that sum has been invested in Government bonds, the interest on which, amounting to $1,000 each year, is paid over to the Children's Pavilion in connection with the sanitarium on the Qu'Appelle lakes in the province of Saskatchewan. So it will be seen from this example alone that we have not got very many Bolshevik tendencies in our organization.

speechtext: Nobody said you had.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
However, I will proceed to show that we at least attempted to do our part in that time of national crisis. The House may not remember, but the farmers of Western Canada remember very well the first action the Government took in dealing with the wheat of the West. They commandeered several million bushels in fact all of the standard grades of wheat then in store at the head of the Lakes. That wheat was paid for at a price $1.20 per bushel or which approximated two-thirds of the subsequent value of the wheat of that particular crop. The farmers made no particular outcry. They took the view that if it was absolutely necessary for the Government to pursue this course, well and good. But I will have a little more to say in connection with that if I get time to touch on the appointment of the proposed commission to inquire into the grain trade. Then further action was

taken subsequent to the appointment of the Board of Grain Supervisors. Reprenta-tives of the agriculturists of Western Canada were called into conference in the city of Winnipeg, and were asked to name a price that they thought would be fair for their wheat. That conference was held and a price was submitted. The minimum price was $1.50, the maximum price was $1.90, but a flat rate of $1.70 per bushel was considered preferable. As a matter of fact the actual price which the farmers of Western Canada were paid for their wheat under the Board of Grain Supervisors' recommendation was $2.20 per bushel. So you will see that even from a mercenary point of view they oifered to take fifty cents less for their wheat than what the Board of Grain Supervisors thought was a fair price.
Now, we will go on a little further and relate another instance. In that peaceful province of British Columbia where the people are so peaceful that they raised no objection to accepting all the products of the Western farmer, on which their is no duty, or to letting us, in turn, have the products of their orchards in the form of apples and other fruits, in connection with which there is a nice little profit to them by way of duty. Nevertheless, peaceful as they are, trouble started in Vancouver. It gradually filtered through until it got into Alberta; it went from there to Manitoba, and a serious situation was arising. At the height of that trouble the one man in Canada more particularly charged with the maintenance of law and order in Western Canada than any other man came to the executive of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Organization, which was in session in the city of Regina, and, in confidence, laid the whole matter before them and asked their hearty co-operation should the worst come to the worst. In fact, he told us he was convinced that the agriculturists of the West-our organization-was the only organization that he believed could successfully cope with the situation if the worst came to the worst. Now, this man, who knows the West, I believe, better than any other man, has no thought in his mind of any Bolshevists, seditionists, or anything else of that kind being in that organization. I am citing the case of the Saskatchewan organization simply because I am quite familiar with what was done there. But I have alsolutely no reason to believe, and do not believe that any different spirit existed in the other provincial organizations.
[Mr. Maharg.I

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the sitting was suspended, I was dwelling on the actions and attitude of the farmers of the West during the war period, and I want to go just a little further in that respect and say a word or two regarding their actions and contributions towards patriotic efforts during the war. The one great patriotic movement was, I believe, the Red Cross, and as regards provincial contributions towards the Red Cross, the province of Saskatchewan came second in the Dominion of Canada. A further contribution which I have in mind at the present time was that undertaken by Dr. Robertson on behalf of the relief of the devastated areas in France, and the contributions from Saskatchewan towards that fund took first place in the Dominion of Canada.
I come to the election of 1917, the crucial test of the entire Dominion as to just what action and attitude our people were going to take as regards the steps necessary for the successful prosecution of the war. What was the result in Saskatchewan? We have in that province sixteen constitu-

encies, and every one of them returned to this House a man instructed by the vote behind him to give his fullest support to everything necessary for the successful prosecution of the war. There were no vacancies whatever; the front was a solid one, and I think I can go further and say that in proportion to the vote taken, the majorities given in that province exceeded those given in any other province in Canada. I want to go just a little further to show what was the attitude of even this group, although it was referred to by the Prime Minister himself as not representing the farmers; indeed, his words as quoted, were that "the Crerar bunch did not represent the farmers." I am not going to argue the point as regards representing the farmers; evidently, the idea that he was trying to impress upon the people by his words was that we were more or less of a Bolshevik class. To disprove any such idea as that, I think I have in sight sufficient evidence, namely, the fact that 50 per cent of the total group of crossbenchers had sons in khaki during the war. That should prove that they are not too bad a kind of "Bolsheviks," even if some people should try to tag them with that name.
I come to the last feature, the final proof of their attitude and their sincerity. A couple of months or so ago at our convention in Saskatchewan, we unveiled an honour roll which, I think, for a provincial organization, cannot be exceeded in numbers by any other organization in Canada. We had a scroll in the neighourhood of four feet square, and it was covered with names as closely written by a pen as it was possible to write them. I have not the exact number, but I should say that it contained the names of close to one thousand men who had made the last and supreme sacrifice for their country. It seems, indeed, rather strange that, while the heart-wounds were still bleeding, the Prime Minister of this country should endeavour to hold up the fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters and others closely connected to them, as a group of people seeking an alliance with those who had not the best interest of our country at heart. Such action comes with very bad grace from him; further, it very ill becomes the Prime Minister of this country, or even anyone supporting his Government, to talk of "alliances." Most of us have a very vivid remembrance of an alliance made, I think, in 1911, by the
then Conservative party. We may be accused of a number of things, but I do not think anyone can accuse us of forming an alliance with those who were prepared to shoot holes in the Union Jack as did the Conservative party at that time.
The Prime Minister started on his Western tour, and he was met in Winnipeg by a committee representing citizens of the province of Saskatchewan. The primary cause of the appointment of this committee was the discontinuance of the Wheat Board. There was held in a town in Saskatchewan a public meeting to which representatives of the different boards of trade of the towns along the line, municipal officers and the public generally were invited, and were present at that meeting. A committee of three was appointed, one of them being the mayor of the town in which the meeting was held and the other two being representative farmers of the districts represented at that meeting. This committee proceeded to Winnipeg to endeavour to impress the Prime Minister with the importance of reestablishing the Wheat Board. They had an interview with him, and, amongst other things, he told them that the re-establishment of the Wheat Board had never been asked for, either inside the House of Commons or out of it. I think most hon. members who were here last year know very . well whether the re-establishment of the Wheat Board for another year was asked for or not. I will take the liberty of quoting from Hansard one or two things that I said myself in respect of the Wheat Board. I will be as brief as I can. Speaking on this subject in the House of Commons I said (Hansard 1920, p. 2636) :
Just so long as the pooling arrangement exists on the other side where our wheat is marketed, we must have a similar arrangement here; if Governments are going to buy, the Governments will have to sell.
So that the Prime Minister will not be of the opinion that he was not in the House at the time I was speaking, I will quote from my remarks in connection with the Wheat Board at the time when the enabling legislation was before the House, and the Prime Minister was in his seat just across the floor from where I was speaking. The gentleman who had preceded me had been trying to convince the House that the farmers themselves were not satisfied with the Wheat Board, and in reply to that, and speaking on behalf of the farmers, I said (Hansard 1920, p. 4131) :

We are perfectly satisfied, and we have been satisfied, with the method that had been adopted in handling the grain. I should have been pleased had the hon. gentleman furnished some proof in support of his statement. If it is not satisfactory to them (the farmers), why are they, as a body, from one end of the country to the other, asking that this enabling power be given .... At their convention they went further; they asked not only enabling legislation, but that the Government continue the Wheat Board for another year. The Canadian Council of Agriculture passed a similar resolution, and recently, through their executive they have again stated that as long as there is Governmental control of buying in European markets, we must have Governmental control in Canada in regard to disposing of our wheat.
There are several other quotations I could give. Here is one (Hansard 1920, p. 4133) :
We have been told that this is paternalism. In what way is it paternalism? We have been told that we are asking for protection. I have stated in this House more than once that we never asked for protection; never asked for a fixed price to the producers. We never asked for that at all; all that we are asking for now is: Since you have forced it on us; since you have disorganized conditions, and since the price was fixed for one purpose or two purposes at the utmost, you must continue this so long as conditions remain as they are in European countries.
There are several other passages I could quote from different pages, but my time is limited. I think I have quoted enough to show that the Wheat Board had been asked for both in this House and outside.
The Prime Minister on his tour visited several western cities. I heard him speak in the city of Moosejaw on his way west, and on his return he spoke in the city of Saskatoon. When speaking of the Wheat Board there after being persistently questioned as to why the Wheat Board was discontinued, and he is reported in the Saskatoon Star of November 13, 1920, as follows:
Stand on Wheat Board Question.
He reviewed the circumstances which led to the organization last year of the Wheat Board. Immediately after the passing of the Act he was attacked in the West on its account, and up to the time control was dropped the government had no word of commendation. In the House they were criticized by those supposed to represent peculiarly the farmers' views.
Now, I have absolutely no recollection, and I do not think Hansard will show, that one word of criticism was offered from those supposed specially to represent the farmers. The report continues:
This year the board was discontinued because careful investigations showed, he said, that further control was not in the public interest. He gave as reasons the absence of whes t control in the United States and the abseace of controled buying in Britain.

Now I state, and I defy contradiction, that at the time this enabling legislation was passed there was control in the buying of wheat in Great Britain-full government control. At the time the Minister made this statement in Saskatoon, exactly the same control existed, and it exists today. I think my right hon. friend, as First Minister of this country, should be a little more conversant with the facts before he undertakes to discredit the representatives of agriculture in Western Canada.
I want to say a word or two as to the results of the discontinuation of the Wheat Board. In the first place, at the time the market was thrown open, things were going along very nicely in Western Canada. We had in sight, as we supposed, good and substantial reasons for continued prosperity throughout the West. While we did not have a heavy yield, we had a fair average yield, and the price at that time was such as to allow a fair return to the producer over and above the cost of production. But immediately the market was thrown open, or shortly after, the prices started to slump, and the result was that business so far as the West was concerned became stagnant. For the sake of illustration, I might quote a conversation I had with a merchant in one of the towns. He told me how business had been going on, and to mark the contrast he instanced several articles, among them fruit. He said that previously to the slump in the price of grain his customers were taking out apples by the box, two or three boxes at a time, but, he said, within a week after the price of grain slumped, his customers instead of buying apples by the box, were buying twenty-five and fifty cents' worth at a time and taking them home in paper parcels. He said the same was true of sugar, tea, and in fact, all the staple commodities. His customers instead of taking supplies sufficient to last two or three months were taking just enough to keep them living from hand to mouth. It was only a matter of time for the stagnation to spread, and soon the wholesalers were hit, then the jobbers and manufacturers, and eventually the labourers when the manufacturers ceased to produce. I think you can trace the general stagnation in business very largely to the fact that the Wheat Board was discontinued.
We have heard a lot about the adverse balance of trade with the United States. In my opinion, the discontinuance of the Wheat Board will be responsible, before the entire crop is marketed, to the extent

of at least $100,000,000 of our adverse balance of trade with the United States.
I do not think I am exaggerating one bit when I say that the amount of grain purchased from Western Canada by the United States at the reduced price consequent on the discontinuance of the Wheat Board will amount to at least $100,000,000 before the season is over. That is one hundred million less will be paid by the United States on account of the drop in price.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend contend that the price of wheat is fixed by the Wheat Board, or was when the Wheat Board was in existence, or by the European market-the Liverpool market, as it is known.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to admit that it was the European market, and I think the European market would have been very satisfactory this year if the Wheat Board had been continued, but it was not. I might ask the hon. gentleman a question. Why is it that wheat went away down to $1.25 a bushel and then rose close to $2.00 a bushel? Had there been any change in the European conditions?
I am speaking of the price paid to the farmer at the initial point. Large quantities of our grain were sold for $1.25 at the initial point. Was there anything in the conditions of the European market or anywhere else to justify that. I might go a little further on that point. We all remember that the Winnipeg grain exchange representatives came here during last session and how the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) assisted them very materially and how caustic he was in his remarks about the Wheat Board. We have a vivid recollection of these things. They, the Winnipeg grain exchange representatives, told us that if the market were thrown open, we would get $4 or $5 a bushel for our wheat. Of course, we took that with a grain of salt, but we were prepared to continue the Wheat Board and let them secure the world's market for us. That price, however, never materialized.
Last fall, in order to be in some degree consistent with their previous statements, the Winnipeg Grain Exchange undertook to give reasons why the market had slumped, or why these prices had not been paid, and they had to take the prospective crops of the large producing countries, such as Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, and India, in order to make anything like the showing there was the previous year, and even then they were some 60,000,000 bushels short. But what was the actual
result? The market went away down while the harvests of these countries were merely in prospect, but when these crops were assured definitely and some of them harvested, that is, when the prospects had become a reality, the price started going up again until it reached 50 cents, 60 cents, and even 75 cents a bushel higher than it had been on the prospective results. Will my hon. friend say that the European market or world conditions had anything to do with that? I do not think so. We shall have to look elsewhere to find out why that happened. It happened simply because of the non-existence of the Wheat Board to steady the market in order that there might not be five, ten, or twenty thousand sellers to one or two buyers. No one was expecting big prices from the buyers, but we were expecting the stabilization of prices so that those who were unable to get their wheat out early would receive at least a fair proportion of return from the whole crop.
Now, another statement which the Prime Minister made in the West was that we never had the courage to move the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture as an amendment to the Budget. Well, he might have gone a little further, if he wanted to be fair, and told them that why we did not move it as an amendment for the reason, as this House knows very well, that a second amendment to the Budget is not permissible, owing to some old custom whose origin I do not know but which I think must have been conceived in medieval ages, for it is as far behind the times as anything can possibly be, and why it should continue I cannot say. Had it been in order, the platform would have been moved as an amendment. However, the next best thing was done and the Prime Minister must know that it was placed on Hansard by myself, I think in either the first or the second session I attended Parliament. It is on Hansard as public property and every one is free to scrutinize it to his heart's content, and the more that is done the better we shall like it, for we have nothing to fear.
I want to touch upon one or two remarks of the hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie), who, I am sorry, is not in his seat at the present moment. One of the strangest attitudes which any person could adopt was the critical view which the minister took of the speech of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). He criticised that hon. member rather severely because he ventured to take up some of the

time of the House in dealing with the fiscal policy of Great Britain. He thought he might have been better engaged discussing the fiscal policy of Canada. Well, I am not going to say that I disagree with him there, but there were certain conditions that led up to the hon. member for Red Deer discussing the fiscal policy of Britain. During the last session of Parliament no less a personage than the present Prime Minister himself spent considerable time discussing Britain's trade policy, and drawing attention to the results of that policy as he saw them; and, among other things, Great Britain was represented as a land of paupers and incompetents, all on account of its fiscal policy. Now, I wonder if there are any Canadians small enough to deny a gentleman, especially one who hails from the Old Land, the privilege of stating to this House the exact position of Great Britain in relation to pauperism and incompetency. I think this House will agree with me that the hon. member for Red Deer very ably answered the arguments of the Prime Minister and demonstrated to him that far from pauperism and incompetency being the condition of Great Britain, matters had gone in the other direction continuously for years and years and that a change had come very shortly after she had adopted the free trade policy.
I think it very unfair for any one to try to deny any member of this House the privilege of defending not only the land of his birth but the particular part of a country in which he might have resided at a particular time.
The Minister of Militia went a little further in his defence of the Government and said that the Government must be judged on its record since last July. That is all very well, but it should work both ways. While the Prime Minister was out West speaking to the electorate there, I think he took credit for almost everything that the Conservative party had accomplished since away back in 1878. Now, if he is going to take credit for the good things which the Government preceding his own Administration achieved, then, logically, he must assume responsibility for some of the other things that do not look so well. The member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) instanced the five by-elections that have taken place since July last, asserting that the Government had won three seats out of the five. I do not need to dwell on this point, as it has been touched on by some of the speakers who have addressed the House since the minister made his speech.

But there are one or two of the elections which we might refer to briefly, such, for instance, as the contests in East Elgin and West Peterborough. These seats were not selected by the Government; the other three, or at least two of them, were, and, Sir, I think we are safe in concluding that the Yale seat was very carefully considered before it was thrown open. Had there been any fear so far as that constituency is concerned, I think the present representative would have been expounding the gospel of protection through the columns of his paper rather than from a place on the floor of this House. But, Mr. Speaker, they deemed it a perfectly safe seat, and I will ay that we are very glad indeed to have the present representative (Mr. Mc-Kelvie) with us. Now, what about West Peterborough? I do not know whether it is true or not, but word has trickled through to Western Canada that there was some promise or other in connection with a dam that was to be built there. I have not heard the rumour contradicted, and I take it for granted that there must have been something to substantiate it. Well, dams are, of course, supposed to be built to stop flows. It is quite evident that that dam did not stop the flow of voter's in West Peterborough. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I think that instead of damming the flow of votes it had the result of damning the Government to a certain extent, and I think it would have been wise on the part of the Government to have been more circumspect in their promises. Of course, whether the dam will be built remains to be seen.
Now, I come to another part of the speech of the Minister of Militia, a part which I think was uncalled for. I think that I can prove to this House before I conclude that instead of the United Grain Growers' Company being the chief sinner there are others equally as bad, although their professions would lead you to think that they were almost sprouting wings so far as this matter is concerned. The hon. gentleman maintained that the United Grain Growers' Company were dealing solely, or practically so, in American implements. Reasons were given a year ago by myself on the floor of the House why farmers' companies were dealing in American implements, the prime reason being that the Canadian manufacturers absolutely refused to sell any kind of implement to the Farmers' Co-operative Companies. Now, Sir, I know whereof I speak, for about fifteen or sixteen years ago we formed a Co-operative Farmers'

Company locally in our own district. Among other things we decided that we would handle the large implements and carload requirements of the district, and we undertook to see if we could secure implements. Sir, we could not obtain even a wheelbarrow or a hand cultivator, let alone the big implements for the farm. We had to go to the United States to get every single one of them.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They would not even sell to the returned soldiers.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Sir, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) a few nights ago illustrated what the Drury Government were doing in the purchase of their graders. He said they were using American road graders. I venture to make the assertion that it is quite possible the same principle extended even to the matter of supplying a Farmers government with the necessary implements for taking care of the roads. It is just possible something of the same spirit may have been manifested there; and it would be well if the member for Brantford would look into the question. It might also be well for him to inquire into the matter as regards previous governments. Are we to understand that the Whitney government never had occasion to use a road grading machine during their term of office? Or is it a fact that the Canadian machine was of such a character that it would not do the work, and when a progressive government came in they had to obtain a grader of a suitable type? There are several features in connection with this matter that are well worth looking into.
Now, while the hon. member for Brantford is in my mind I want to thank him for the kind compliment he paid to our little Group here.
