speechtext:
You left out the word
" and ".

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The National Liberal and Conservative party. Let us take the national part of the name first. The National party is a party that deserves well at the hands of the Government. Had it not been for the National party in 1911 the Government would not be in their places to-day. It was Mr. Bourassa who acted as Cyrano de Bergerac to the then leader of the Opposition, and got him into power. He reached My Lady's Chamber with the assistance of Mr. Bourassa, and no person else, and we know how Mr. Bourassa was treated a few weeks afterwards. Still, it appears the Government have some kindly feelings for their old friend, and when they came to give the child a name, he was given for a first name "National," in remembrance of the kindly act of Mr. Bourassa and his National followers. Then we have the name "Liberal." What does that mean? Is it worth calling a party by a name simply to salve the conscience of three hon. gentlemen who have left this side of the House and crossed to the other? I do not think it is. It is the custom in our synagogue, Mr. Speaker, to call our children after the names of our dead relatives. These three Liberals certainly are dead ones, and my friends on the other side have evidently adopted some of our Jewish customs. I am glad they are doing so, and I hope before I am here very much longer they will follow others. Then comes the word "Conservative." I suppose they are entitled to call themselves the Conservative party, because after all these Nationalists and these Liberals are really Conservatives. They have been swallowed by the Conservative party. They have "returned from their ride with the lady inside and the smile

on the face of the tiger." A motto which I would suggest to the Government would be the one Mr. Vanderbilt used on one occasion when he was asked "What will the public say?" He replied "The public be hanged." That is a motto which I suggest should be adopted by this new Government. A famous French general in the Crimean War, I think it was Marshal MacMahon, in a communique to headquarters stated that he had taken the Malakoff redoubt. He explained the situation in a very few words, "J'y suis, j'y reste"-"I am here, and I intend to remain here." That is good tactics in war, Mr. Speaker, and I suppose, this being a war government, they feel they can righteously adopt tactics of that kind and say "J'y suis, j'y reste." '
Evil communications corrupt good manners. The Conservative party is not the Conservative party it was before it became contaminated by these elements. I would ask my hon. friends on the other side if they have Mr. R. B. Bennett's opinion of them. He is a gentleman who practically used to sleep with the former Prime Minister, who could not go anywhere without Mr. Bennett. Whether he was afraid to leave him in Canada when he went abroad I do not know, but Mr. Bennett used to travel with the Prime Minister when he went abroad, and he was the recipient of many favours from the Conservative party. It would be interesting to know what Mr. Bennett's views on this party are, and also those of the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, the former Minister of Militia, (Sir Sam Hughes). It would also be interesting to know what the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) thinks of this once great party. A story is told of a student of zoology who was asked by the professor of his college to define what a lobster was. He said: "A lobster is a fish, is red in colour, and walks backwards." The professor said: "That definition is perfect except for the fact that the lobster is not a fish, is not red in colour, and does not walk backwards"; and it might be said adopting the student's definition with a slight variation that this Government is the greatest lobster we have ever had in this country.
I do not know why it is that the Government was not satisfied to revert to the old name of "Conservative" when the so-called "Union" label was discarded from the title of the present party. The Conservative party stood for a great deal in this country. It was the party of Sir John A Macdonald, and my hon. friend the 
Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) was instrumental in forming that party into an important fighting force in Canada. Why is it that they have cast aside that name and now seek something which they think is just as good? The new name indicates the hybrid origin of this Government; but like everything hybrid, I am afraid it is not destined to come to much. A definition was giver recently of this National Liberal Conservative party, in which it was likened to tht mule, in that it had no pride of ancestrj and no hope of posterity. Our chief objec tion to this Government is that it was formed during war time and consequently is saturated with the war spirit; and you never can do anything in the matter of re-establishment on a civil basis unless you get rid of the war spirit and everything it implies. And I propose to show in the few minutes at my disposal that this war spirit still permeates and impregnates in its entirety every Department of the Government. I have only to refer to the Department of Marine, which is presided over by my good friend the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Ballan-tyne). In passing, I may say that I am glad to think that a member from the city of Montreal should be appointed to this high and important office. This department started building ships during the war. It may have been necessary that we should have ships- during the war. No one could tell how long the war would last; it was practically an impossibility to predict its duration; and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and Naval Service cast about him to see that we should have as many ships as possible for the purposes of the war. But the hon. gentleman has evidently forgotten that the war is over, because he is still going on with the building of ships, or at any rate is completing ships which were started after the war. Is not that an indication of the war spirit which permeates the Department of Marine? We want these ships no more than a man wants a third leg; they are useless to us. Shipping in every part of the world is at a standstill. I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to a couple of telegraphic despatches which appeared in the newspapers only a few weeks ago touching the situation with regard to ships throughout the world. I shall quote from the Montreal Star, a newspaper by no means hostile to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Rotterdam, January 7.-Forty-nine ocean steamers, mostly Dutch, are laid up at the present time at Rotterdam because of lack of

cargoes and the low freight rates according to Burgomaster Zimmerman. He also announces that while more ships entered Rotterdam last year than previously the actual tonnage was only 58 per cent of that of 1913.
Side by side, in a parallel column, I find the following:
Vancouver, January 7.

The keels of two new Government steamers, the Canadian "Transporter" and the Canadian "Trader" were laid at the Coughlan shipyards here yesterday. Seven hundred men are engaged in the yards.
Then on January 7th, the same day-
I am still quoting from the Montreal Star 

there appears this item:
Prince Rupert, January 7.-A meeting of the creditors of the Prince Rupert Dry Docks and Shipbuilding Company was held hero yesterday. W. E. Hodges, who presided, read a statement showing approximate total liabilities exceeding $800,000.
A few weeks earlier in the newspapers, the following appeared:
The Canadian Engineer reports that the Mexican Government has placed orders with the Prince Rupert Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company for thirty-seven vessels. A form of the proposed contract is now before the Marine Department, Ottawa, for approval.
How is it possible, if this contract for 37 vessels was placed with the Prince Rupert Dry Dock Company in November, that in January this company should have gone into liquidation? That is something which I cannot understand, unless it he that when the creditors of the Prince Rupert Company found that Mexico was seeking to buy 37 vessels from Canada they felt it was high time to close up the works. This only goes to show-and I could cite numerous instances-the moribund condition of shipping and shipbuilding throughout the whole world. And yet the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has committed us to nearly $100,000,000 in the matter of the building of ships. We are, and have been for some time, groaning under the railway incumhus, hut the Minister of Marine and Fisheries evidently is not aware of the fact, because, notwithstanding that burden, he is still putting on our shoulders a policy that will mean to this country, before the eyes of the Government are opened to the situation, a loss not of $100,000,000 but perhaps of $200,000,000. How long are the Canadian people going to stand this? Are we not quite right in demanding an immediate election in order to test the feeling of the people as to whether they want shipbuilding started, when the country is almost on the verge of bankruptcy? Now, that is an indication of
the war spirit which, as I have said, still permeates the members of the Government.
May I take another Department, about which I know something, the Immigration Department? We have on the statute books and in Orders in Council certain laws respecting immigration, which are the most extraordinary and grotesque that it is possible to imagine sane people would enact. I make this statement advisedly, and shall show you what some of these laws are. For instance, we have an Order in Council respecting immigration which declares that any immigrant who wishes to come to this country must come direct from the country of his birth, be it the Balkans, be it Ukrainia, be it Poland, or be it any of the countries of Central Europe. If he comes direct from the country of his birth he will be permitted, under certain conditions, to land in this country; but should that man and his family have left the country of his birth and gone to England and have lived in England say for fifteen or twenty years, brought up his family there under English customs, and taught them English ideals and the language of the country-if that man attempted to land in Canada with his wife and family he would be debarred from entering the Dominion. Now, I am not saying this as a jest, Mr. Speaker. It is not something from a libretto of Gilbert and Sullivan, or something from Alice in Wonderland-it is an Order in Council of the Department of Immigration. Now here is another thing:
No person will be permitted to land in this country unless he is possessed of $250 in cash on his person at the time he presents himself for examination before the Immigration officer at the port of entry.
He must have in his possession $250 so that he can keep himself alive until he obtains works. But if the man is coming to relatives who are worth say half a million of dollars and who are prepared to give bonds to the Government that he will not become a public charge it is not sufficient. This man may use his $250 for living expenses and he may then become a public charge but that is of no consequence to the Government. If he lands with $250 that is sufficient; but no matter what bonds another person is prepared to give, or what bonds his relatives are prepared to give he is not permitted to land without $250.
Now there is another rule. In times when there is little work people are permitted to

Yes. Why is that department not represented by a minister in this House? I am aware that the Government is in such a position that they dare not open any constituencies, and that is one of the reasons, we say, why we ought to have a general election and put affairs on a proper basis. We cannot accommodate this Government very much longer. We are willing to do what we can, but in the name of public decency we owe it to ourselves to see that the Government is dug out of its hole and driven to the country.
The Department of Militia is another department that indicates the permeation of the war spirit. We have a new Minister of Militia who is not a military man, he is not a Son of Mars. The only "fighting" he ever does is to make a "fighting" speech in the House, and he follows that rule of fighting in which discretion is the better part of valour, because he finds it is well to fight and run away so he may live to fight another day. This gentleman, in order to show that he was in sympathy with the war spirit, promptly jumped our expenditure in the Militia Department from something like $8,000,000, which I think it was before the war, to about $20,000,000, if we include the Northwest Mounted Police.
Here we have the League of Nations, and we have my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the former President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) going across the Atlantic ocean to settle all the ills to which flesh is heir-to bring peace into the world and not a sword. But on the other hand, we have the Minister of Militia and Defence, who is left at home, jumping the estimates from $8,000,000 to $20,000,000. I understand that our share of the cost of the League of Nations is about $200,000 a year. Does my right hon. friend not think that it would be better for us'to spend $20,000,000 towards the upkeep

of the League of Nations and $100,000 or $200,000 for our militia? Perhaps it would do more good.
I could go on and show how in every branch of the Government service we have the war spirit. The Naturalization Act, the Franchise Act, and other Acts which we passed last session had the war spirit breathed into them.
But I find that I have already taken up more time than I intended, and I shall resume my seat in a moment or two. Before doing so, however, I should like to say a word or two about the threatened Royal Commission to investigate the grain trade. I know nothing about the grain trade, I cannot talk in terms of wheat, and it goes against the grain for me to talk about it. But I was rather astonished to find that this important question should have been relegated to the gentlemen who occupy seats in the rear of this chamber. It came on rather suddenly. One day the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) threatened the Agrarian group with a Royal Commission of inquiry into the grain trade; next day another hon. gentleman took it up; next day still another hon. gentleman took it up; and finally all along the line we found a wonderful similarity in the addresses of these hon. gentlemen, until one could not but conclude that some person higher in authority than these gentlemen was giving them their cue; they spoke in such parrot tones that one might very well come to the conclusion that they were under the tuition of the professor of par-rotology in the Government; but of course that is one of the mysteries into which we are not permitted to delve. I am inclined to think that if a Royal Commission is to be appointed the gentlemen from the Agrarian group will be able to give a pretty good account of themselves. They look to me as rather decent, honourable and respectable citizens.

speechtext:
If they are not, so much the worse for them. It is a matter with which we on this side of the House are not concerned. But, as I said before, I believe they are well able to take care of themselves.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the talk of conciliation towards the province of Quebec? I come from that province. I represent a division which is largely French Canadian, and I think I understand the mentality of those people. They were sufficiently tolerant and wide in their

views to elect me to be their representative in this House-an example which I have yet to see from other parts of the Dominion. From time to time we read in the government press articles of a conciliatory character with regard to Quebec. We are told that the people of that province are safe, that they are sane, that they are progressive, that they are conservative and that they have all the virtues which it is possible for a race to possess. A great change has come over this people since 1917, evidently. But, Sir, do you think that the province of Quebec is going to be won by mere lip service such as is indulged in by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House? When you find positions to which French-speaking Canadians are rightly entitled taken from them and given to English-speaking Canadians, when you find them ignored in the filling of public appointments, do you think those people have for the rest of the country, and particularly for the Government, those "Christian" feelings which you would like to inculcate in their breasts? Let me take, for instance, the appointment recently to the International Joint Commission. One of the three positions occupied by representatives of this country had been held by a French Canadian ever since the Commission was established, the first gentleman appointed being Mr. Aime Geoffrion, of Montreal, the second hon. Thomas Chase-Casgrain, and the third hon. P. B. Mi-gnault, who is now a judge of the Supreme Court. The vacancy caused by his accepting a judgeship was filled by this Government appointing Sir William Hearst. A poor Tory politician out of a job-a discredited Tory politician with nothing to do, is appointed as French representative on the International Joint Commission. That is a sample of the attempt at the conciliation of Quebec. Is it at all surprising, Mr. Speaker, when hon. gentlemen on the other side invite Quebec to give them support, that, as my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) said, the poor fish from St. Hyacinthe is the only one that they landed.
Then, let me take the case of the appointment to the Senate last year of a gentleman to take the place of the late Senator Landry. Senator Landry typified a certain element who are very strong in their views with regard to certain questions-the Catholic school question particularly. He was a gentleman of very high intellect and of considerable ability. He died in due course of time and was

gathered unto his fathers, and the French Canadian who took his place was a gentleman named Lome C. Webster. Then, there was the case of the ill-fated Board of Commerce, which was born with the seeds of death in it. No French Canadian was appointed to that Board; perhaps that is why it died so early, because French Canadians are long-lived people. That ought to be a lesson to my hon. friends on the other side; it should cause them to see to it that they appoint to positions of that sort men who are noted for vitality. The failure of the Government to appoint a French Canadian on the Board of Commerce was keenly resented throughout the whole province of Quebec. I could go on naming other instances in which traditions have been broken down by this Government-traditions which had been consecrated by fifty years of custom. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite ask us of the province of Quebec to come in, and lend them a hand when they are in dire straits. It is expecting too much of flesh and blood to ask Quebec to do anything for this Government under the circumstances, and so long as such treatment is meted out to them, just so long shall we have on this side a solid block from that province opposing the Government tooth and nail, until we have them on the run-which I think, Mr. Speaker, we have succeeded in doing at last. The Government, Mr. Speaker, is tottering to its fall. No power on earth can now save it; it is moribund. It is said that of the dead we should say nothing but good. All I can say of the Government is, in the words of Shakespeare:
Vex not his ghost; O, let him pass; he hates him,
That would upon the rack of this tough world Stietch him out longer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising at so late a period to make a few observations in this debate, I am sure it will not b6 possible for me to offer much that is new. However, I feel it my duty to occupy a few moments of the time of the House before the vote is finally recorded.
Before proceeding, let me offer my congratulations to the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) who has since last session been elevated to the high position of Prime Minister of this country. I do not hesitate for one moment in saying that as a new member I have admired the great efforts he put forth during the period of the war in his desire to serve our country
and the Empire. Since assuming the high office he now holds, his courage and resourcefulness have been greatly admired, even by those who do not agree with his policies or with the pretensions of the multi-named party which he leads.
Lest I should be accused of violating a time-honoured custom in this debate, allow me, Mr. Speaker, to extend to the mover (Mr. Mclssac) and the seconder (Mr. MacKelvie) of this motion, my felicitations. I would be remiss in my duty if I did not extend my congratulations also in another direction. Since this Parliament last met an incident has occured which is of far reaching national importance:	I refer to the fact that the hon.
member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has been selected by a very large portion of the people of this country as leader of the new National Progressive Party. In my opinion their selection of a leader has been a wise one, for in the member for Marquette we have a man of very wide business experience in Canada, a man who has risen from the ranks of the people, who is thoroughly conversant with their problems through knowledge gained from personal experience, and, most important of all, a man whose integrity and honesty of purpose is beyond reproach.
Lest I should forget it later, I wish to express my appreciation of the kind references made in regard to this group by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. (Mr. Jacobs) :	I trust that we shall not disappoint him. I merely wish to thank him for his kind words.
I shall not attempt to follow along the by-roads into which this debate has led us; I will endeavour to confine myself for the most part to one or two items of national importance. The country has been very considerably agitated by the introduction into the House of Representatives and Senate of the United States of a measure which, in its effect, aims at the vitals of one of our chief industries. I refer to the Fordney Bill. Too much importance cannot be placed upon the effect that that legislation may have upon the agricultural industry of this country should it become law. I am informed that three quarters of the wheat exported from this country last fall found its way into the United States. Had a measure been in force such as is contemplated in the Fordney Bill it is my opinion that the result would have created a financial panic in a great portion of this country. The effect upon the grain-growing industry would have been disastrous; it would have shut out prac-

tically the only market we had for our grain. The surprising feature of this situation, Sir, is that during the time this most important legislation was before Congress, Canada, which, we are told, has assumed the status of nationhood-and I sincerely hope it is true-was without official representation in that country. Not only that, but even the good offices of the British Ambassador were not available owing to his absence overseas. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has informed the House that it has been decided to appoint an ambassador at Washington, but the delay is in the selection of a man suitable for the position. It did not seem very difficult to secure suitable men to represent us at the Peace Congress and at the Assembly of the League of Nations at Geneva; surely it dannot be so difficult to find a suitable representative to go to Washington to protect our interests there.
I am quite sure it is not generally known in the country to the south of us that Canada is her second best customer. But that condition is easily understood when we realize that our Canadian interests have not been properly represented in the United States and that therefore the importance of the Canadian market is not appreciated.
I would urge upon the Government the necessity of the immediate appointment of a capable ambassador at Washington. Further delay may mean the placing of agriculture and of the myriad industries that depend upon it in a very precarious condition, which otherwise could in all probability be avoided. We should also have trade representatives in all the large cities of the United States.
The Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie), in his speech the other day, told us that there were two ways in correcting the adverse trade balance: one was to buy less from the United States and the other was to sell more. The latter process appeals to me very strongly. Surely such trade representatives would be of inestimable value in procuring outlets for manufactured goods of Canadian origin. It must be a source of great inspiration to Canadian manufacturers to look to the south and see the great market that exists there for their goods. There is nothing wrong with the goods they manufacture; those goods will compete favourably with any they may meet on the world's markets. What our manufacturers need is a broader vision and, as has been so well expressed by the hon. leader of this party (Mr. Cre-
rar), courage to go out and fight the commercial battle with those who, in most cases, are not any better armed than they. These trade representatives would be of great assistance in guiding their efforts and would act as a searchlight to guide them in securing new outlets for their goods.
There is another matter to which I should like to direct attention. During the period last fall when grain was being shipped to the market from the farmers in western Canada, very great difficulty was experienced in obtaining cars, more particularly along the lines now operated by the Canadian National system. At practically every shipping point along the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is now under the control of the Canadian National system, and which runs through the constituency which I have the honour to represent, grain buyers were instructed to purchase only one car of grain and no more until that car had been finally disposed of. The grain was taken into the elevator for storage, but no purchases could he made beyond the limitation I have mentioned. The result was that in a very short time the elevators were filled, and the farmer who needed money to meet his financial obligations found himself in a position where he had the value in grain to meet those obligations, but he could not find any market for it. In the meantime, the market value of wheat was going down at an alarming rate, and the loss sustained by those men was very serious. The cause of this condition seems to have been the great shortage on the Canadian National system of cars suitable for shipping grain. In many districts that I visited last fall, the farmers were hauling their grain many miles beyond Grand Trunk Pacific points in order to get to the Canadian Pacific where cars were available.
I am pointing this out more to acquaint the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) with the facts, than for the sake of offering criticism, in the hope that this condition may be remedied before another crop is placed on the market.
Besides the serious loss that has been suffered by the farmers on account of the shortage of grain cars on the Canadian National system, there is another important feature. A very substantial increase in freight rates was granted to the railway companies last year, but owing to the shortage of cars in the early part of the wheat shipping season, our National system was not in a position to take full

advantage of this increase. As a result, we have been called upon to pay a greatly increased freight rate, largely to the Canadian Pacific railway, and on top of that, we shall have to get down into our pockets and pay the deficit on the Canadian National system, thus paying twice,, whereas, had there been sufficient cars to earn the additional revenue mentioned, we would have had to pay only once, to some degree at least.
I now come to a subject which, up to a day or two ago, seemed to be a rather dangerous one for a member sitting in this group to approach. I refer to the Canada Wheat Board. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been patting themselves on the back for the success of the Wheat Board, and they have tried to make it appear that every member in this group was diametrically opposed to it. That is not the fact, as I am sure they are convinced now after the proofs that have been placed on Hansard by previous speakers. Every member of this group was in favour of the continuance of the Wheat Board for another year, and if my hon. friends opposite pat themselves on the back because of the success of the board, what have they to say about its discontinuance? Nothing. As soon as it was seen in the West that the board was a success and a great boon to the farmers, we asked for its continuance for another year; but the Government, supported by those hon. gentlemen said: "No; we will not allow it to continue," this, notwithstanding the fact that the same or practically the same system of buying by Government commission, axisted in 1920 as existed in 1919. Even in the statement read by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Blair), there is no proof that Mr. H. W. Woods, President of the United Farmers of Alberta, was opposed to the Wheat Board if it were kept clear of politics. Mr. Woods, at the Moosejaw convention of the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, stated that, in his opinion, if the Canada Wheat Board had been continued for another year, that is the year 1920, it would have saved the farmers of western Canada at least $50,000,000. That is the statement also made by the hon. member for Battle River. I do not know whether he obtained his statistics from Mr. Woods or not. I see he shakes his head, but he will agree with Mr. Woods on that one point at least. I well remember in the debate which took place upon the Wheat Board last year, that the hon. leader of this party hesitated to commit himself to the endorsation of the Canada Wheat Board as a permanent in-33
stitution, but he made a strong plea for its continuance during 1920 until selling conditions became more normal. Compare his attitude with that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), and what do we find? The leader of this party asked for the continuation of the Board for another year; but the Minister of Trade and Commerce absolutely refused, no doubt on the strength of representations made to him by parties interested in the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and in other lines of com* mercial endeavour, who draw their incomes from the grain produced on the farm on its way to the ultimate consumer.
The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) appears to have made a great discovery. In his speech the other day, amid the tremendous applause of those who sit around him, more particularly those from Western Canada, be announced that there were abuses in the grain trade in Western Canada. Well, that was not at all surprising to those sitting in this group, and I would remind the hon. gentleman that in the very first remarks I made in this House on the Budget of 1918,
I drew the attention of the Government to that very fact. It is now suggested, with a blare of trumpets, that a commission is to be appointed to investigate the grain trade in Western Canada, I have this to say to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders), who seems to be heading this agitation on the Government side and also to the Government: that if this Commission is appointed, and if it is composed of practical men capable of investigating the grain trade, men of integrity, men free from political influence, it will have my entire support; but I would remind the hon. member for Macdonald and the Government, that the people of this country are becoming somewhat tired of the continual procession of commissions that have been appointed since 1917 and before, and which have professed a very great deal, but, in the estimation of the people have accomplished very little. The only real accomplishment, Mr. Speaker, that I can call to mind has been from a commission which is not precisely a Government commission; I refer to the Board of Railway Commissioners. They have succeeded in raising the freight rates. I do not think under the circumstances that hon. gentlemen sitting in this group can be accused of being overly suspicious if they suggest that the appointment of this commission to investigate the grain trade in Western Canada is being



urged more for political purposes than for any real good that may come to the farmers as a result of its investigations.
The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), in what seemed to me to he a very able address this afternoon, pointed out a very patent fact, and I think the same fact was pointed out by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), namely, that the commission under whose jurisdiction the grain trade of Western Canada is at the present time, is a Government commission entirely 1 under the control of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). Therefore, if this new commission finds anything wrong with the grain trade, I fear that the censure will fall on the heads of hon. gentlemen opposite.
A few days ago we had a speech from the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rou-ville (Mr. Gauthier). I am sure we all thoroughly enjoyed that speech as an oratorical effort. With regard to the main portion of his speech I have nothing to say, because it had to do with what is more or less a family quarrel in the official Opposition party; but I find on page 86 of Hansard a reference which he made to so-called foreign-born living in Western Canada, and I think it is my duty as a representative of some of those foreign-born, and as a citizen of Western Canada, to draw attention to the hon. gentleman's remarks. He said:
Sir, I have no objection to the people of the West; none at all. I respect them. They came her to draw from the soil the wealth which Providence has stored there for those who are sturdy enough to work and obtain it. I have no objection to their helping us to develop the country. But, Mr. Speaker, figures are figures, and I have before me figures that show that west of the Great Lakes 63 per cent of the population are not British born. This is not my fault, but it is a fact. Am I going to preach an alliance with those who have not the same ideals as we have and who do not love our institutions? No, Sir, I cannot do that; for one, I will not consent to it. Everyone, of course, is at liberty to choose his own ally.
I am choosing mine, and I shall try to make my people see as I do in this matter.
Taking into consideration the fact that from year to year the various governments have spent a considerable amount of the people's money in an effort to bring immigration to this country, and have been very successful in obtaining a great number of foreign-born settlers in Western Canada, I think such references are unfortunate, to say the least. We in Western Canada fully realize that before we can have a thoroughly united people, these

people of foreign birth must be assimilated into our population, and must be taught our Canadian ideals. I have travelled among these people to whom my hon. friend makes reference, and from my own personal experience I wish to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I have none of his apprehension. I would remind him of the fact that a great many of these so-called foreign-born have come into this country to escape oppression in their native land, and thoroughly appreciate the freedom and the privileges which they enjoy in Canada, and they are true and loyal to our institutions.
I wondered when I heard the hon. gentleman's remarks if he referred to the American-born in Western Canada. We have thousands and thousands of Ameri can-born citizens in Western Canada, anc we have no finer settlers there. These people have practically the same ideals that we have. They are industrious and they are making splendid citizens of this country. I call to mind an instance which will go to prove the statement that these people are rapidly becoming true Canadian citizens. A few years ago a family came to Western Canada from the State of Indiana. There was a young girl in that family. She completed her education in the province of Saskatchewan, and later was employed as a school teacher in the district in which I reside. I have had occasion to go many times to that school house. I have taken a particular interest in it, as I do in most of the schools in my constituency, and I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no school teacher in this country who is more zealous in teaching the love of Canada and true Canadian ideals to her pupils than that little girl from Indiana.
There comes to my mind another instance. Another family came from the United States to Saskatchewan. The head of this family had been at one time President of the Senate in one of the States of the American Union. He brought with him two sons. The father took up a considerable tract of land, and is one of the largest farmers in the district where he resides. He is a respected citizen, a man who takes a keen interest in all our local institutions. He is keenly interested in all the political affairs of this country, and has given every evidence of loyalty to our institutions. His sons publish a weekly paper in a town in Saskatchewan. I am a subscriber to that little country paper, and I want to say that in its editorial columns I have read just as strong a defence of Canadian and

British institutions as I ever read in any periodical published anywhere in Canada by men who are British or Canadian-born.
I happened to come across one of these editorials to-day, and I shall endeavour to read without mentioning the names which appear in it. I merely quote this article to show the class of editorials that appear in this paper, published by sons of a man president of the Senate in a certain state in the American Union and who has come to Canada and settled here. The occasion that brought forth this editorial was the dedication of a community hall in the town where these people reside. A certain gentleman was asked to make an address at the meeting and he made the statement that he found himself in a district in which the majority were of foreign origin. A letter was published later in this paper commenting on the address of this gentleman and the editorial comment was as follows:
But there is one reference in Mr. Griffin's letter that the Despatch takes exception to, and
that is where he states that Mr 

 found
himself in the midst of a foreign majority.
Mr. 
was not in any such place at the hall
He was visiting a Canadian town and was surrounded by Canadians. And we venture the opinion that Mr. 
 knows that he could
travel the length of Great Britain and her possessions and nowhere would he find a community living more in harmony, more loyal to Canadian institutions, or more proud of British freedom. The fact that we are not natives is, strictly speaking, something that we all have in common. But our people are naturalized in law and in heart and would resent by an overwhelming majority at the poll any candidate who sought to curry favour by introducing sectionalism.
That is the sentiment expressed by some of the so-called foreign born. It has often occurred to me, Mr. Speaker, that the difficulty we encounter in Western Canada in assimilating the foreign-born, lies not with those people themselves but with our own Canadian-born and British-born subjects. It appears to me that what we need is a broader and stronger Canadian national spirit. When you find men who are always vaunting their birth-place and proclaiming from the house-tops the fact that they are descended from fathers born in England, Scotland, or Ireland, as the case may be-when you find Canadian-born men walking around and calling themselves Englishmen, Scotchmen and Irishmen, what can you expect those who come from Germany to do? Why, the German-born settler in western Canada will say " I am German;" and why should he not? What we want in this country, Mr. Speaker, is more
33i
people who will boldly declare, when asked concerning their nationality, that they are Canadians.
In connection with this subject I should like to cite a personal incident that occurred when the last census was being taken in Canada. It may be of interest to those who have charge of the present work in connection with the forthcoming census. I was in the town of Unity, Saskatchewan, when the Census Commissioner came and requested the necessary information in order to compile his statistics. We came to the point of nationality and the commissioner asked me, of course, what my nationality was. I told him I was Canadian. "Yes," he said, "I understand that; we are all Canadians. But you must be descended from people of extraneous origin. " Well," I replied, " I am not descended from any other nationality at all; I am just a Canadian." " What was your father's nationality?"-he then demanded. I said: " My father is a Canadian." The next question was:	"Was he born in Canada?"
I said "yes.u " Well then," he said becoming rather annoyed, " Where was your grandfather born?" I replied:	"He was
born in Canada and you may go back one of two generations more and I will give you the same answer." Then he said: " Well, we have no column in this return for Canadian nationality." And my answer was: " If I am not a Canadian, I am nothing, and you may call me a Negro or a Chinaman or anything else you choose. My answer is simply, I am a Canadian."

Now, Mr. Speaker, I regret very much having occupied so much time, but I desire for a moment to refer to a paragraph in the speech delivered the other day by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). I had not the privilege of hearing the hon. gentleman's speech, but on looking over the report of his address in Hansard, I find that it was more or less an attack of a rather violent nature against this party and particularly against our leader (Mr. Crerar). I should like to read one paragraph of the hon. gentleman's speech. On page 306 of Hansard, the hon. member for East Algoma is reported as follows:
What has been the attiude of the hon. member for Marquette, their leader, towards the farmers of this country? The hon. gentleman was Minister of Agriculture for at least a year and a half at a period when every Government in Canada, provincial and federal, backed by the whole body of public opinion, was bending

its energies to increase production, when the Dominion Treasury one might say, was wide open for the hon. gentleman to use its funds in any way that would stimulate our agricultural production. Can he point to one single Act that passed through this House at his suggestion to improve the condition of our farmers? Not one single Act or suggestion.
We see expressed in that paragraph the opinion of the hon. member for East Al-goma of the hon. leader of this party. Without further comment, let me read the opinion of another hon. gentleman of this House, the right hon. member for Kings, Nova Scotia, (Sir Robert Borden), the late Prime Minister, of whom the leader of this party was at one time a colleague. On June 4th 1919, on the occasion of the resignation of the hon. member for Marquette, the right hon. member for Kings wrote as follows:
My dear Mr. Crerar, I have received with deep and unfeigned regret your resignation as a member of the Government but I entirely appreciate and respect the sincerity of the convictions which have impelled you to take that course. It will be my immediate duty to acquaint His Excellency the Governor General with your decision and to request his authority for the acceptance of your resignation. During the period of nearly two years in which you have been one of my colleagues your high sense of public duty, your fine ability and indefatigable energy have made your service to the country especially valuable. Within that period problems of an exceptionally difficult character have continually presented themselves, and I am most grateful to you, and to all my colleagues for the loyal assistance and earnest effort which on all such occasions have been of invaluable assistance to me in the consideration of such questions.
My association with you as one of my colleagues will always be to me a happy memory and I know that I may express this to you on behalf of all the members of the Government.
I am very grateful for your kind words in respect to my own part in public affairs since it has been my privilege to have you as one of my colleagues.
With every good wish Believe me,
Dear Mr. Crerar,
Yours faithfully,

speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have here the opinion of two members of the House with respect to the leader of the Progressive party. The first is the opinion of the member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). It is quite possible that he may hold his opinion in higher esteem than he does that of the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) but I reserve the right to use my own judgment in the matter, and for my pa.rt I prefer the judgment of the former leader of the Government.
I would like to refer for a moment to the speech delivered a short time ago by

the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie). It will be remembered that the Minister of Militia followed the hon. member for Red Deer in this debate. The remarks of the Minister of Militia in reference to the splendid speech delivered by the hon. member for Red Deer were very scant indeed. He had no answer to make to the criticisms offered by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clark) and I think there was a very good reason for it-he could not find any arguments against them. He brushed aside the splendid effort, the magnificent speech of the hon. member for Red Deer, with the statement that this country was not very much interested in British politics, that it was much more concerned with Canadian politics. Well, we all agree with that statement, but did the minister not realize that in speaking as he did he was passing censure upon the Prime Minister. Practically the whole of the recent speech of the hon. member for Red Deer was a reply to a speech delivered by the Prime Minister at the last session of Parliament, when the latter made a comparison between British and Canadian politics and drew his own inference therefrom, and in the opinion of a good many, the premier's conclusions were not very well founded.
I would like to pass on to a paragraph in the speech of the Minister of Militia in which he referred to the commercial activities of the organized farmers of Western Canada. On page 43 of Hansard we find that the minister made the following statement:'
But there is another point of view in regard to this matter. It is said that we in Canada are to-day suffering, to some extent at least, from unemployment. Is it a patriotic thing, or a sound thing economically, to take the money of the people of Canada at this critical period, to send it across to the United States to give employment in the factories there, to pay wages and keep employed citizens of the United States, while so many good Canadians during the past few months have been looking for jobs in this country? Would it not, in the first place, be a more patriotic thing, and in the second place, a sounder thing economically, if the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and his friends of the United Grain Growers would look about them in this country to the scores, yes, even hundreds, of Canadian manufacturers who can supply the goods they require, and try to make terms with them, spend their money in this country and thus give employment to unemployed Canadians.
That sentiment meets with the approval of all. I do not need to go into any details as to why the United Grain Growers' Company did not handle Cana-
10 p.m. dian goods. That question was very thoroughly dealt with by

the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) this afternoon. He stated that on the organization of the commercial activities of the United Farmers' they went to the Canadian manufacturers and tried to obtain Canadian goods. They could not do so because the Canadian manufacturers would not sell to them. Now, in all fairness I would say this: There may be a good reason why the Canadian manufacturers could not supply them, but they have never considered it worth while to make that explanation. When the Minister of Militia was reading us this lecture across the floor of the House perhaps it would have been more to the point for him to have turned about and addressed his remarks to the manufacturer members who sit behind him. If anybody is to blame for the condition that exists, for the quantity of American goods that is being handled by the Grain Growers' Organization in Western Canada, it is those very manufacturers who refuse to supply Canadian goods. I wonder if the Government are so keen and so anxious as they profess to keep their money in Canada and in all cases to purchase Canadian goods. We had a short time ago the case of the Government wishing to re-organize the Civil Service. Did they employ a Canadian firm to do that work? I think not. It appears to me that I heard a faint whisper somewhere that they went to Chicago and obtained the services of the Griffenhagen Company to carry out this work of reorganization, or disorganization, or whatever it may be. In this connection I would like to refer to another case. I am told that there is a garage maintained in the city of Ottawa in which are housed a number of automobiles for the use of Cabinet Ministers, Government cars paid for by Government money. I am not criticising that. It may be all right to buy these cars for the ministers; they may be perfectly entitled to use them. That is not the point I want to bring out. It is well known to you, Sir, and to hon. members that quite a number of splendid automobiles are manufactured in Canada by Canadian labour. Did the Government purchase cars of Canadian manufacture for the ministers' use? I think not. It strikes me that one of the makes that they run is called the "Cadillac," and I never heard of a "Cadillac" car being manufactured in Canada.
Another example comes to my mind. I remember very well a year or two ago when the Department of the Interiorwhich was then presided over by the present Prime Minister-decided to plough certain wild prairie land held by the Department of Indian Affairs and it was necessary to purchase machinery for the purpose. Did the hon. Minister of the Interior of that day, who is now the Prime Minister, insist on the purchase of Canadian made machinery for that purpose? Oh, no. He purchased Rumely traction engines, six of them, manufactured in Laporte, Indiana, notwithstanding the fact, which is very well known, that good traction engines are manufactured in the province of Ontario by Canadian labour, using, I presume, Canadian materials.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have already taken up more time than I intended. I just wish to make a few remarks in regard to my stand on the vote which will shortly be taken. I was elected in the general election of 1917 to support-not the present Government but the preceding government for the period of the war. I wish to emphasize that point, it was for the period of the war that I was elected to support the Government then under the leadership of the right hon. member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden). We met in Battleford constituency-the executives of the two old political parties-and we came to an understanding to form a union of forces for a specific purpose-for the purpose of electing a member to come to Ottawa and support a Union Government for the period of the war, the specific purpose being the winning of the war; no other issue whatsoever entered into the arrangement. I remember on one or two platforms the tariff issue was mentioned, and the answer was given that we were not concerned about the tariff at all; the point in our minds was whether the money derived from the tariff would be spent in the Dominion of Canada or in Germany. That was the .sentiment all through the campaign. I believe that I am properly expressing the sentiments of the vast majority not only in the constituency I have the honour to represent, but in all of Western Canada, and, I think, in a good deal of Eastern Canada as well, when I say that, regardless of any constitutional aspect of the case, the people of this country believe that the Government has outlived its mandate and that there should be a general election.
I differ from the Government on their tariff policy, and I take it that that is the chief issue in the speech of His Excellency. Therefore it will be my duty to vote want of confidence in the Government.
