speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to
take to myself and to offer to the House and to the country a comforting thought. I think that in the strife of party politics men sometimes magnify the evil which is to be wrought upon their beloved country if their own particular notion of public affairs should not happen to prevail. It is as well perhaps that we should guard against an error of that sort, and while each of us may press as earnestly as be likes his particular line of thought, it will be better, I think, if we keep in mind the fact that even if our view shall not prevail the sun will still rise and the King's Government will be carried on.
Naturally, from my point of view, I think the best kind of Government that this country can have is a Liberal Government. I think the traditions and history of the past show that. And if we may have a Liberal Government at no distant day, I trust that it may be as successful in the future as it has been in the days that have gone by. But perhaps that admirable condition of affairs is not attainable; it may be that we cannot have the blessing of a Liberal Government at an early day, and we may have to be content with a Farmer Government. It is quite conceivable, it is quite possible. Now, the prospect, if you so regard it, of a Farmer Government sitting in the seats of the mighty here, does not alarm me in any way as it does hon. gentlemen opposite. I cannot subscribe to the Farmers' view on all things, but I decline to regard the farmers of this country as Bolshevists, or Anarchists, or Communists, or any other kind of 'ists except good Canadianists. I have an abiding faith that if in the movement of events our Farmer friends should be entrusted with power the sense of responsibility which will then come to them will lead them to pursue a moderate course, and that though we may not agree with it on one side or the other, I cannot conceive that from that course there will flow any particular disaster to this Dominion. So a Liberal Government is the first choice; and a Farmer Government would not be too bad; and I will go so far as to say that if the worst comes to the worst-and that means if we have a Tory Government-the country could survive event that. The truth is, it is a case in which the patient, that is, the Dominion, is so strong that it can stand the doctoring schemes of any one of these parties and still survive.
I join most heartily in what has been said in congratulation of my right hon. friend

the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) upon his attaining at a comparatively early age the high position which he now occupies. It has been my misfortune often to differ with the right hon. gentleman, and I am very much afraid that our conceptions of public affairs are such that our difference will continue; but that should not prevent me recognizing, as I do in all sincerity, that he will bring to the duties of his high office great qualities-first, the quality, the superb and highest of all qualities, high personal character; he will bring to it marked ability, of which we all have had evidence; and he will bring to it untiring industry. These are great qualities. May I not say too-and that is where the comforting thought comes in- that we have similar qualities in the two hon. gentlemen who lead the other parties? In my hon. friend who sits at my side, the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Mackenzie King), and in my hon. friend the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), the leader of the Farmers' party, we have men who have also youth on their side, who have character, who have talent, who have industry. And from that I draw this thought, that no matter what may occur, this country cannot go so very far wrong when it comes under the leadership of any one of these three gentlemen. These qualities that I have mentioned-personal character, great ability and great industry -are indeed splendid qualities in mankind; they are qualities which each of these gentlemen brings as an asset to the Party which he leads: they are qualities which they all bring as assets in the common service of our country.
Among the subjects that have been discussed in this debate on the Address, not the least interesting has been the question of the League of Nations. It is true, as my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) said yesterday, that our representatives at the League of Nations have valiantly defended in this House that which nobody is attacking. This House is unanimous in its belief in the League of Nations. I myself am most cordially in favour of the League. I am not only in favour of it in principle, but I am in the main in favour of the machinery whereby the League of Nations is created. It may be within the recollection of the House that when the question of the Treaty of Versailles was before Parliament I gave expression to some views concerning Canada's participation in the League of Nations, in which I was careful to say that I spoke for myself only. I differed from the hon.

gentlemen opposite and I differed from many of the hon. gentlemen surrounding me. I want to be permitted again to state briefly my position in that respect.
I have said that I warmly favoured the League of Nations. It has not accomplished all that was hoped for; it has disappointed some people, and many look upon it to-day with very great gloom. I do not take that view. I regard the League of Nations as a noble scheme for a noble end, and even though it may not accomplish all that was intended, I regard it as a case, indeed, in which it is better to have tried and failed than not to have tried at all. Although the League of Nations has disappointed me in some respects, and although it is particularly disappointing in the failure of the United States to join-I can hardly conceive of its being a success if that nation stays out-nevertheless, with all the criticism that is offered, I still desire to be counted as a warm admirer and supporter of the League of Nations.
My difference was with regard to the manner in which Canada was participating in that League. Again let me remind the House that I am speaking entirely for myself on that particular point. My view of the matter was this: in all that makes for our Imperial relations; in all that concerns the relations between Canada and the Mother Country and other portions of the British Empire, in what I may call the inner circle of our Imperial family, I want Canada to occupy, as she has occupied for many years, a position of ever-increasing weight and influence. When we come to deal with foreign affairs, I am not desirous that Canada shall play a part of her own, separate and apart from the British Empire. I want the British Empire, when we come to deal with foreign affairs, to enter every conference as a unit, not as representing several places. Even in matters concerning Canada alone; even in Imperial matters in which Canada is particularly interested, my desire would naturally be that Canada should be, as she has been, represented by Canadians, but I would have them go into the conference not merely as Canadians, but as representatives of the British Empire. I expressed the fear-and I am not going to withdraw that expression today-that with the best of intentions-and I do not for a moment question the good intentions of the gentlemen concerned-this declaration on the part of the Dominions that they must have a separate existence in all these conferences, and a separate existence in the League of Nations, was not
making for that Imperial unity that we should desire, but was paving the way towards separation. I have seen no reason to change my view in that respect.
There is a small party in Canada which desires the separation of this country from the British Empire; which desires the independence of Canada; which desires Canada to withdraw from the Empire and set up as an independent sovereign nation.
I have spoken of it as a small party; it may be larger than we know. I speak of it as a small party because only a few gentlemen have identified themselves publicly with that movement. They are gentlemen of high standing, gentlemen of ability, gentlemen whose sincerity we can respect, even though we may not agree with their conclusions. But I want to call the attention- of the House to this significant fact:
I find that so far as I have come in contact with or learned the views of these gentlemen, every advocate of the independence of Canada looks with approval upon Canada's position in the League of Nations because he regards it as the beginning of a movement for the separation of Canada from the Empire.
That view is not held by me alone. There are several things occurring in relation to the proceedings of the League of Nations, to some of which I will draw attention. The speeches of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), of the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell), our three representatives at the League of Nations, were very interesting. They gave us some information and presented their case as gentlemen of ability always do. But there were some things going on in the League of Nations about which they did not tell us; and it is a pity that we have to look to outside sources for some of the information that we ought to get here. I think that as the consequences of our action unfold themselves, there will be a revision of some of the judgments hastily formed a year or two ago-I think I see evidence already that on both sides of the House light is breaking.
There is a financial side to the question which some members will regard as important. The League of Nations is a rather expensive luxury. I hold in my hand an article which describes what is called by responsible men the "great extravagance'' of that body. I will trouble the House only with the headlines:
Fat Sinecures on Paid Personnel of Commissions. Allied captains receive much more

than Marshal Foch, state French. Flagrant Injustice. Most Scandalous of Anomalies Inaugurated by Versailles Treaty. Princely Chauffeurs.
Now, of all that extravagance Canada pays her share. I am not presenting that as a serious side of the matter; by-and-by some members of the House who feel more keenly interested in that class of question than I do may draw attention to it. I only mention it in passing; I do not regard it as the gravest situation. The gravest position arising out of our action with respect to the League of Nations is that we are having the unfortunate spectacle-the word is not too strong-of the represen-1 tatives of Canada and the representatives of the Empire quarrelling in the eyes of the public at the Peace Conference and at the League of Nations. There is evidence of that, and as the hon. gentleman did not give us a full report of all these things, we have to resort to the press. I find the following report from Geneva, dated December, 1920:
During yesterday's voting the British Empire was divided on nearly every question, Canada and South Africa voting against Great Britain regarding Armenia, and Australia abstaining from voting when the question of Bulgaria was before the Assembly.
Canada and the Empire voting against one another, quarrelling before the wide world, and showing that there is not that unity of the Empire which all should desire to bring about. Well, there is further information along the same line. I have before me a quotation from a New York journal. Careful observers in the public press are noticing what is happening in these proceedings; they are noticing the quarrels between the representatives of the Mother Country and those of the Dominions, and every enemy of Great Britain and the Empire is getting aid and comfort from these quarrels-which, I say, are not creditable to Canada, not creditable to the dominions generally. Here is an article from the New York World:
The Dominions disagree not only with the Mother Country, but with one another. England wants the Council to be supreme; Canada, South Africa and India claim equal rights for the Assembly. Canada is supporting the compulsory adjudication of international disputes, as urged by Elihu Root, which England opposes. On the questions of admitting Germany to the League and disarmament, as to which England has expressed no final opinion, the dominions are sharply in conflict.
Again we have evidence that the differences and quarrels between the representatives of the Mother Country and the representatives of Canada and the other domin-

ions are attracting the notice of the outside world; and who shall say that conditions of that kind are making for Imperial unity? Let me quote another passage. We are all acquainted with that venerable labour leader, whose eloquent voice we heard down in the Museum two or three years ago, Mr. Samuel Gompers. There is much in his record that I admire; but in this particular instance, I regret what he had to say. He said:
"It was my experience," continued Mr. Gompers, "and I look upon it as something of a dependable guide, that the votes of the representatives of these Dominions and Commonwealths were more often with the United States than with Britain."
That is the fruit of Canada's participation in the matter-insisting on having an opportunity to play her own game. I know every hon. member in this House feels as I do in regard to the need for Imperial unity. I do not ascribe anything but the best motives to any hon. gentleman who differs from me, but I ask my hon. friends to think seriously over the situation as presented where, instead of having an Empire with a united front to promote peace, we have the representatives of the different sections of the Empire quarrelling in the eyes of the foreign world. It may be remembered that in discussing the League of Nations in this House, some of us took exception to one particular clause. In the particular point that I have been speaking of for the last few minutes, I have been speaking for myself, and I do not wish anybody now to endorse what I say. There came a moment in that discussion, when in the name of the Liberal party in this House, I made a motion in the House concerning the League of Nations. There was in that League one section known as Article X, which, if I may be permitted, I will read. It reads:
The members of the League undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all members of the League. In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression, the Council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
We did not undertake, although we did not like that clause, to move an amendment to it. We recognized the fact that a treaty, a bargain signed by a number of nations, could not be amended by the will of one. We did not even adopt the Washington practice, the method adopted there, of making reservations. All that we proposed to do was to say that there was a vagueness about that clause, and

that it would be the part of wisdom if, while adopting the Treaty, while confirming it without any qualifications, we should place on record our understanding of what that clause should mean. Therefore, with the consent of my friends around me, I moved the following motion:
That in giving such approval-
That was the approval to the Treaty-
-this House in no way assents to any impairment of the existing autonomous authority of the Dominion, but declares that the question of what part, if any, the forces of Canada shall take in any war, actual or threatened, is to be determined at all times as occasion may require by the people of Canada through their representatives in Parliament.
That seemed a reasonable proposal. How were we met? The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) denounced the motion. He declared that Article X and the Covenant generally were all right; that the instrument was a perfect one; that he would not have any interference; that it was a Holy of Holies; that it must not be touched, and so we were voted down and the League of Nations, including Article X, was approved. What do we find now? The right hon. gentleman, who would not listen to our representations in this House, went across the seas and deliberately proposed to strike out Article X altogether. The House may remember that when the question first came before the House, when the Prime Minister of that day, the hon. member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden), delivered a speech in explanation of the Treaty which he was submitting to the House, I ventured to ask him the question what would happen if the House should neglect or refuse to endorse the Treaty. My right hon. friend said that in that case there would have to be a change of Government, and he would have to go out. So this was such a sacred document that interference with it in any degree would have brought on us that dissolution which some people seem to be so much alarmed about to-day. No words seemed to be too strong for my right hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) to utter in denouncing our proposition, which was not an amendment, not a reservation, but merely a declaration which we thought would make clear what should be the attitude of this Parliament in relation to any question of war. At that time, the Minister of Justice gave us his views as to how the matter should be dealt with. He said that it was highly improper that we should attempt to make any reservation or amendment or declaration of any form. He said that the treaty must go as it was; that it was all right. There was no word of doubt on his part. Then he went on to say that if it turned out by experience that there was something wrong about the treaty, if it needed change or amendment, there was a way in which that could be done. I quote from his speech:
X think that with what I have pointed out with regard to a better opportunity that will come for dealing with this Covenant, if it requires improvement as soon as the League of Nations has been brought into existence-with that present in our minds, and with this further fact present to our minds, that if any of us consider modification essential or of great importance, or if this House upon further consideration-
Observe that-
__should come to the conclusion that modification in connection with Article X or any other provision is necessary, it will be perfectly open and competent to this House, when it sends its representative to the League of Nations, to send him there with Instruction as to the amendment, whether it be this or ^ any other that, in the opinion of this House, is essential or necessary or desirable in the interests of Canada.
So the Minister of Justice pointed out that the proper, and the only proper, course for an amendment was that instruction should be given by the Parliament of Canada. What instruction did this Parliament ever give to the minister to go overseas and demand that Article X be stricken out? Article X and the whole treaty constituted a solemn compact to which this House became a party, and I deny the right of the Minister of Justice or anybody else, without the authority of this House, to go to Geneva and undertake, in the name of Canada, to move to amend that contract. The Minister of Justice did not even have instructions from his Government. I asked the question: What instructions were given? I asked the Government to bring down the Order in Council. They brought it down, and it simply set forth that a meeting of the League of Nations was to be held, and that the right hon. Minister of Justice, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Poster), and the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell), should be chosen as representatives of Canada. Not a line of instruction. By the very method that the Minister of Justice himself laid down, he should have come to this House for instructions, and he should not have tampered with that Covenant in a single line. His action in that regard was a specimen of the autocracy which this Government

is manifesting all the time. It was an exhibition of the contempt that the Government has for Parliament, and it is one of the reasons why every man who respects the rights of Parliament will be justified to-day in voting no confidence in this Administration.
I have heard no effective answer, Mr. Speaker, to the contention advanced by the hon. leader of the Opposition at the beginning of this debate, that this Government no longer had a mandate to conduct public affairs, and that they were carrying on public affairs without any good reason to believe that they had the confidence of the country. I said I have heard no effective answer. Of course there has been one answer. It has come from many quarters, and has always been the same. They tell us that our right to sit here is within the law. They point to the British North America Act which says that Parliament "may" sit for five years, and they in effect translate that "may" into "shall," and make it appear it is our duty to sit here for the full term of five years. Sir, that is not the spirit of the British constitution. It is not enough in these days to say that a thing is within the law. That which is within the law is not always expedient. That which is within the law is not always honourable. I think it was the right hon. the Minister of Justice who pointed us to what was occurring at Washington. There, he said, was a government which was defeated four months ago, and is still in power. Well, the American system has its merits, or they would not have it, for they are a pretty intelligent people, and it is a fair assumption that for everything that exists in their system there is some good reason. But their system in that respect is not ours. There is a rigidity in the American system which no doubt has its purpose. They provide that their election shall take place on a given day, and you cannot change that at all. I do not say it is wrong; it is their method, and as I have said, it must have some merit or they would not have it. But our system is just the reverse. There is an elasticity in the British system which has its purpose and the purpose is not that we shall sit out for the full term of five years, but that as there become evidences of change of public opinion in the country Parliament may be dissolved in order that the Government of the day may ascertain whether or not Parliament possesses the confidence of the country. The argument advanced by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition 
was fortified by many others, and particularly in the very able speech of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) yesterday. What thoughtful man could have listened to that speech without seeing that the whole spirit of the British constitution was against hon. gentlemen who hold office at the present time?
The Prime Minister and one or two other gentlemen speaking on that side made allusion to my own experience in Nova Scotia as having some bearing on this question. Why, they said, when the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was Premier of Nova Scotia and resigned, there was no election necessary. That is true, but the conditions were not the same. I was for twelve years the premier of that province. I had made a record. The people thought it remarkable. I remember one kind friend, who was willing to pay me a compliment, although we differed on political questions, said the Government was all right so long as I stayed, but when I left, it would go to pieces. Well, I left it, and turned over the affairs to Mr. Murray, and he has been there for 25 years. Here in the changing scenes of this Ottawa climate, men may come and men may go, but down in Nova Scotia a good Liberal Government apparently may go on forever.
None of us on this side have contended that a change of leadership necessarily calls for an election. There is no such argument. When Sir John Macdonald died in 1891, nobody claimed that dissolution of Parliament was necessary. There had been an election only a few weeks before. When, at a later stage, Sir John Abbott passed off the stage, and Sir John Thompson succeeded him, nobody thought that an election was necessary. There was no change of policy, merely a change of the individual. And in later years, in every case of the kind where change in leadership takes place not involving any change in policy, there was no reason for having an election. Nobody contends that the mere fact of a change of leader creates the necessity for an election.
But what is the situation here? We have a new leader of the Government; there is no dispute about that. We have a new name; we have a new policy. Now it appears to me that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is on the' horns of a dilemma: either we have a new policy, or we have not. If we have a new policy, if it is a new Government, with a new leader, and a new policy, then no argument is

needed to show that you must go to the country and obtain a mandate to support that leader and his policy. Oh, but, some say, it is not new, it is the same old business, there is no change, so you do not need an election. Well, there is a change of name. Mr. Speaker, a change of name to an individual or to a corporation is a grave and serious matter. The man who undertakes without lawful authority to change his name, the man who travels under an assumed name without lawful authority, the man who travels under a false name, furnishes presumptive evidence that he has fraudulent intent. If this is the same old policy, what justification have they for calling the party by a new name? Is it not presumptive evidence of camouflage, or something described by a stronger word? If the right hon. the Prime Minister says it is the same policy, the same Government, the same group of men, the same old thing, he cannot say that and at the same time justify the change of name. There is no escape from that. Either this is the old policy under a false name, or a new policy on which they are afraid to appeal to the country.
Several hon. gentlemen have expressed their personal opinions as to the understanding at the time of their election. A, B and C say: There was no bargaining with me. I was elected for the term of five years; no conditions were imposed, and therefore I assume it is right for the Government to go on. Many of us can probably say that, but what was the experience of any individual, where the matter was not discussed at all, is not important. What is important is, what was the general understanding in the country everywhere, and surely it does not admit of debate that the general understanding in the country was that the Government was chosen for the purpose of the war. Necessarily there had to be a laying aside of controverted questions in order that the Unionist Government might be formed. For what period were those controverted questions laid aside? I can imagine the interview of the Prime Minister of that day with one of my Liberal friends. "We must come together, gentlemen," he says, "for the winning of the war." "Certainly," says my Liberal friend. "Well then," says the Prime Minister "we will hang together till the war is over." "Yes, that is all right. We will lay aside controverted questions for that period." "Hold on," says the Prime Minister, "I want you to agree to put aside
these matters for four years after the war." I do not believe that even my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) would have accepted the condition if laid down in that way.
It is perfectly evident that the Unionist Government was formed for a period during which reasonable request could be made for laying aside controverted questions, but the war being over, the moment events so shaped themselves that these controverted questions were thrusting themselves up for consideration, that moment the mandate of the Government to conduct public affairs ceased. I do not see how that can be a matter of dispute at all. Oh, some may say, it is a very foolish thing, this proposal that the Government's mandate has ended. Well, if we are foolish people in contending that, we are foolish in pretty good company. The Hon. Mr. Carvell, the former member for Carleton, New Brunswick, was a very active member of the Union Government, but Mr. Carvell felt that the mandate of the Government had ceased, and he retired. He is not a foolish man. He has received one of the highest offices in the gift of the Government. That, at all events, is a testimony to his sagacity and his capacity. There are others. My hon. friend the member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), who so ably and so satisfactorily, I may say, discharged the duties of Minister of Militia and Defence, must have felt that the mandate of the Government had ended, for he resigned.
The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) also felt that the mandate of the Government had expired, that now questions having arisen, it was incumbent upon him to resign. Similarly, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), the moment they attempted to deal with the troublesome question of the tariff, found that he could not agree with them and therefore resigned; and he is not a fool. And the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell), a very active and prominent member of the Union Government, evidently took the same view. He is not here to-night, but I should be doing him no injustice to say that the action he has taken proves that he regarded the Government as having exhausted its mandate, for which reason he has resigned. Now, in the face of the general understanding which cannot be disputed, in the face of the action of all these members of the Liberal party who were in the Government, it is evident that we on this side of

the House are justified in saying that the Government has exhausted its mandate and should appeal to the country.
These things are so patent that when the new Leader of the Government was called to his high position, it would have been, it seems to me, the part of wisdom for the right hon. gentleman to have said at once to his colleagues: "Gentlemen, I must appeal to the country, for I do not feel that I ought to carry on in this way." However, some of them apparently persuaded him to keep on, at a time when conditions were not at all propitious for such a course, He would have been well advised, I think, and it would have been far better for all concerned, had he, at the time the change was made, declared that the conditions were such as to compel him to appeal to the country.
Now, hon. gentlemen opposite try to comfort themselves with the belief that all is going well. A dozen members have spoken and have said that all is well. They ask: "What is the need of a change? The Government is all right; everything is going well; why make a change at all?" Well, they might comfort themselves with that belief, but they will not comfort any unbiased friends outside. Let me read an example of the opinions that are expressed by those outside of this House. This is what a good Conservative newspaper says:
Cabinet reorganization, so essential and so long deferred, must be faced by the new administration without much further delay,
Mark you, "essential and long deferred"; and that was in November last. At that time it had long been necessary, and now it is immediate and pressing.
What is the paper?

I am reading from the Montreal Gazette, through its Ottawa correspondent. After some complimentary remarks to the Prime Minister, indicating that his visit to the West has strengthened him, and so forth, this correspondent goes on to say:
He can now devote himself to organization of his Cabinet and the initiation of constructive measures. It cannot be denied that reorganization in essential for the further success of the new administration. Some members of the Government, through age or ill-health, desire to retire; others should be retired; and others again must give way to men in whom the party and the country have greater confidence. There should be at least five changes in the Government. There is a long stern fight ahead of the administration, and in that fight success can only be attained by men of strong physique

and mentality who have confidence in themselves, and in whom the people have confidence.
That was four months ago. At that time reorganization was overdue; it had long been needed. And now it is absolutely necessary. This newspaper tells us that five changes were necessary. How many ministers do I see present? Let me see, -one, two, three-I believe there are just five ministers sitting on the benches tonight! Now, I should not like to have the task of selecting the five whom this correspondent thinks should go. I am perfectly willing to vote them all out en masse, bag and baggage; I should not like to have to choose from among these genial and estimable gentlemen and to determine whose heads should go upon the block. But when they console themselves with this soothing delusion that all is going well; when they see such unmistakable evidence before them day by day, in the by-elections, of the trend of public opinion and public desire; when they see public opinion reflected in the utterances of their candid friends everywhere, telling them that they have outlived their usefulness, I cannot for the life of me understand why the Prime Minister of the day can complacently hang on to the last moment. Someone remarked today that the Tupper Government had held on to the last moment. Yes, and the result was a catastrophe; and if this Government should hang on to the bitter end, depend upon it the catastrophe will be greater. I think, therefore, every argument that has been advanced in support of the contention that the Government should obtain a mandate from the people is absolutely well-founded and well-supported.
But we are told that we ought to support the Government for all the good things it has done. Well, we have a little difficulty in determining the time at which we should begin the accounting. One minister has said that the Government is only responsible for what has happened since July last, while other hon. members have contended that this Government is the successor of all governments that have been in power since 1911; and that is the sounder view. My good friend, the Prime Minister, may to-day properly be held responsible for the policy of the Conservative party from the year 1911 down to the present time. He was associated with the late Prime Minister and was always ready to defend that hon. gentleman's government. I think, therefore, we shall be doing him no injustice if we hold him responsible for that government's conduct. But, hon. members

say: Look at the noble and patriotic action of this Government in regard to the war! Well, Mr. Speaker, it if a great thing, if you want praise, to shout about the war. But I want to remind my hon. friends that the war did not begin with the general election of 1917. The war had already been in progress before that and we have to go back earlier.
I pass over the manner in which the Government obtained power in 1911; I pass over the unholy alliance which they made with the Nationalists of Quebec which was the foundation of all the trouble that has occurred in that province since; I pass over the slogan of "No truck nor trade with the Yankees" which so aptly expressed their policy at that date; I pass over the breach of faith they committed when, after being elected to prevent free wheat, they put free wheat on the list; I pass over the breach of faith which they committed also in regard to potatoes-I pass over all these things and come to the war. The war began in 1914 and lasted for four years and a quarter, and for three-fourths of that time the Government led by the right hon. member for King's, Nova Scotia, the late Prime Minister, carried on a partizan Administration with all the evils attendant upon partizan patronage. For three years out of the four they made no attempt to form a Union Government, and they made overtures in that direction only when they were in extremities and were likely to be beaten.
That is the whole story-four years of war and only one year of Union Government. For three years they took the money which the people of Canada voted through this Parliament so liberally and patriotically for the purposes of the war and expended it with the help of every patronage committee of Canada. And that is patriotism! That is the record of this Government in wartime, Mr. Speaker, and when the people of Canada some day look into it they will see what a sorry record my hon. friends opposite have made. If we are going to have in this debate the history of the Government's action in the war, let us have the truth, and let us not be told that the Government is a patriotic body, when for three years out of four it carried on partizanship in all its extremes.
Now, I have no desire to detract from anything that has been accomplished by my right hon. friend from King's, Nova Scotia, in his capacity as Prime Minister. He occupied that high position for a long period in the midst of exciting scenes, and
it is but reasonable to believe, as I believe and willingly admit, that he has much good legislation to his credit. On the great question upon which the parties broke, on the great question which was the basis of the formation of the Union Government, I agreed with him and I supported him, and I have no regrets to express for that course. But when we are told that he and the hon. gentlemen associated with him pursued a patriotic course throughout the war, I join issue on that assertion and reply that for three-fourths of the time the Government played the game of partizans and not of patriots.
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that I am occupying more time than I intended, but there are two or three other questions that I should like to refer to.
With regard to the Washington representation I am not going to offer any criticism, but in all sincerity and respect I desire to offer a word of advice. The Minister of Justice, I think rather smarting under some chaff that came from this side of the House, said that the Government would appoint an Ambassador to Washington whenever they found the right man. Well, I suppose he was obliged to say something like that, but my hope and belief is that the Government have revised their judgment in that matter and that they have concluded not to send an Ambassador to Washington. I am not criticising their action, I am merely venturing, in all sincerity, to offer a word of respectful advice. I know something of how work is done at Washington. Have commercial agents, as many as you like, where there is business to be done,-I offer no objection,
__but I affirm that if Canada sends an
Ambassador to Washington he will degenerate into nothing better than a clerk under the British Ambassador-that is all he can become.
I submit that the arrangement which exists to-day is a far better one. If there is a real question between Canada and the United States the Ministers-in-Council deal with the question, they thresh it out; and a minister leaving Ottawa this afternoon will be in Washington tomorrow afternoon and able to present the Governments views to the American government, or to whomsoever he may be dealing with. A minister of the Crown coming in that way fresh from Council, fresh from consultation with his colleagues, is more useful and more likely to be an efficient representative than any clerk dawdling around Washington, and half the time doing nothing at

all. I am not finding fault with anything the Government have done. I am in all earnestness and all sincerity, in the light of my experience, advising them to drop the Washington business.
Then there is the Imperial Conference. Now I think the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) was not quite fair to the Government. He asked the Government to bring down to this House a statement of the policy which they intend to pursue at the Imperial Conference. Mr. 11 p.m. Speaker, you cannot take the Breeks off a Hielan man.
You cannot get from anybody that which he does not possess. I do not say it offensively, I do not say it by way of censure, but I believe this Government does not know about any policy with which to go to the Imperial Conference. There is nothing to confer about. There is a great deal of rubbish talked about these Imperial Conferences-a great deal of rubbish. I agree that conferences between Imperial ministers and overseas statesmen, the meeting together of these men and the exchange by them of opinions, each one learning how the science of government is worked out in other countries, all make for a good purpose, and I do not for a moment wish to be regarded as opposing a conference. On the contrary, I say that, from time to time, such conferences are exceedingly proper.
I do not hesitate to say, however, that from the point of view of Canada there is no question to-day which requires to be submitted to an Imperial Conference. Mr. Lloyd George may have some schemes over there which are referred to in recent press cablegrams. Mr. Lloyd George makes picturesque speeches, but they are not always followed up by anything practical. A good able man he undoubtedly is; but if Mr. Lloyd George has something to-day to propose over there, we want somebody to watch him. If Mr. Hughes, of Australia, if that gallant soldier-statesman from South Africa, General Smuts, has anything to propose, of course it is our duty to listen; but I take the responsibility of saying now that there is no question to-day before the Parliament of Canada which needs to be referred to any Imperial Conference.
Why, it sometimes happens when these conferences are held, when the members come together, that they wonder what in the world they are there for; and if you look over some of their proceedings you will be surprised how many resolutions have been passed which never amounted

to anything. They were academic resolutions; they never came to anything. The truth is that there is a body of people over in England, not a very numerous one, that I might describe as the "Grand Order of Fussers." They are talking about a new constitution to come before the Imperial Conference. They are always talking about what Canada wants, and about what Australia wants. Sir, Canada does not want anything. I say again there is no question pending to-day that this Parliament knows of-and we have a right to know if there is any question-there is no question which needs an Imperial Conference at all [DOT]-absolutely there is none.
We have one little question of importance in its way in regard to the cattle embargo. We think that the British Government are wrong in their attitude. We believe they are wrong, but we may as well let it go because, if we are maintaining the right to regulate our own trade and commerce, we are not going to claim the right to dictate to the British Government how to regulate their trade and commerce in their own way even if it does not happen to please us. But, apart from that question, no man in this House could tell us to-day what there is that requires an Imperial Conference so far as Canada is concerned.
Of course, if the conference is to be held, and if my right hon. friend the Prime Minister should still be in office in June, I think it is quite right that he should go; but he is not going to have a very happy time. If I am not mistaken, my right hon. friend will find himself in a curious position. Every other government representative at that conference will represent people who have expressed their views in recent years and since the war-I think that is correct. If that be the case, what will be the position of my right hon. friend? He is in the position that he does not represent the people of Canada. It is a weak position. He will be a lonely sparrow on the housetop, a solitary pelican in the wilderness. I should think it would be a humiliating position for my right hon. friend to occupy, and-one of my colleagues says-humiliating to the country. I do not mean for a moment to be understood as opposing a conference. I say again, conferences are needed from time to time. Conferences of men on trade and commerce are good things, and as a result of them men understand each other better. I would have Canada from time to time represented at a conference. But I do not hesitate to say

that for my right hon. friend to go over to England in June, with things as they now stand, and to undertake to represent Canada with the full knowledge that he possesses-because he is too intelligent a man to doubt the fact that he does not represent the people of Canada-is to place himself in a position that he ought not to occupy, a position that he will always regret.
We were told that we should support this Government because of the things they have done. I have spoken briefly of their general war record. I heard one hon. gentleman-I forget now who it was-speaking of the wonderful record of this Government-say, "Look, they have given votes to women." They did not. Looking back in my mind's eye to the elections of 1917, there are two households that I recall. One was a family of ladies who had votes. They had a son and a brother who had gone to the war, and it was right that they should have votes. But, close by, there was another home where there were three ladies who had.no brother to send to the war, but who were giving their days and their nights, and their money and their energy, to all the good works that the women of Canada were doing. They had no votes because the Government did not put them on the voters' list. Was that patriotism? Was that statesmanship? Ah! but it is said, they have given the votes now to women generally. No, they have only pretended to give them votes. They have put a provision in the statutes giving them the votes, but they will have to wait until 1922 before they get a chance to vote. No, the things which my hon. friends opposite describe as tributes to the Government's wonderful policy will not stand examination. The Government has outlived its usefulness, as has been contended by many hon. members.
There is only one point more I think I will speak upon, because I believe there are other hon. gentlemen who desire to express their views to-night. One of the things we are told this Government has done for which we should give them great honour is the abolition of patronage. Well, I am not going to deny the Government some share of credit for that matter. If any hon. gentlemen in this House are anxious to have the control of patronage again, I am not one of them. I am net complaining if I have not any patronage. I do not want it. It is better to be without it for many reasons. If the Government has abolished
patronage, I want to give them credit for it, but I must say this: No sooner do they agree to do these things than they begin to try and evade their own laws. I think it was the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who described them of being guilty of infanticide-they were always killing their own babies.
Well, with all the cry they have made about abolishing patronage, what is the situation? The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is to-day claiming the right to exercise patronage to the extent of 15,000 officials in this Dominion. I had a letter from a man down in my county who had heard somewhere that the census officials were going to be appointed on the nomination of the members. I wrote him that I thought he was mistaken, but that I would inquire. So I inquired of the proper department. I thought: If this is going to be done by the Civil Service Commission I am not going to complain; but if it is not going to be done by the Civil Service Commission, perhaps it will be well for me to ask if the members irrespective of politics are to make the recommendations. The assurance I got from the official authority is that they have gone back to the old patronage game; they are going to appoint the census officials on the nomination and recommendation of members supporting the Government. That is patronage. Why, Sir, in almost every claim the Government set up we discover that while they are making great professions of virtuous policy they do not live up to them.
For all these reasons I say the position taken by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in this amendment is the correct one. This Government have no longer a mandate to conduct the affairs of the country; they have no longer any right to believe that they have the confidence of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to follow the very good example set by a number of the preceding speakers and extend my sincere congratulations to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) on his accession to the very high office that he now occupies. I can remember in 1909, I think it was, when I first heard him speak as a young man, at that time a private member, I predicted that he would go far; that prediction has been realized. I further predict that if he desires to remain in public life he will always fill a very prominent position.

We have now a brand new Government with a brand new name and-I say it with all respect-a brand new Prime Minister. But, Sir, we find that they have a very old policy. I would have thought that a new government in such a new country as this, where conditions are changing, might to some extent modernize their policy. However, I will quote a passage from the speech of His Excellency, delivered as the mouthpiece of this Government. He said:
It is the opinion of my advisers that in such revision-
Speaking of the tariff.
-regard must be had to the necessities of revenue and as well-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is so much conversation on the floor of this Chamber as well as in other parts thereof that it is absolutely impossible for the Speaker even to follow the hon. member who is now addressing the House. I must ask hon. members and others to refrain from talking.

I was quoting a part of the speech of His Excellency regarding the tariff. It reads:
It is the opinion of my advisers that in such revision regard must he had to the necessities of revenue and as well that the principle of protection to Canadian labour and legitimate Canadian industries, including agriculture, which has prevailed for more than forty years in this country, must be consistently maintained:
That is a very old policy-as old as the country. I am afraid that I cannot support it. At the same time I commend the Government for their frankness in stating exactly where they stand on the tariff. It is another story with regard to what we call the official Opposition. It is very difficult to say where they do stand with regard to the tariff. Liberalism, as I have always understood it, meant "no special favours," which are conveyed, of course, under protection. But from the expressions of prominent Liberals in public and private and their attitude generally, we have come to the conclusion that a majority of them do not stand upon their own fiscal platform. And it is a very good platform in some respects.
It has been claimed that this little group here, which I believe sincerely stands for free trade in many respects, for instance, in regard to tools and implements that are used in developing natural resources, free food, and so on, and a low tariff in other respects-it has been claimed, I say, that this little group should affiliate politically with the present Liberal party; but as long
[Mr. MacNutt. [
as there is that distrust amongst our group -I can speak for myself and, I think, for the rest of my colleagues-there is not very much chance that there will be any such fusion. Recent by-elections have shown that we are not very likely to fuse. And, besides, a great deal of evidence has been brought forward to show that there is more than a doubt as to where the Liberal party as a whole stands on the tariff. In support of this assertion I wish to quote some newspaper reports of statements claimed to have been made by prominent Liberals. This is the first report:
The recent speech by the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux at Ste. Martine, Chateauguay county, has attracted considerable attention in the East. In this address Mr. Lemieux said: "It is possible that in the West Liberals think that we should have a policy of free trade. In a word, Mr. Speaker, since the hon. gentleman has entered the political field in Canada, he has always shown himself to be the representative of the most Tory traditions which we have in this country. His leadership is dangerous, and the sooner it is terminated the better, in the interests of this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the question which is before the House is after all a very simple one. It is this: Has this Government a mandate to further govern Canada? And, secondly, has this Government the confidence of the people of Canada? I intend briefly to discuss these two questions. As to the first-has the Government a mandate to further govern Canada?-that question is one of great importance and moment. It is important for us to know whether responsible government in Canada shall be maintained. Any student of constitutional history is aware of the struggle, the long and bitter struggle, that was fought in England in order to obtain responsible government, and before the principle of constitutional and responsible government was recognized, the head of Charles I had to fall. In Canada, we have also had a

struggle. That struggle lasted from 1828 to 1847, and the names of the leading actors in it who led the fight to secure for us liberties and the freedom which we enjoy are the names of those most held in honour by every patriot in our country. Is this government to be permitted to rob us of those privileges? Is it to be permitted to abolish the prerogatives won after such a hard struggle? That is really the question which is before the House.
The Liberal principle, as expounded by my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), has always been the same; it has never varied, and that principle is that the Government should remain in power not merely so long as it is supported by a majority of the House of Commons, but so long, and only so long, as that majority in the Commons is an exact reflection of the opinion in the country at large. The Tory theory is altogether different. That theory in substance is that a government has the right to remain in power, notwithstanding the will and the desire of the people, so long as it can manage to muster on a division sufficient votes to secure a majority, no matter how slim that majority may be. That Tory principle has been put into practice not only by this Government but by the Administration .of the late Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) since 1911. Since 1911, has the Government conducted affairs in accordance with the mandate given by the electorate of Canada? I answer that question unhesitatingly, Mr. Speaker. I say that the Government of 1911, the Government of 1917, and the Government of 1920, have none of them ever conducted the affairs of this country according to the mandate given by the people.
In 1911 an appeal was made to the electors of Canada by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and it was met in Ontario and in other provinces by the allegation that the Laurier administration was endangering the British Empire and that it was time for Canada to save itself from dismemberment from the Empire. In our province of Quebec it was stated by the Nationalists that Canada had no obligation towards the Mother Country, and that it was time she should secede from the Empire if remaining in it meant further obligations. The appeal to the prejudices of the people carried the other provinces; the appeal to sectarian nationalism carried to a certain extent the province of Quebec; and the party led by the late Prime Minister, who had received a
mandate from the English Provinces never to forget our obligations towards the British Empire, the day after the election was over, turned round and made an alliance with the Nationalists of Quebec. Since that alliance was formed, never has the Government which was originally elected in 1911, carried on any policy in keeping with the promises made to the electorate of the English provinces nor, on the other hand, in fulfillment of the pledges given to the electors of Quebec.
In 1916, the Government applied for an extension of the parliamentary term, and that extension was granted provided that during the additional period no legislation of a controversial character should be introduced. A mandate was given by Parliament to the then Government. How was that mandate respected? The Government respected it by first introducing conscription when the Prime Minister had expressly promised that there would not be conscription in Canada. Secondly, the Government respected it by bringing in the War-times Election Act; and thirdly, the Government respected it by taking advantage of this opportunity to form a Union Government. In 1917 the Union Government was formed and an appeal made to the country. This appeal was based solely and exclusively on one question, the carrying on of the war. The Prime Minister declared to the electors of Canada, and his ministers made the same declaration, that the Government was for one purpose, the carrying on of the war, and that the moment the war was over the Government would consider that its mandate had expired. The elections were won by means and by methods which are well known to the people of Canada. The Government carried the day, but what did it do? In 1918 the war was over but did the Government resign? Not only did the Government not resign but despite a promise to the electors not to bring in during the war period, or during the period of its existence, any domestic question which could be controverted, it introduced the railway policy upon which the people of Canada had never been consulted. Further, the Government now wishes to introduce redistribution, although it has absolutely no mandate. Nay, it wishes to proceed further by sending representatives to attend the Imperial Conference in London and make decisions binding Canada, when the representatives who are to sit in London have absolutely no mandate from Canada, and absolutely no authority to speak for this country.

As to whether this Government has a mandate or not I will only say this: In 1917 the Administration called the Union Government was elected. Where is that Government to-day? It has disappeared. In 1917, during the war, the then Prime Minister led the Government forces in the electoral struggle, and the Union Government carried the elections. Where is that leader to-day? He has resigned. In 1917 a programme was submitted to the electorate of Canada. Where is that programme to-day? Mr. Speaker, that programme has been cast aside and a new programme has been propounded. In 1917, Mr. Speaker, a special franchise was passed, and nearly every member in this House sits as a member elected under the provisions of that franchise. Where is that franchise to-day? That franchise which gives life and existence and legal authority to this Parliament to sit has been taken out of our statutes, and the reasons why are well known to the people of this country. Not only has the Government disappeared, not only has the programme disappeared, not only has the leader disappeared, not only has the franchise disappeared, but even the issues have disappeared out of our public life.
To-day there remains absolutely nothing in this Praliament connected with the elections of 1917, but the fourteen members who were elected by the provisions of the War-time Elections Act when they were defeated by the electors of their constituencies. Mr. Speaker, this is true. There is not one man on the Government side that can deny the truth of what I have just affirmed. Nevertheless, this Government clings to office; this Government refuses to go before the people; this Government refuses to give to the electors of Canada the chance to decide who shall have the direction of public affairs. I have studied the history of England, I have studied the history of my own country, I have studied the history of the United States-nowhere in any of these countries do I find a single example of action on the part of a government which is to he compared with the action of the Government of Canada to-day. Only one precedent, Mr. Speaker, may be found and that precedent is to be found in the most unhappy and unfortunate period in English history-I	refer
to the period in England from 1640 to 1660. In those days there was a Parliament, a Parliament which was elected at first in a moment of public enthusiasm, as was the present Parliament. But it had outlived its usefulness. Al-

though the people of England did not want that Parliament, it nevertheless persisted in remaining. It was called the "Rump Parliament" and I think the only proper appellation for the present Parliament would be the same title. The Rump Parliament had to be thrown out by a Cromwell. Will this Government wait until a Cromwell throws it out? I think the Government should be careful; the people of Canada have been patient. The people have displayed lots of forbearance, but the patience of the public like the patience of the individual has its limits. The Government has overstayed its usefulness, the Government should disappear.
Another question is as to whether this Government has the confidence of the people of Canada. I do not wish to discuss this point at great length, former speakers have discussed it much more ably than I can do; but I desire to recall to your memory, Mr. Speaker, that
12 p.m. since 1918, if I am not mistaken, fourteen elections have been held and out of that number ten have gone against the Government. I do not wish to further discuss the meaning or the significance of the result in Peterborough. I simply wish to say that the electors of Peterborough voted in such a way as to give to this Government an imperative order to quit office. Peterborough has spoken in a most emphatic and unambiguous manner, and I hope the Government will at least understand the desires of the people as expressed by the electors of that constituency. It has been said that this Government is too weak. The Government knows that it has not the confidence of the people, and although its weakness is known to its own members, although the Prime Minister knows and acknowledges that his Cabinet should be reconstructed, he does not dare to do it. Why does he not? Because the Prime Minister knows that should the new ministers go to the country they probably would not be returned.
The situation is most unfair. I see opposite to me the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid). This hon. gentleman has been working very hard for his country; he has been in office since 1911. Very often during our prolonged debates I see the hon. gentleman turning yearning eyes towards the Senate Chamber. Is it not time, Mr. Speaker, that he should have his rest? On the Government benches I also see my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), for whom

I have great respect. He, too, has worked arduously for his country. Very often, I am sure, he thinks what a beautiful and restful place the Supreme Court would be in the evening of his life. I see, for instance, my hon. friend the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). He is full of energy, he is full of activity, he is full of zeal. If these old servants of the public do not get their reward, and if the young bloods like the member for Fort William and the very devoted Chief Whip do not get Cabinet portfolios in these days, it is because the Government knows its own weaknesses and does not dare to face a by-election anywhere.
For the last year there has been discussion in this House and in the press as to the situation of the province of Quebec. The province of Quebec in 1917 was a traitor. The province of Quebec in 1917 was compared to a province where open rebellion existed. No appeal to prejudice was strong enough against our province and against our people. These appeals to prejudice had their results-the Government carried the general election in that year. But if the Government carried the election, it lost any sympathy that it might have possessed in my native province. The war is now over. The big interests are appealing to this Government for high protection. The Government knows that the rest of Canada is opposed to protection. The Government knows that sentiment in Ontario is antagonistic to that policy. The Government wished to have new allies, and although, Mr. Speaker, you will be surprised, the Government turned their eyes upon this very province, inhabited by traitors, to find these new allies7 to find this new blood which will give them new life. The press of Canada, which is heavily subsidized by the Government, as we all know, has published articles declaring that nothing is too good for Quebec, that Quebec
is the sanest province in the Dominion. Quebec is being cajoled. We are told every day that we represent the best traditions of Canada and the highest Canadian aspirations. It is with great regret that I have mentioned my hon. friend. In my native province we have fought many a battle side by side in favour of the principles which the Liberal party represent. My associations with the hon. member have always been of a very friendly character, and when I saw him rising to his feet, and when I heard the speech which he delivered, I can say that the feeling I had, Mr. Speaker, was a feeling of heartfelt sympathy and sadness.
In 1917 when I waged in my province a fight for Canadian autonomy, for Canadian spirit, for Canadian nationhood, when I ran against the former Minister of Inland Revenue, the Hon. Mr. Sevigny, one of the speakers during that campaign who enunciated the most Canadian of Canadian sentiments was the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe. The attitude of my hon. friends towards our province is an attitude of promise, an attitude of flattery. But the papers of Montreal, particularly the Montreal Gazette, have announced Jthat the Government, unless Quebec yields to their demands, will assume another attitude. That attitude would be a threatening one; to use their own expression, the Government would open a "barrage fire" upon Quebec. Their fire we are awaiting without fear. Mr. Speaker. Unyielding to promises, we shall

not bend to fear. We represent in this House an indignant province which has been insulted, and never will our province give in to the Government until a fitting apology is forthcoming from public men in this country for the crime committed against Quebec.
Their barrage fire has already been opened, by a gentleman, who claims to represent his province in the Cabinet, the hon. Mr. Blondin, Postmaster General of Canada. Represents the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker? He no more represents Quebec than I could claim to represent New Zealand in this House; he no more represents Quebec than I represent or claim or wish to represent the city of Toronto. Mr. Blondin is an outcast from our province. In 1917, having betrayed the most sacred interests of our province, he has come amongst his own people and to use the words of the gospel, he has "passed amongst them and has not been recognized." In some place the hon. gentleman has chosen to declare that never has he uttered disloyal words in the province of Quebec. The hon. gentleman has a very short memory. In 1910 during the election in Drummond and Arthabaska, on the same platform where I was discussing public affairs with him, in the parishes of Maddington Falls and St. Louis de Bland-ford, the present Postmaster General of Canada shot holes through the British flag. In the election of 1917 in my own constituency the hon. gentleman said to the people of St. Rose de Watford: "What does conscription matter to you gentlemen? You are close to the American border; should conscription be enacted you can escape over tne border to the United States." If the Government wishes to retain the Postmaster General as one of its members it is free to do so, but I ask the leader of the Government, if he lets Mr. Blondin remain in the Cabinet, not to let him call himself the representative of Quebec. Another gentleman has opened a barrage fire on our province, and that gentleman is the hon. Mr. Robertson. The hon. gentleman in another place-
