speechtext: The hon. member cannot escape the well-known rule by making a veiled reference to a debate in the Upper Chamber by saying that it occurred in "another place." I think he would be well advised to adhere to old parliamentary traditions and not refer to hon. gentlemen in the other Chamber in terms of disrespect.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to refer to any other hon. gentleman in terms of disrespect. I simply wish to direct the attention of the House to certain statements by ministers or members of the Government, bearing on questions before the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The' hon. gentleman would not be in order in doing so if the statements to which he refers were made in the other House of Parliament. That rule is well known.

I bow to your decision, Mr. Speaker, but I was under the impression that the rule was to the effect that we had no right in the House of Commons to quote from speeches delivered in the other Chamber, but that hon. members were perfectly free to discuss declarations of members of the Government as connected with Government responsibility and as connected with the attitude of the Government on public matters.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman would be perfectly in order in doing so if they were matters of record, but if he starts to traverse a speech made by an hon. member of the other House, he is not in order.

Mr. Speaker, I have
read in the press that hon. members of this Government have started an attack upon our province, describing the condition of Quebec in 1917 as having been worse than that which exists in Russia. Any member of the Government who so represents the conditions in my native province in 1917 is not stating the real condition of things. When the Military Service Act was being put into force in 1917 the greatest agitation existed in the province of Quebec. The then Minister of Militia came to the city of Quebec, and the reception accorded to him at that time showed that if the people of that province were firm and solid in their principles and convictions, they also knew how to respect the laws of their country. It was represented by members of the Government that houses were burned and that dynamite was used. I say that the only dynamite used in Quebec in 1917 was dynamite bought with Government money and used by Government agents as Was done in Montreal.
The hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) during the course of his speech in this debate, referred to the Liberal party on this side as being the remnant of a party. So far as we in this House from

Quebec are concerned, we represent those who in the greatest struggle ever fought by Sir Wilfrid Laurier remained firm, solid and loyal to Liberal principles. In this political fight of 1917, young and old members from Quebec were like the soldiers who had fought many battles under the guidance and direction of the great Napoleon. When the time and the hour of defeat came on the field of Waterloo, although the old guard was not numerous, in the face of obvious defeat those soldiers remembered the glories of former victories through their leader and protected him. When an English general, addressing those soldiers, and assuming the same attitude as the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) did the other day, called on the old guard to surrender, that English general was answered by the sublime word which has immortalized Cambronne, and I say that the province of Quebec, answering the request of the Government, uses that same sublime and immortal word.
The province of Quebec will hold in Canada the balance of power at the next election. No government can carry on the business of this country without the support of the province of Quebec, and the members from Quebec will see to it that never again in the history of Canada, if we can prevent it, will a government be given the power of the strength to try to crucify a whole race and a whole province. Our forefathers came to Canada as the pioneers of civilization; we love our province as we love our mother; we love the vastness of its forests; we love the romance and the grandeur of its rivers; we love the beauty and the picturesqueness of its landscape; Quebec is our mother; Quebec has been insulted, and it is useless for any member in this House to ask us to forget. We shall not forget.
Any man who states that Quebec can be disregarded in Canada's affairs is a man who shows his ignorance of Canadian history. Canada has been built up by the combined efforts of the great men of the other provinces, and of the great men of Quebec. No matter how far you go back in history, always amongst the most prominent workers for the grandeur and advancement of Canada, you will find French Canadian statesmen and politicians from Quebec. Who wanted constitutional government for Canada? The French Canadian statesmen who sat in the Legislative Assembly in 1791. Who carried to the battlefield the cry of responsible government? Who shed their blood for that principle?
The French Canadian heroes of 1837, who, under the Union government obtained from England a full acknowledgment of responsible government-Lafontaine and Baldwin. Who rendered possible Confederation in Canada? Sir George Etienne Cartier. Who consummated Confederation and made of the nine provinces in Canada a nation united? Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It is needless to try to cast aside the French Canadian race in this country. We are the pioneer race and we intend to remain so. We have done things in the past; we are doing things in the present; we expect to achieve even greater things in the future, and intelligent statesmen, instead of trying to threaten Quebec, should try to conciliate Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, in making my contribution to this debate, I wish to follow the time-honoured custom of congratulating the mover and the seconder of the Address on the able manner in which they have acquitted themselves, and I also wish to join with them in extending congratulations to my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who has attained to the high position of Prime Minister of our country.
I intend that my remarks shall be brief. Since becoming a member of this House, the thought has often occurred to me that a large portion of many of the speeches, which are devoted to calling down the opposing party or parties, might very well be either cut out altogether, or the same effort applied to something constructive for the country's weal. It has been said that one of man's greatest advantages over the brute creation is the gift of language with which to conceal his thoughts, and, Sir, one is sometimes forced to wonder what the real thought behind some of the statements made in this debate might be. Consequently, Sir, I will be as concise as possible and as plain as possible.
In congratulating the leader of the Government, I wish it to be distinctly understood that I do not agree with some of the policies laid down by his party, and that I emphatically disagree with the policy of protection as outlined by that party and embodied in the speech from the Throne. This being the case, I could hardly be expected to vote for the motion unless I swallowed my convictions, which I have no intention of doing, and yet the amendment as it stands does not comply with the thought uppermost in my mind in regard to the present situation. But I feel forced

to follow the old advice that of two evils, or possibly, I might say in this case, of three evils, choose the least. Consequently, I will support the amendment. In doing so, I am fully aware of what the consequences may be, but I have no hesitation in telling the members of the Government that the situation has been created by them, and on them the verdict will fall.
In all fairness there is one thing I wish to give my right hon. friend the leader of the Government credit for, while he filled the portfolio of Minister of the Interior, and that is the establishment of the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and the placing of thousands of returned men on the land. The hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt) has given the figures relating to the whole Dominion, and has made a plea for generous treatment of the returned men. I heartily endorse his sentiments in that respect, and I should like to give some figures particularly of the work done by the Board through the office at Prince Albert. The constituency of Prince Albert to-day has many soldier settlers who are making good in comfortable homes, and who are owners of fertile farms. These men are located not only in the district tributary to the city of Prince Albert, but you will find them all the way through the famous Carrot River valley right to the Manitoba boundary. Undoubtedly some are heavily encumbered, but taken broadly, the scheme has been a success both from the point of view, of the re-establishment of the returned soldier, and that of land settlement and increased production. The office at Prince Albert reports 1,200 established settlers, with only some fifty adjustments, leaving 1,150 soldier settlers in actual residence, occupying in all 265,000 acres, and producing last season over 450,000 bushels of grain. Of these settlers 538 are married men; 164 of the wives are overseas brides, and there were at that time 1,002 children. So, Mr. Speaker, you will readily see that the element of increased production has not been overlooked.
Education has been handicapped in the settlement which was formed in that portion of the Porcupine Forest Reserve which was opened for soldier entry. Owing to the fact that the Government retained title to the land, debentures for the purpose of erecting schools could not be sold, and a condition exists there which should not be allowed. There are over one hundred children in this settlement, over sixty of whom are of school age but there is no school. Let me say in passing that in my opinion there is nothing the Government or
[Mr. Knox. [
this House can do for the returned man that would repay him for the sacrifices he made during the war, and when we find men who, after all the turmoil and upsetting experiences which they have undergone, are ready and willing to settle down on the land, or willing to qualify for the benefits of the Act, surely it is up to us to give them all the assistance and encouragement in our power.
But the one big want most keenly felt is the lack of transportation facilities. Some of these settlers are tremendously handicapped for lack of railways, but no worse than the civilian settlers who surround them. An extract from the report reads as follows:
Transportation facilities north of Tisdale and north of Prince Albert are poor, and a railway-operated at an early date would be of untold benefit to these areas. A line from Turtleford to Shellbrook would open up a very fine tract of country. The centre of this district is fifty miles from railway facilities, yet settlers are favourably reported upon.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I most strongly urge upon the Government and upon this House the support of any scheme whereby these people may get the necessary assistance in connecting them up with the outside market. I believe the whole West has a grievance in regard to the heavy freight rates, but the high rates of transportation, individually, sinks into insignificance in comparison with the situation of those people who have no transportation at all.
I would like to say a word about the freight rates. In the West our lines of railway are much more easily and cheaply constructed, and with long unbroken hauls in bulk lots, much more easily and cheaply operated than similar lines in the East. You will easily see that both the producer who has to ship his products over thousands of miles to eastern markets, or what is more likely, eastern ports, and the consumer, who in most cases is also a producer and has to ship his supplies in over the same long route, is heavily handicapped by the situation-handicapped to such an extent that if there is any possible way of surmounting the difficulty, the West demands to-day that it be surmounted.
There is a way to overcome the difficulty. The natural outlet for the Prairie Provinces was provided by an all wise Creator in the shape of the Hudson Bay, and it only remains for the hand of man to supply the necessary transportation facilities, the funds for which have already been largely provided by the sale of western lands set aside for that purpose. The

work on this was proceeding fairly satisfactorily, even through most of the war period, but was finally stopped in 1918, and the present Government declines, or neglects, to complete the project, even though the West has, in season and out of season, been pressing for it. The Senate Committee which took evidence in connection therewith last year decided in favour of the scheme. I would impress upon the leaders of the Government that the West demands that the Hudson Bay route be completed.
In the matter of the investigation of the grain trade, I am sure that this group will gladly join in giving all the assistance in its power, and in that direction I wish to inform this House that it was the iniquities of the grain trade in the first place that forced the farmers of the West to organize in self defence, and I can assure you, Sir, from personal experience, that the fight in those days was an up-hill one. Where were the champions of the farmers' cause then who have lately come forward on the Government side, asking for an investigation of the grain trade? I venture to say that, with one or two exceptions, none of them knew or cared what the outcome would be at that time, but if the Government can make any improvement in the conduct of the grain business, the milling business, the shipping business, the textile business, the agricultural implement business, the packing house business, the sugar business, or any other business that affects the common good, it will get all the assistance possible from this group.
I wish to speak of another matter. Two days ago the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) referred to his speech in South York and made this statement, which will be found in Hansard on page 445:
I said that the movement had its /Genesis among the American farmers in the great west.
He was referring to the origin of the Farmers' movement. I want to tell the minister that his information is absolutely false. I have been intimately connected with the Farmers' movement since its inception in 1902. It originated first in the province of Saskatchewan. I have myself been for eleven years a director on the Board and I had the high honour of working in conjunction with the men who originated and organized the movement. I think it might be interesting to the House to learn the nationality of some of these
men. As I look backward over the years and try to recall the outstanding men connected with the movement, it is possible that some of them may escape my memory; but I shall give the names of those who occur to my mind at the moment. Of the Canadian-born directors whom I can remember on the board some have been presidents and some vice-presidents. Of the Canadian-born, there are:	Hon. W. R.
Motherwell, Mr. E. A. Partridge and his brother Mr. H. O. Partridge, Mr. John Miller, Mr. Peter Dayman, Mr. Levi Thomson, Mr. E. N. Hopkins, Mr. David Railton, and, last but by no means least, Mr. John A. Maharg. The British-born are: Sir Richard Lake, Lieutenant-Governor of Saskatchewan, Mr. Allan Hawkes, Mr. F. W. Green, Mr. F. M. Gates, Mr. Matthew Snow, Mr. J. A. Murray, Hon, C. A. Dunning, Provincial Treasurer in the Saskatchewan Government, Hon. George Langley, Minister of Municipal Affairs in the same government, and, in this category, last also, but not by any means least, the hon. member for Mackenzie who sits on my left (Mr. J. F. Reid). In all these years there was not a single American on the board, so far as I can remember, not that there is any reason why they should not have been there. The fact remains, however, that at that time very few Americans had come into the Canadian West. Many have entered the country since and some are on the boards, but they are in the minority, and the American idea has never influenced the movement at any time. I make this statement for the benefit of the minister who made the accusation. It has been stated by the hon. member for Last Mountain, (Mr. Johnston) that had the present situation and the present fiscal policy of the Government been predicted in 1917 in Western Canada, a very different result would have been recorded. And I quite agree with him. But no such policy and no such situation were in sight, nor were they considered in any way at that time. The Minister of Militia admits that the old Unionist party has passed out of existence and that a new party with an attenuated name has taken its place. This being so, and having no confidence in that party, I will support the amendment.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, as this is the first occasion on which I address the House in French, I feel that I should offer a word of explanation, if not of apology, to those who, no doubt, believe in all sincerity, that

the French Canadians are in the wrong every time they do not address this House in their mother tongue. I understand and still more appreciate, such feelings on their part, for I do not forget that I once felt as they do, and that, until I had the honour of being elected to Parliament. Until then, I was one of those who believed that French Canadians should fully avail themselves of their right to speak their own language in the House of Commons at Ottawa, whatever the outcome. However, I must say that, as soon as I had acquired some experience in Parliament I soon had to alter my views; this I did at the very first session. It was then that I realized that, whatever our rights to the use of French in this House, if we wish to take a prominent part in the debates of this House, we are thereby under the necessity to speak, not our own tongue, which is ever dear to us, but one that is not our own. And it is for that reason, and at the expense of great sacrifices, as well as great efforts on my part, that, until the present time, I have spoken English in this House. Yet, as I believe that it is my duty to pay a modest tribute to the French language, I am taking the liberty to impose a French speech upon hon. members within these precincts.
Were it necessary to quote authorities in support of my assertion that, notwithstanding our right to the use of the French language, we are compelled for purposes of discussion to speak another language, I would but quote*the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, our lamented leader, who, though he spoke one language as fluently as the other, used the English language almost exclusively during the time that he was a member of Parliament, that is to say, for nearly half a century. We could find only a few instances in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's political life when he spoke in French in this House.
What I have just said of our regretted leader might apply equally well to all the great and illustrious ^French Canadians of the House of Commons of Canada. I might say the same of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland); of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) ; and of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) ; I might also mention that Mr. Bourassa, who has made it his business to champion the French language in the province of Quebec-for which I am grateful to him-very seldom,
CM. Denis.]
if I am rightly informed, spoke French in Parliament.
At any rate, the question is settled; whoever wishes to take part in the debates of the House of Commons must use the English language; once more I say that if I have to offer any apology, I am quite ready to do so; my only excuse is the necessity which exists and will continue to exist in the future for all French Canadians to use a language which is not their own, however much they may regret having to do so, if they wish to join in parliamentary debates.
Mr. Speaker, were I to neglect to congratulate the right hon. minister on his accession to the high position he now occupies, I would be unfair both to him and to myself. Whatever be our opinions, whatever be our likes and dislikes-as far as I am concerned, I do not dislike any one-we are bound to admire and acknowledge talent at all times and wherever it may be found, particularly in our country.
It is an undisputed fact, Mr. Speaker, that the right hon. Prime Minister is a man of great ability, and that this great ability has won for him the high rank he now enjoys, and, saying this of one who is yet a young man is giving him the greatest praise that his fellow citizens can bestow upon him.
Mr. Speaker, I have read very carefully the speech from the Throne. Must I repeat what has already been said so often in this House, that this speech is quite insufficient and incomplete? During this period of reconstruction, at a time when Canada needs all her vital strength and an effective legislation, must it be said that the speech from the Throne has failed altogether to reach the object in view? The great problems of the hour have not been provided for.
The speech from the Throne is a dry document which was presented to us as a simple matter of course; it is a food which has no fragrancy, flavour or taste. The Government, in presenting it, confessed their inability and weakness as well as the instability of their policies.
We are told that this is a new Administration which has been in existence only a few months and that our criticism, if we have any to offer, should not apply to the actions of its predecessors, because the present Government would not be responsible for the blunders committed by the previous administrations.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I hold a different view, and, moreover, it was not the attitude taken by the right hon. Prime

Minister throughout the country and in this debate before the House. It is one of two things: The present Government is either a new government or the continuation of preceding administrations. If it is a new government, then the question which the House has been discussing for the last three weeks, namely, that such a government must submit their new platform to the people, ought to be considered as being a fair proposal since the Government admit themselves that they are a new administration. Such is not, however, the stand taken by the Government.
The hon. Prime Minister says that this Government is nothing but the continuation of the preceding administrations, therefore, if we take him to his word and supposing, for the sake of argument, that this Government is nothing but the continuation of previous administrations, they are responsible for whatever their predecessors have done and they must bear the consequences thereof.
The right hon. Prime Minister has travelled throughout the country to state his policy or rather, as it is commonly said, to talk politics. The hon. gentleman knew that the preceding government was no longer in touch with the people, in other words had lost their confidence. Upon being called suddenly to lead the Government, the hon. gentleman, possessed as we know he is, of youth, ability, initiative and courage, started on a journey throughout the Dominion.
What was the result of that campaign? Have the arguments of the hon. Prime Minister convinced the people of Canada? Has public opinion changed? Has confidence been restored? Have the people of Canada any more faith in this Government than they had in the previous administration five or six months or twelve months ago? The question answers itself; you will find it in every tongue and in every heart. The people throughout the country, are asking just for one thing; that is a general election in which they will have the opportunity to express their sentiments. Hon. gentlemen opposite answering the leader of the Opposition in a somewhat ironical mood absolutely lacking in sincerity said: "You are asking us to vacate our seats for your own benefit."
To put the question in that way, Mr. Speaker, is to distort the truth. That is not the question. The question we are putting before the House and which we shall submit to the people of Canada in due
time, is the following: Fellow citizens, you are called to elect the men who will form a new government. If they should be taken from the ranks of the Conservative or Unionist party, it is all very well. The moment the people have declared themselves, we shall be satisfied with the verdict, because they are the supreme masters of our destiny and they are to decide in last resort as to who shall rule the country. It is often said that the people get the government they deserve. I do not think it would be fair to make the same assertion now, because the people, for ten years at least, as I shall explain it later, have not had any opportunity to select their government.
All that we ask from the Government is to enable the people to select their representatives.
Once the people have voted, if they choose our friends opposite, those amongst us who are returned will be glad to come back and to work as we have done heretofore for the good of the people. Then our friends opposite will not have to submit to such humiliations as they must necessarily feel over a debate like the present one. I for one should not like to occupy a seat on the other side and listen to all that is said from this quarter. It is true that it can be claimed that this is politics and that what is said from this side is said for political objects. One may perhaps find a certain consolation in that, but if one wishes to go to the bottom of things, to examine the question sincerely, one is forced to admit that the position of our friends on the other side of the House is not only precarious, but also humiliating.
I remember that, about twelve years ago, when the British House of Commons was moved into Supply, Mr. Lloyd George insisted on elections taking place and thus taunted his opponents: "What! You are afraid to submit your Budget to the electors of Great Britain! Is it then so precarious that you, the Government in power, have neither the strength, nor the courage, nor the self-reliance that could induce you to submit this Budget to the electors of the country?"
Mr. Speaker, the same argument might apply at the present time, to our friends on the other side of the House. We might say to them, "You, gentlemen, who have been called to power barely three years ago, with a majority of more than 70, you who have won the war and covered yourselves with glory, you who claim to count in your midst the best informed and most capable politicians in the country, you who

receive almost with derision the arguments of the members of the Opposition, why then, is your policy so tottering, have you become so weak, that you fear to present yourselves to the electors and ask for a new mandate?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, after all that has been said during this debate; after all the challenges, more or less to the point if you like; after all the invectives which have been hurled from one side or the other; suppose that the right hon. Prime Minister would now rise and say to this House, speaking at the same time to all Canada, "Gentlemen, I have had enough of your taunts, I have had enough of your challenges; I have the right to remain at my post for two years more since I have behind me a majority in this House; notwithstanding this, I renounce the right, the privilege, not my own but that of this House, that of the Canadian people. Taking for granted that there may be some truth in all that you have said, I give you the benefit of the doubt, and I ask you to assume the responsibility of the stand you have taken. You summon me to go before the people; very well, I consent to do so, I am ready to go forth and give battle before the people and prove that the party of which I am the leader still has the confidence of Canada."
And suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the right hon. Prime Minister should ask for the dissolution of Parliament, should go to the people and find he had a majority; what a humiliating situation for us of the Opposition, the Liberals and the Farmers' party! Cannot you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the return to this House, in two or three months, of the member who would be re-elected? Cannot you see those of us who for the last three weeks have been talking against the Government, returning, crest-fallen to salute the new Government, recognizing that they had the confidence of the people?-recognizing at the same time that we had wrongly accused them in clamouring, for three weeks, or a year, or two, that they did not represent the opinion of the people! I vow that if such an event took place, the Government that would return to power would he the strongest since Confederation. They would have the right to impose their will, for they would have given the people, in a period of tranquility, their chance to vote for or against them.

There would then be no ambiguity and no evasion. It would be useless to say: "You have stolen the election during the war or otherwise. It would not be an election on the platform of reciprocity, it would resolve itself into a question of confidence. And if the hon. minister, after having advocated his policy all over the country, as he has been doing for several months, could get it endorsed by the electors, he would be one of the strongest men we have ever had at the head of the destinies of this country, since Confederation, and this while being still in the prime of life, while we, ourselves, on this side of the House, would be astounded and absolutely helpless for a long while to come.
One must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the challenge emanating from this side of the House is of as much consequence to the challenger as to the challenged. One must not imagine, for one moment, that the Liberals who are daring the Government to go before the people, "are not taking as great a risk as the Government would in accepting the challenge. Theoretically, the chances are even; but the Government does not wish to go before the people, because it knows beforehand, and has the intuition born of its deep knowledge of things, and of men, that it is impossible for it to come back to power, and that is precisely the reason why the Government does not pick up the gauntlet which has been thrown.
I have said that the right hon. Prime Minister had toured the country. I must remind you here that he came to the province of Quebec, and I extend my congratulations to him for the courage he has shown in paying a visit to our province.
The hon. Prime Minister knows that he has very few followers or partisans in the province of Quebec, and yet he came; he stated his policy, and, I must say, with great courage. On the other hand, the right hon. Prime Minister should not deceive himself as to the feelings of the province of Quebec. Our feelings are not those of spite, still less of hatred.

(Translation.)
Hear, Hear.

(Translation.) The province of Quebec is the pivot on which revolves Confederation. Not only is the province of Quebec the pivot of Confederation, but it is also-I would have preferred that the compliment came from an outsider however I say it is the pivot of common and good sense in the Dominion.

When a year ago, or more, the Government was in fear of bolshevism; when strikes and disorders spread from city to city, in certain parts of Canada; when excitement was high and hearts were low, we saw our friends on the other side of the House turn and place their hopes in the province of Quebec and recognize that our province was as I have just said: The pivot of Confederation, of stability and of good common sense.
The province of Quebec is essentially conservative, if you consider that word in its broadest sense, which means the conservation of what we have, the esteem of what we possess, the belief in our traditions, and the attachment for our past. Such is the meaning of conservative, as applied to the province of Quebec.
Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that in the present circumstances, and on a particularly burning issue which I most certainly have no desire to discuss at the present moment, is it any wonder that the province of Quebec should have been of a different opinion from that held by the other provinces? Is it, forsooth such an extraordinary thing for a province, to differ on certain matters from the other provinces?
Since the beginning of the session, and more particularly since the beginning of the present discussion, we have heard many of our friends on both sides of the House declare, and that very rightly, that the opinion of every one must be respected, and that there is no harm in entertaining a different opinion from that of the majority; such is precisely the argument of our friends of the Agrarian party, when they start to discuss in this House problems which, evidently are not in accordance with the opinion of the great majority of this House, either on this side or the other.
The province of Quebec has its own ideas; it has its traditions, its inclinations, its affections. Unfortunately, the hon. Prime Minister has never understood what are the ideas, the affections, the inclinations and the traditions of the province of Quebec, and that is precisely the reason why he has always remained a stranger to our province.
That is also the reason why the province of Quebec has always stood aloof from him. I mean so far as politics are concerned. Outside of politics, we have all due regard for him and we acknowledge him as a capable and worthy man. But between that statement and political allegiance there exists quite a chasm and many things will happen before that chasm is bridged.

Mr. Speaker, since the last session of Parliament there has been an assembly of the League of Nations at which the Canadian Government was represented by three ministers, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the hon. member from Durham (Mr. Rowell), then president of the privy council. I am pleased to see the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce in his seat, the more so because I know that, having learned the beautiful French language, he will no doubt be able to hear and understand the compliments which I am about to shower upon him. It has been said on both sides of the House that Canada had been worthily represented at that meeting. Speaking with that moderation and fairness which I intend to maintain at all times, I would be doing an injustice to these hon. gentlemen who were our representatives on that occasion were I to neglect offering them heartfelt congratulations for the manner in which they represented us.
The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is endowed with an eloquence which younger members of the House should always emulate, and it was sufficient for us to hear him, a few days ago, reporting what had been going on at that meeting to understand how brilliantly and creditably he represented us. I must add that what I just said of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is equally applicable to the hon. gentlemen who accompanied him. Yet, was it not unfortunate that Canada should not have been represented by a French Canadian at that meeting? In this country French Canadians make up a third of the population in round numbers. This meeting of the League of Nations was held in Geneva. French and English were the official languages. I say French and English and I designedly put French in the first place because that language was chiefly resorted to. We had that admission from the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce in his speech, an admission willingly made. With his usual frankness and outspokenness, when answering a question which I put, he said in a very candid manner that French was in much more common use than English at that meeting. However, this was already known to me, having myself had the privilege of attending for a week or over, sittings of the international labour conference, which was

held at Washington in the month of November, 1919, and seeing that the international labour conference was composed of the same nations represented at the meeting of the League of Nations, I had noticed that French was resorted to much oftener than any other language. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, French Canadians accounting for a third of the population and seeing that two thirds, at least, of forty odd nations assembled, spoke French, would it not have been reasonable, and I shall say proper, to have a Frendh-speaking representative there? At that meeting which was held quite near Paris, at the intellectual centre of Europe, largely made up of peoples speaking the French language, would it not have been proper to make it known that there is in Canada another race than the Anglo-Saxon race-notwithstanding all the respect for this race, I shall go further -that there are men of high attainments and of great ability among that race forming a third of the Canadian population? Would it have been impossible to the Government to select as a third representative a French-speaking man who could have been a credit not only to the Government, but also to the French tongue and the French Canadian race? No, Mr. Speaker, such a step would have been two upright in the eyes of the Government, they did not think fit to select a French-Canadian representative and thus they led Europeans, at least those who do not know any better, to believe, that Canada is a country inhabited only by Anglo-Saxons and people who cannot speak any other language than English.
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a point of order. The hon. member is reading his speech and I believe that this is against the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Text) I understand , that the hon. member (Mr. Mackie) raises the point that the hon member for Joliette is reading his speech.

(Translation) Mr. Speaker, never has a point of order been raised with so little justification. If there ever was an occasion in my life when I did not read my speech that is the present time, when I have barely a few notes before me. I would not like to leave the House under the impression for an instant that I am reading my speech. I would rather believe that my hon. friend (Mr. 
Mackie) is of my opinion when I claim that a French-speaking representative should have been sent to that meeting of the League of Nations.

(Translation) Yes, I
agree with you.

(Translation) Being
aware that my hon. friend knows French well, I think he is not forgetful of himself perhaps and believes that he should have been sent to that meeting. This is why, I surmise, he interrupted me, but I shall take no notice of his interruption and shall continue-I was about to say, Mr. Speaker, that it would have been proper, eminently proper, for the Government, if the right hon. Prime Minister had wished to prove that he had some consideration and friednship for the province of Quebec, to have had a representative of the French Canadian element at this meeting of the League of Nations. At the International Conference of Labour, much less important, no doubt, which took place in a city nearer than Geneva, Washington, the Canadian Government was represented by two ministers, the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) and the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson.) 1 do not know whether any of these gentlemen were qualified to represent either the French element or the French language, and as I said just now the predominant language at the International Conference of Labour was French. The delegates of the forty-one nations represented there met daily, continually exchanging views, at banquets and elsewhere-and we had there only two representatives, very worthy ones, but who knew not a word of French. Mr. Speaker, I know for instance, of a banquet at which were present the South American delegates and at which French was almost exclusively spoken-Canada's two representatives were present, and did not understand what was being said-I do not reproach these gentlemen with not knowing French-it is hard to learn a foreign language-but I reproach the Government. Each time that an important occasion presents itself they try to give the impression to foreign nations that Canada is an English country in which there are only English-speaking people, and that the French-Canadians are a negligible quantity unworthy of representation.
( Translation) Hear, hear.

(Translation) If it were
for no other reasons than these, I would say that the right hon. Prime Minister could not expect much sympathy from the province of Quebec. When the right hon. Prime Minister will have proved to the province of Quebec that he is ready to do it justice, not only by words but toy acts, then perhaps that province may in part turn to him, because Quebec is not prejudiced, but is sincere, and the opinions it holds are not those of a day, but fundamental, based upon its traditions and its history. And if one looks back one finds that the province of Quebec was for many years Conservative. How does it happen that these old Conservative traditions have been abandoned and the province of Quebec has become what it is to-day? It is because, with the same reasoning and the same good sense, the province of Quebec at this time has no confidence in this Government. It feels that it has had enough of the Conservative party, and slowly but surely it has broken away from it.
As it has taken a generation and even more for the province of Quebec to detach itself from the Conservative party, so will it be before Quebec places its confidence in another party than the Liberal one, unless, and this we cannot foresee, the Liberal party by misdeeds should prove unworthy of its confidence.
I mentioned just now that the speech from the Throne was a very meagre document. If ever there was a question which should have been submitted or at least discussed in this speech, specially as it . has been brought up in this debate, it is surely the financial standing of the country.
Mr. Speaker, we do not realize to the full extent the financial state of our country. The hon. members of this House must bear in mind that' for the last twelve months our public debt has been about two billion and a quarter and while our revenues are daily decreasing, the debt is steadily on the increase.
Mr. Speaker, if such is our financial situation, with revenues steadily going down, where will this lead us to? The Government has both the responsibility and the duty to balance the finances of this country and from the moment it acknowledges its inability to do so it should make way for another Government. The present mismanagement conducing the ruin of the country Would suffice to warrant us in demanding the dissolution of Parliament. Mr. Speaker, has it ever entered the head of the hon. members of this House that we are at present, and are becoming daily more and more dependent economically out of the United States. Probably this utterance displeases my hon. friends on- the opposite side of this House. These hon. gentlemen are ultra loyal to England and when we say that we are becoming an economical dependency, the expression naturally wounds and shocks them. It is not a pleasure for me to use these words; however, one must admit the evidence of facts. We are at present and are becoming more and more an economical dependency of the United States. At present, in order to maintain our commerce, our industries, to meet our daily requirements and support our family we are forced to import to the extent of nearly one billion dollars a year. On the other hand our exports hardly amount to a little over half a billion. We buy from the United States in round figures for a billion and in return sell to the amount of five or six hundred million dollars.
Mr. Speaker, where will this state of affairs lead us to? We are simply drifting to bankruptcy or probably I may be more correct in saying, we are drifting towards annexation, that is we are becoming every day more and more an economical dependency of the United States. At the present time in order to trade with the United States we are losers to the extent of one hundred million dollars per year. For the products we purchase from them by paying the difference of the rate of exchange which has varied between 8 and a fraction, 19 and a fraction since 1912, we make them a present of one hundred million dollars per year. In other words when buying one billion dollars worth of goods, we pay naturally the billion dollars, but over and above that amount, we make them a present of over one hundred millions.
(Translation.) It is extortion, not a present.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, that is the situation we have to face at present. How will we stand in three, six or twelve months? No one knows. There are astute observers amongst the financiers of this country who contend that it is possible that the rate of exchange which was
19	and a fraction three months ago, might again attain that figure and perhaps reach
20	and 25 per cent. Should this happen, we should be absolutely at the mercy of the United States, for the simple reason that we are at present compelled to purchase
(Translation.) Hear, hear.

(Translation.) And our opponents were proclaiming everywhere; "The government we have is a coalition one composed of Liberals and Conservatives; it is not a government which is expected to last long." Everybody knew at that time that it was a government which would not last forever, that it was a provisional government, a coalition in order to "win the war" as the saying was at that time. I have the greatest respect for the views of those who then formed themselves into a group to promote a policy which prevailed, but it must be admitted that the means they took were far from being legitimate.
To-day, that question having been settled and the war being over, we have to decide whether or not in 1917 the elections were held upon the general policy of the government. ^ The following answer cannot be gainsaid:	In 1917 the elections were not
held upon the general policy of the government, but upon a single issue-then a burning one which is not so now, that is, in what manner were we to endeavour to win the war. That is precisely the ground upon which the elections were fought in 1917.
Now, events having taken another turn; the war being won, we may justly say that there have been no elections since 1911 because the people of this country were not called upon to give their verdict since then. However there is something more forcible and I would say more amusing, if I may use that term: it is that during this session we shall have to decide upon the fiscal policy of this country. Now, I ask the hon. gentlemen opposite whether or not Canadian electors ever thought that the representatives they were electing in 1917 would be called upon to decide the fiscal policy of Canada?
I remember that on many occasions when we came to this House in 1918 certain members on the opposite side raised fiscal issues and each time when questions of this nature were brought forward, interested friends, no doubt of those who made these enquiries, would rise and appeal to the whole House for support-each time such an issue was raised in 1918, immediately a minister of the Crown, or an hon. member would exclaim: We are not here to discuss fiscal issues, we are here to win

the war, this Government was elected to win the war and when this is done, we shall settle our accounts.
Is it not a fact that what I have just mentioned not only was said once, but twenty-five times in this House?
In 1918, our friends on the opposite side admitted that they were not here to discuss fiscal issues, but to carry on the war. Well, so far the war was concerned, the hon. members on the right were in perfect agreement because they were elected on a definite programme and they acted accordingly. They followed their programme as long as the war lasted, and I have no fault to find, they were consistent with their former stand. However, hardly was the war over that we witnessed their disaggregation. Hon. members followed one another declaring that, the purpose of the election was to win the war, but as the war was over, parties should return to their old lines; that those at present holding office had not been elected to govern the country in time of peace or to settle the fiscal issues, or to decide on questions which cropped up presently-it was a war government whose existence depended upon the war and the problems involved with it. Mr. Speaker, I beg to be excused for having-taken up so much time. I might bring forth further arguments, but I am not so conceited as to hope that I could alter the views of my hon. friends opposite. I crave the indulgence of those I may have somewhat tired by this lengthy speech. I hope that when the vote is taken in a few minutes the Government will realize, that an Administration returned with seventy of a majority in 1917 and reduced to what it is at present, should examine their conscience, consider the necessity of returning before their masters and seeking a new mandate to present themselves before this House. But, Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much if this mandate will ever be granted to them.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take any part in this debate, but as the hour is early-we have the whole day before us!-I would like to offer a few remarks in reply to some of the suggestions that have been made by several hon. members on the other side of the House.
In the first place I think it is my duty to offer my congratulations to the Prime Minister, as the right hon. gentleman

came into this House at the same election as I did. I had the pleasure of journeying with him to Ottawa. At that time we had about the same ideals, the same aspirations, and we did believe that perhaps we might in some way work for the benefit of that great western country whence we came. For the first session or two we got along very well together. At that time I was interested in the stock business in the West, and as conditions were not very favourable I put a resolution on the Order Paper in favour of a cold storage system to be operated by the Government. I received the support of every hon. member from the western provinces, but the best support came from the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Government. As I say, at that time we shared the same ideals, but since then we have been drifting apart. I have watched my right hon. friend climbing upwards on a different path, and he has now reached the peak.
Mr." JACOBS: And is going down again.

Yes. He has got to the peak of the greatest autocracy that ever controlled the destinies of this country. I suppose in the opinion of the masses he has travelled faster than I have and has become a much greater man.
No, no.

But I stayed where I was, believing in the common people, still retaining the beliefs that I held when I came here, and which he also held at that time. I have stood where I was; he has advanced. Perhaps he imbibed a different spirit after coming down here. Believing, as I did, that certain things were in the interests of my country, I have been satisfied to stay where I still am, rather than attempt to follow my right hon. friend to the high position which he now holds. However, in all fairness to my right hon. friend I will say that only by his energy and his industry has he attained the highest honour Canada can give him, and if that position is to be held by any hon. member on the opposite side of the House, I do not believe there is anybody more deserving or more fitted to hold it than my right hon. friend.
I also wish to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address. In my observation extending over fifteen sessions I have never seen that duty performed in a more creditable and able manner. But my reason for rising to-night, Mr. Speaker, is not particularly to congratulate the mover and seconder of the

Address, but rather to offer some observations on certain features of the debate.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) discussed some grievances from which the western farmer suffered and dealt with the matter of the car shortage in that country, The hon. member pointed out that there was a shortage of equipment on the Canadian National railways and that the farmers suffered a great deal in consequence. I agree with every statement he made in that regard. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Blair) followed the hon. member for Mackenzie, but he seemed to think that the disadvantages the western producers laboured under were due to the operations in grain. The hon. gentleman delivered a splendid speech. It was his maiden effort and I congratulate him upon it. But he must know better than to advance such an argument as he did. He and I were on two delegations that met the Prime Minister when he visited the city of Edmonton last fall.
The great grievance complained of then was not the spread in prices, or the matter in which the grain business was handled, but the car shortage. Had there been in the proper sense of the term adequate railway equipment, the spread of prices which the hon. gentleman mentioned would not have cut any figure at all. The producers were in the independent position that they would not have needed to deal with the line elevators, and might have ignored the street prices; they could have shipped their grain independently if they could have got the cars they needed. Had sufficient cars been available they would not have been affected by the spread in prices; they could have shipped their grain to the terminal elevators and sold it there. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) has made the statement that he ordered about double the number of cars contracted for by the Canadian Pacific Railway and had done twice as much as that company to relieve the congestion. Well, if that were the case, and if the cars were available, they certainly did not reach our part of the country. Every western member knows that the congestion of cars was felt all along the line of the Canadian National, Railways. We were told by the General Superintendent at Edmonton that with the equipment possessed by the Canadian National Railways it would take three years to move the crop according to the estimates he had received. My hon. friend from Battle River was present at the meeting and heard Mr. Brown make the statement.
A demand has been made for a new Grain Commission to be appointed to deal with the existing difficulties. As my hon. friend from Red Deer pointed out, we already have a Grain Commission composed of men of ten or twelve years' experience. Surely another commission is not needed to deal with the matter. However, the point upon which I wish to lay stress is that had sufficient cars been available the spread of prices complained of would not have bothered the producers and they could have sold their grain in the open market. I raised considerable grain myself last year, in fact I come from a section where their was a bumper crop. We are holding that grain to-day because we could not dispose of it by reason of the lack of adequate equipment on the Canadian National railways.
The real grievance of the West to-day along the Canadian National Railway lines is lack of equipment. The member for Battle River (Mr. Blair) knows well that the prices are from seven to ten cents higher in the districts covered by the Canadian Pacific than they are along the Canadian National railways, because it is recognized that along the Canadian Pacific, where proper equipment is available, the grain will be brought out in the early part of the season, so that advantage can be taken of lake transportation. The suggestion on the part of my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Henders) and other hon. gentlemen opposite that the great detriment to the producers in the West has been the spread of prices and that kind of thing is only a bugaboo; the real difficulty arises from car shortage. The hon. member for Battleford (Mr. Wright) was present at the meeting when Mr. Brown stated that if the estimate of this year's crop was correct, the Canadian National could not move it out with their equipment in less than three years. I would like to know how many farmers will go very far in the matter of production next year under circumstances such as these. Let hon. gentlemen who represent the western districts forget their party affiliations and truly represent the sections of the country from which they come; it is a simple matter.
There may be a great deal that is wrong about the grain business, and if a commission can be appointed that will make things better for the producer, why, I am willing to support anything that could be done along that line. But I take the same view as that expressed by the member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), when he suggests

that there is no reason why we should appoint one commission to investigate the doings of another. We already have a commission on the job; why appoint another to find out some imaginary wrongs, particularly when every producer knows what the real cause of the trouble is. We can get away from grain commissions altogether if we have proper transportation facilities for the shipment of our grain to the open market. The Minister of Railways says he has put into commission double the number of cars that the Canadian Pacific have put on their road. Well, if he has, they are not in evidence.
Some hon. members have spoken of redistribution. I want to make an honest statement in regard to this. Everybody will agree that the West is not bothering very much about redistribution. In fact, the West believe that they are not properly represented in the House to-day. There are very few members here to-day who represent the actual sentiment of the West. Who believes that hon. gentlemen from the West on the Government side represent the views of the people of the West? Nobody believes it. The real sentiment of the West to-day is represented on this side, not only by the two Liberal members from the West, but by what is called the Progressive group. They represent western opinion; there is no doubt about that-and the Government know it; let them test it and find out. The views of the West to-day are very well expressed by the Calgary Albertan, which says: We would like to have more representation in the West, but we would rather take a chance right now than wait to see how many more representatives we might have. No one will have the audacity to stand up and say that hon. gentlemen sitting behind the Treasury Benches represent the voice of the West.
What is this Agrarian group to my left? Ho you not think, Sir, that this is a body of intelligent men who, when they found that they were not representing public opinion, left their party and crossed over to this side? No better evidence than that could be offered of their intelligence. I do not contend that I, as a Liberal, represent the whole sentiment of the West; there is no doubt that others were wise enough to know what public sentiment was, and when they found out that the people were not satisfied with the Government, they crossed over to this side. They did not cross over to this side to defy the electors of their constituencies; they crossed over because they considered they were f Mr. W. H. White.]
the servants of the people. When they found that the people had no confidence in the Government, as honest, sincere representative's of the people, they followed public opinion and cut thmselves free from hon. gentlemen opposite. Nobody can believe anything else to be the case.
In conclusion, I want to say that, perhaps not in a very eloquent manner, but in the simple language that comes easy to me, I have tried to make an honest statement to both sides of the House. Although I know hon. gentlemen opposite are looking for their support to other sections of the country than that from which I come, I am trying as honestly as I can to represent the views and sentiments of the people who sent me here.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, which has already lasted over two weeks, and especially at this stage it would be impossible for the humble member that I am to throw any light on the matters under discussion. But after reading in the Montreal Gazette of February 28 that the Opposition had failed in this debate to point to any wrong-doing on the part of the Government, I decided to endeavour to show, in as few words as possible, some of the innumerable pieces of mischief that have disgraced the record of this Government, elected in 1911 and reelected, by accident, in 1917. The Gazette challenges the Opposition in the following words :
The debate on the address, as .have all debates for three years, has been remarkable in that there has been no suggestion of wrongdoing or maladministration on the part of the Government. Either the Opposition is too dense to perceive errors, or the Government has given Canada a wonderful example of administrative capacity and probity. The old charges of scandal no longer obtain. Nor are there likely to be any charges. The Government may have made mistakes, but no one has the courage to say that its members permitted the treasury to be plundered by themselves or party friends.
We on this side of the House were profoundly amazed when we read those wofds. We would never have imagined that the Government's friends would be bold enough to challenge the Opposition to reiterate the many scandals and numerous feats of maladministration that stained the Borden Government, and for which- the present Administration rightly admits responsibility. For the sake of Canadian pride, we of the Opposition would have very much preferred to avoid publishing those terrible national misdemeanors, more especially

when it is a well-known fact that in other countries during the war those who dared to indulge in similar mischievous acts were either very severely punished with penalties or imprisonment or very often shot as traitors to their country, while in this country of ours the guilty remained undisturbed, when they were not held in favour for Canadian or Imperial positions of trust. But we accept the challenge and I will, therefore, give a list, though incomplete on account of the late hour at which I am speaking, of some of the very numerous scandals that we have already charged and that we claim to have proved against the Government.
There is a first group, known to the country as " war contract scandals," as investigated by the Public Accounts Committee of the House of Commons in 1915. It was proved before that committee that war contracts were let without any tenders, or any kind of competition whatever, and that the Government's purchasing system was loose, irregular and illegal. The Auditor General, before the committee on March 17, 1915, speaking of purchases, said:
It was worse than that; they were not made in compliance with the Act.
Indeed, war goods amounting to over $1,000,000,000 had been bought without Orders-in-Council, as required by law. It was also brought out in evidence that the Tory patronage system then existing compelled the use of middlemen in all contracts. I shall give a very brief nomenclature of those scandals that the Gazette claims not to exist or to have been forgiven or forgotten:	The horse scandal,
which brought about the resignation of a Tory member of this House; the drug scandal which caused the resignation of another Tory member of this House; the binocular scandal and many others that will pass over without mentioning; the nickel scandal, which raised in this House a debate in which several members and especially one on the Government side laid considerable blame on the Government; the shell scandal and the fuse scandal, which alone meant a million dollar rake-off.
In another group not connected with the war, I might mention several other deeds of maladministration, such as, for instance, the padlock scandal, in the Post Office Department; the Carslake scandal in the same department; the Dorval military camp scandal in the Department of Militia, and the extravagant payment of several hundred thousand dollars to foreigners, Arthur Young and Company, and the Griffenha gen
and associates, to perform a so-called civil service re-organization which could only have been properly performed by the heads of departments together with our Civil Service Commission.
Why, Mr. Speaker, the Montreal Gazette reporter has already forgotten all these wrong-doings! Is it not in this very same paper that I read, in an editorial of June 14, 1920, under the title " a con-demnable contract," the following charge against the Cabinet in connection with the above expenditures:
The whole episode reflects ministerial incompetency in a most unusual way, and the Government cannot too soon repair its mistake by terminating a contract repugnant to National pride.
And again, what about the creation, by Order-in-Council, on July 15, 1920, fourteen days after prorogation, of a Central Purchasing Board, a scheme which had encountered during a debate last session, the hostility of the great majority of this House? How many other scandals have there been, Sir, the mention of which would be much too long for my purpose? The gentleman who represents the Montreal Gazette in the press gallery is at liberty now to send again to his home office a despatch stating that we on this side of the House are "too dense to perceive errors."
It has been stated by previous speakers in the course of this debate that the people of Quebec would forgive, but could not forget, the treatment that they received from the Government. Well, I venture to say that the people of Canada at large will neither forget nor forgive those numerous scandals which have been detected and proved against the Government, whether they have been perpetrated with the connivance or through the gross negligence of the Government. In closing my remarks on this point, I wish to give credit to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) for his frankness in admitting, in a speech delivered in Winnipeg, on October 22, 1917, that he, as a member of the Conservative Government, was bound to share all the responsibilities assumed by the former Government, replaced, in the fall of 1917, by the Union Government.
During the recess and in the course of this debate, much has been said of the feelings of the province of Quebec towards the - present Ministry, and of the very affectionate and touching friendship entertained by the same ministry not only for the province of Quebec, but towards the three million French-speaking citizens of this country.

The very eloquent member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), in beautiful and forcible, though mild and courteous language, has laid before the House undeniable evidence, showing to what a great extent the friendly words uttered by the right hon. the Prime Minister and by his colleagues are flatly contradicted by their own acts and deeds, when it is up to these same gentlemen to give concrete form to their flirtations with our French-speaking people.
The hon. member for Beauce mentioned several instances of recent injustice done to the French-speaking people by the Government. He particularly inquired from the ministry why not a single representative of the French Canadians had been invited to join in with the ministers who represented, or at least assumed that they held a mandate to represent, Canada at the Peace Conference and at the Assembly of the' League of Nations.
I would go one step further, and ask the Government the reason why, if any, the only French-speaking member of the Cabinet was not invited, and even induced to attend those conferences as the representative of one-third of our population? If the hon. gentleman, who occupies the position of Postmaster General, was not then available, why did they not invite the very distinguished French Canadian who is the present Speaker of the Senate, and who is also, I am told, a member of the Privy Council? Has he not the confidence of the present ministry?-and what about the hon. Senators Beaubien, and Chapais? These also are two very brilliant French Canadian supporters of the present ministry. And, Mr. Speaker, a like courtesy to one-third of our Canadians would not have necessitated an election in Quebec!
May I be permitted to add a few more instances as a sequel to those brought forward by my hon. friend, the member for Beauce? When the late lamented Hon. S. N. Parent, the father of the hon. member for Quebec West, resigned from the National Transcontinental Railway Commission, in October, 1911, he was replaced by Major Leonard, an English Canadian, and the French Canadians were left without representation on this board, which was managing a railroad traversing the province of Quebec for several hundred miles. When the French Canadian head of the Government workshops at Sorel, in the county of Richelieu, Quebec, was compelled to go out of office, he was replaced by one Mr. Jackson, an English Canadian. When the late Thomas Cote was asked to 
resign, after September 21, 1911, as secretary of the International Waterways Joint Commission, he was replaced by one Mr. Burpee. Mr. Justice McDougall succeeded the late Judge Champagne in the French judicial district of Hull. Chief Justice Landry, in New Brunswick, was replaced by Mr. Justice Chandly. Mr. Blount succeeded Major Chapleau as clerk of the Senate, although a French Canadian was there available, in the person of the deputy clerk, who had been holding office for many years. Senator Webster succeeded the late Senator Landry in the Senate.
Who sat, may I ask, as a representative of the French Canadians, on the Public Records Commission; on the Board of Grain Commissioners; in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; on the War Trade Board; on the Canada Food Board; on the Canada Registration Board; on the Pensions Board?
Is it not a well-known fact that out of thirty "Trade Agents" that we have in foreign countries, the French Canadians are given but one representative? The hon. the Postmaster General recently stated elsewhere that he is representing in the ministry the hundreds of thousands of French Canadians, who, according to him, voted for the Government in 1917.
I beg to submit that it would seem obvious, from the statements which I have made that this hon. gentleman is satisfied with holding a public office for his own self and sake, and that he lacks influence with his colleagues whenever an opportunity arises for him to exact the appointment of a French compatriot to an office of public trust. This failure in the hon. the Postmaster General's duty of procuring for his French fellow-citizens their just share in the public trusteeships reminds me of a statement made in October, 1917, by Sir John Willison, in a letter of appreciation of the Coalition Government to "The New York Tribune." This writer, a stalwart Union supporter, alluding to the present Postmaster General and to his former colleague from Quebec, now politically deceased, wjote as follows:
In the new Cabinet there are only two French ministers, and these are among the least weighty of its members.
Is this statement a reply to our inquiry as to why this French minister was not invited to the Peace Conference or to the League of Nations with his English colleagues ?
And, by the way, Mr. Speaker, while I am taking the liberty of dealing with the

hon. the Postmaster General, who holds this office as a member of the Senate, I would very respectfully suggest to the right hon. the leader of this House that the present vacancy in the county of Yamaska, Quebec, affords a unique and splendid opportunity for the Postmaster General to secure for himself a comfortable seat in this beautiful chamber. Indeed, this constituency of Yamaska happens to be the hon. gentleman's native county; he has even been residing therein as recently as a few months ago. Then why not try his chance there just now?
I will go still further in this connection.
I assume, from the wording of the Electoral Act, as it now stands, and also from the amendment made to the House of Commons Act in the second session of 1919, that it would seem to be your own duty, Mr. Speaker, immediately to issue your warrant for this election. Let me explain myself.
Section 9 of the House of Commons Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, Chapter 11, reads in part as follows:
If any vacancy happens in the House of Commons by the death of any member .... the 'Speaker, on being informed of such vacancy by any member of the House in his place .... shall forthwith address his warrant to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for the issue of a new writ for the election of a member to fill the vacancy; and a new writ shall issue accordingly.
Now, under the new law, as drafted last year, the Clerk of the House of Commons holds the office of the former Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. On the second day of this session, as shown on pages 7 and 8 of Hansard, it -was stated by the right hon. the Prime Minister and by my hon. leader, who were both addressing you, Mr. Speaker, that our regretted colleague, the late member for Yamaska, had passed away during the recess. Hence, I take it for granted, Mr. Speaker, that you have been sufficiently informed, under the Act, as to this vacancy, and I very respectfully submit that it is your duty to issue your warrant accordingly.
At all events, in order to remove any possible misunderstanding I, myself, now from my place in this House, beg leave officially to inform you, Mr. Speaker, that the former member for Yamaska, Mr. Oscar Gladu, died over two months ago, and that, therefore, a vacancy has occurred in that electoral district.
It is true that a delay of six months is mentioned in section 11-A of the House of Commons Act. But this is a maximum limit; it was intended to mean that six
months' delay might be allowed during recess. But I humbly submit that, when Parliament is called to meet in session, all the vacancies should have been filled before the opening of the session, in order to give to every constituency the representatives to whom it is entitled. I assume that this is a sound interpretation of this new law.
Now, Mr. Speaker, following again and further the argument made by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) in reply to the statement made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in this House, on the 18th of last month, I will quote from the remarks of the member for Frontenac the following, as they appear in Hansard at page 141:
I challenge the leader of the Opposition, or any of those sitting behind him, to quote one single sentence, one single line, one single thought expressed in words by the present Prime Minister of Canada at any time, in this House or out of it, which has indicated the slightest feeling of hostility or unfriendliness to the people of the province of Quebec.
I will make a compromise with the hon. member for Frontenac; I will agree, but only for the sake of argument, that his honourable leader is, towards French-Can-adians and in connection with the treatment that he has afforded to them, a sinner more by way of omission than by commission. But we feel the injustice just the same, whatever may be the artful mode of procedure adopted by the hon. member's leader when dealing with the Quebec people, or with French-Canadians in other provinces.
Before closing, I would call to my aid in this connection,-to prove that my remarks are accurate on this very important subject, which is a vital one for one-third of the people of this country,-a very remarkable , editorial of the Montreal Gazette of May 17, 1920. This editorial, which was headed "French and the Franchise," had regard to the then pending-debate in this House on the new electoral law. I will omit a few sentences, unfortunately, to save time, but I hope that the hon. the Prime Minister and his colleagues, will read this editorial in its entirety and that, in the future, when boasting that they are giving equal and equitable treatment to all races and creeds in Canada, they will sincerely meditate upon the sound and sane principles of justice, as so thoroughly expounded in this article, which reads, in part:
Several hours were devoted in the Commons last week to the discussion of a subject upon which we think there is no room for controversy, namely, the desirability of having the

Proclamation of an election printed in the French language in electoral districts in which there are a considerable number of electors who understand that tongue, but are not familiar with the English language. The matter was brought up by Mr. Turgeon, of Gloucester, New Brunswick, .who, in a temperate speech urged the desirability of giving to the French population communication in their own language of proceedings relating to the very foundation of popular government, the election of members, and, with customary exceptions, the debate was conducted in admirable mood, though not upon a lofty plane. There was much citation of the Constitution to prove where begin the rights of the French people in respect of official use of their language, and where those rights end, and a disposition to place rigid and narrow construction upon the Confederation Act in a matter that fairly transcends the strict letter of the law. Constantly are we reminded that harmony and cordiality between the two great races, which inhabit ICanada rest more upon sentiment and generous feeling than upon the text of a statute.
The editorial in another place says:
Mr. Turgeon told the House that "French people are sentimental; they appreciate anything that is done in their behalf; "but while sentiment must always receive recognition, there is a yet higher motive to move man, that of justice and of regard for the general good.
Finally it says:	-
It may not be a great matter that in French districts electoral proclamations should be issued in the French language; but it is of consequence that FrenchJCanadians be not irritated by a sense of injustice, that they be not pin-pricked, and that their great part in forming and fostering Confederation should And expression in equitable legislation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. the Prime Minister appeared before the Frenchspeaking people of this country some months ago, did he offer any explanation why he and his colleagues remained mute during the debate in question last year? Did he tender an apology for their refusal to grant, when it was most opportune to do so to the French-speaking minority, "Equitable Legislation," as their organ calls it, and thus to prove in good faith that their legislative acts, if not their administrative deeds, accord with their political performances?
No, Mr. Speaker, the law remained as it was. _ The Prime Minister did not utter one single word of ill-feeling towards the French-speaking people, but he committed another sin of omission.	[DOT]
I believe that I have already spoken too long, and I shall close with the following words:	I shall vote for the amendment
offered by our distinguished leader. I am sure that if the Hon. Robert Rogers were in this House, he who, as a true Conserva-
